notes: Great Britain only - the Employment (Allocation of Tips) Act 2023 inserted Part 2B into the Employment Rights Act 1996 with extent England, Wales and Scotland. There is no equivalent Northern Ireland statute, so do not describe these duties as UK-wide. Three separate duties: (1) allocate the total tips at a place of business fairly among the workers there, having regard to the statutory Code of Practice (s.27D); (2) have a written tipping policy where qualifying tips are paid on more than an occasional and exceptional basis, made available to all workers at that place of business (s.27I); (3) keep a tipping record for three years and respond to worker requests (s.27J). The employer must pass on 100% of qualifying tips - no deductions except tax and NIC as required by law. Independent tronc arrangements are dealt with separately at s.27F. CURRENCY NOTE: a consultation on a revised tipping Code of Practice is live, so the Code (though not the three-year record period or the monthly payment deadline, which are in the Act) may be updated.

title: TUPE: Employee Rights On Transfer

figures.what: minimum notice before the transfer for the transferor to give the transferee employee liability information, raised from 14 days on 31 January 2014
how recent the information must be: accurate as at a date no more than 14 days before it is notified
the MAXIMUM compensation a tribunal may award for failure to inform or consult, under regulation 16(3) — a cap, not an entitlement

figures.value: fewer than 50 employees, or fewer than 10 transferring
figures.what: either test lets the employer inform and consult affected employees directly where there are no representatives
transfers completing on or after this date use the current thresholds; before it, the old fewer-than-10 micro-business test applied
time limit for a failure to inform or consult complaint, from completion of the transfer, raised from three months on 1 October 2026

scope.nation: business-transfer TUPE extends UK-wide. The service provision change limb is GREAT BRITAIN ONLY — Schedule 1 paragraph 2 disapplies it in Northern Ireland, where service provision changes are covered by separate NI regulations.
scope.who: employees on a relevant transfer, with 'employee' defined broadly as any individual who works for another under a contract of service or apprenticeship or otherwise. Two routes in: a business transfer of an undertaking in the UK that retains its identity, or a service provision change such as outsourcing, re-tendering or insourcing.
scope.excluded: anyone providing services under a contract for services, expressly carved out, so the genuinely self-employed and independent contractors are out; share takeovers, where the employer's identity does not change; administrative reorganisations of public administrative authorities and transfers of functions between public authorities; activities consisting wholly or mainly of supplying goods for the client's own use; service provision changes for a single specific event or a task of short-term duration; service provision changes in Northern Ireland; and transfers of assets only where no economic entity keeps its identity. Transfers within the public sector are usually not covered.
scope.from_when: TUPE 2006 in force 6 April 2006; the 28-day rule from 31 January 2014; the current consultation thresholds for transfers completing on or after 1 July 2024
scope.how_to_claim: the transfer of employment, terms and continuity happens automatically on a relevant transfer — no opt-in and no qualifying service. The right not to be unfairly dismissed for a transfer-connected reason still needs the ordinary qualifying service.

notes: Three corrections. The official page is now gov.uk, not Acas. The 13 weeks' pay is a maximum award under regulation 16(3), not an entitlement, and if anything cites regulation 15 for it that citation is wrong — regulation 15 creates the complaint, regulation 16(3) sets the cap. And the small-employer threshold is two alternative tests, fewer than 50 employees OR fewer than 10 transferring, not a single 10-employee test. Transferee and transferor are jointly and severally liable for compensation ordered against the transferor, which is the point that matters to a buyer. Regulation 13(2) requires information 'long enough before' the transfer with no fixed number of days, so do not put a figure on it.

title: Who Must File A Self Assessment Return

figures.what: the tax year covered by the return due on 31 January 2027 (the 2025 to 2026 tax year)
deadline to file the 2025 to 2026 online return and to pay the tax owed
deadline for a paper 2025 to 2026 return (already passed)
deadline to tell HMRC you need to file for 2025 to 2026 if you have not filed before
self-employed sole trader gross income (before expenses and reliefs) that requires a return; HMRC wording is 'earned more than £1,000 (before taking off anything you can claim tax relief on)'
untaxed income in the year that requires a Self Assessment record (State Pension collected through the PAYE code excluded)
untaxed income that still requires a return even for someone otherwise taxed only through PAYE
gross property income band where you contact HMRC rather than automatically register for Self Assessment; over £2,500 gross you register

figures.value: more than £10,000 gross, or more than £2,500 net
figures.what: property/land letting income that is Self Assessment criteria in HMRC's own manual (gross test applies irrespective of expenses)
savings and investment income, or dividend income, before tax, that is Self Assessment criteria (2016-17 onwards)

the 'high earner' total income test: HMRC removed the income threshold for completing a return for PAYE-only taxpayers from the 2024 to 2025 tax year onwards, so there is no £100,000 or £150,000 income trigger for the return due 31 January 2027

scope.who: Individuals anywhere in the UK for the 2025 to 2026 tax year (6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026), filing by 31 January 2027. A return is required if any one criterion is met: self-employed sole trader with gross income over £1,000; partner in a business partnership; Capital Gains Tax due on a disposal; High Income Child Benefit Charge not paid through PAYE; an off-payroll worker repaying a student or postgraduate loan; untaxed income of £2,500 or more; property income over the property tests; savings, investment or dividend income of £10,000 or more; or HMRC has asked you to send one.
scope.excluded: Taxpayers whose income is taxed only through PAYE are no longer caught by any income-level test - HMRC removed the income threshold for completing a return for PAYE-only taxpayers from 2024 to 2025, so a high salary alone (over £100,000 or over £150,000) no longer requires a return. Also not required: anyone with gross trading income of £1,000 or less and nothing else (the trading allowance covers it), anyone with gross property income of £1,000 or less and nothing else, and people whose only untaxed income is State Pension collected through their PAYE code. Being below a threshold does not remove liability if another criterion is met.
scope.from_when: In force for the 2025 to 2026 tax year, return due 31 January 2027. The removal of the income threshold for PAYE-only taxpayers has applied since the 2024 to 2025 tax year.
scope.how_to_claim: You must register for Self Assessment yourself (deadline 5 October after the end of the tax year), then file online at GOV.UK by 31 January 2027 and pay by the same date. HMRC does not file for you, and not receiving a notice to file does not remove the obligation.

notes: The figure people most often get wrong is the £1,000: it is GROSS self-employed income before any expenses, not profit. The old 'earn over £100,000 (then £150,000) and you must file' rule is gone for people taxed only through PAYE from 2024 to 2025 onwards - that is the change to flag this season, and high earners should check the other criteria instead. Income Tax rates and bands differ in Scotland, but the Self Assessment FILING criteria and the 31 January deadline are identical across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, so this subject is safe to state UK-wide; only the amount of tax calculated differs for Scottish taxpayers. This is not the Making Tax Digital for Income Tax rules, which are a separate set of thresholds (over £50,000 for 2024 to 2025, over £30,000 for 2025 to 2026, over £20,000 for 2026 to 2027) for how sole traders and landlords already in Self Assessment must keep records and report quarterly.

title: Crypto Reporting To HMRC Under CARF

figures.what: the date the Cryptoasset Reporting Framework came into effect, from which cryptoasset exchanges and other cryptoasset service providers must collect and record customer details
the first reporting period providers must cover
deadline for a UK cryptoasset service provider to submit its first report to HMRC
penalty a user can face for giving inaccurate details, or not giving details, to a UK cryptoasset service provider - and the penalty could be higher for a non-UK provider
penalty a provider can face for not reporting, reporting late, or submitting inaccurate, incomplete or unverified reports

figures.value: full name, date of birth, address and country of residence, tax identification number
figures.what: the details an individual user must give to every cryptoasset service provider they use, including providers not based in the UK

figures.value: legal business name, main business address, company registration number or tax identification number and country of issue
figures.what: the details an entity user (company, partnership, trust, charity) must give; some entities must also give details of their controlling person

figures.value: user details plus a summary of their transactions
figures.what: what a provider must report to HMRC, as an XML file of up to 250MB per file
The Reporting Cryptoasset Service Providers (Due Diligence and Reporting Requirements) Regulations 2025 - the legislation behind the obligation

scope.who: Two groups. Providers: anyone providing cryptoasset services in the UK - exchanges and other cryptoasset service providers, which HMRC says can be entities or individuals effectuating exchange transactions as a business - must collect user data from 1 January 2026 and report it to HMRC, first report by 31 May 2027 covering 2026. Users: anyone, individual or entity, using a cryptoasset service provider must give their identifying details when asked, and must give them to EVERY provider they use, including providers not based in the UK.
scope.excluded: A provider with no information to report for a year does not need to submit a report. Providers only report on users who are tax resident in the UK or in another country signed up to CARF, so a user resident in a non-CARF country is not reportable. A user who is not eligible for a tax identification number - HMRC's example is living in a country that does not issue them - does not have to provide one. HMRC states the measure 'is not expected to have an impact on the majority of individuals' because the obligation falls on service providers, and CARF 'does not replace or amend existing legislation', so no user gains or loses a tax liability because of it.
scope.from_when: In force. The measure came into effect on 1 January 2026. First reporting period 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2026, first provider reports due by 31 May 2027. HMRC's online submission service for providers was not yet live when this guidance was read.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. Users simply respond to their provider's request for details, accurately and promptly, to avoid a penalty of up to £300. Anyone with gains or income from cryptoassets reports and pays tax as they always have: gains on disposals through Capital Gains Tax (60-day rule does not apply - crypto is not residential property, so it goes on the Self Assessment return by 31 January, or through HMRC's real time service), and crypto received as income through Self Assessment.

notes: The line to hold: crypto gains and crypto income were ALWAYS taxable in the UK, and CARF changes REPORTING, not liability. HMRC's own CARF page says the framework 'does not replace or amend existing legislation' and describes it as a deterrent that encourages correct reporting - nobody owes tax they did not owe before 1 January 2026. What has changed is that HMRC will receive user details and a transaction summary from exchanges, and will exchange data with other CARF countries annually, so undeclared gains become far easier to spot. Two different £300 penalties exist and should not be conflated: up to £300 for a USER who gives inaccurate details or none to a UK provider (potentially more for a non-UK provider), and up to £300 PER USER for a PROVIDER that fails to report, reports late or reports inaccurately. Users must give details to overseas exchanges too, not just UK ones. This is UK-wide and not devolved; Capital Gains Tax on crypto disposals is the same across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, though Scottish Income Tax rates and bands affect tax on crypto received as income.

title: R&D Tax Relief: Merged Scheme And ERIS

figures.what: Merged R&D expenditure credit rate on qualifying R&D expenditure, for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2024. The credit is taxable as trading income.
RDEC rate for ring fence trades (CTA 2009 s104M(2)), unchanged since 1 April 2013 - ring-fenced trades do not get the 20% rate
ERIS additional deduction on top of the normal 100% deduction, giving a total deduction of 186% of qualifying R&D expenditure
ERIS payable tax credit rate on the surrenderable loss. The payable credit is not liable to tax.

R&D intensity threshold for ERIS (CTA 2009 s1045ZA): relevant R&D expenditure must be at least 30% of total relevant expenditure, aggregated across the claimant and all connected companies, for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2024
The OLD intensity threshold, which applies only to claims under the old SME scheme for accounting periods ending on or after 1 April 2023 but beginning before 1 April 2024

Claim notification (pre-notification) deadline: the claim notification period starts on the first day of the period of account and ends six months after the period of account ends. Miss it and the whole R&D claim is invalid.
Claim notification exemption: a company that claimed R&D relief within three years of the last day of its claim notification period does not need to submit the form (subject to exceptions)
The claim notification form is not required for claims made on or after 1 April 2027

scope.who: Companies within the charge to UK Corporation Tax carrying on a trade, with a project meeting the statutory definition of R&D. The merged R&D expenditure credit is the default for all company sizes for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2024. ERIS is the alternative route for loss-making R&D-intensive SMEs: a company is loss-making if it has a trading loss for tax purposes before the additional deduction.
scope.excluded: Companies not trading or not chargeable to Corporation Tax; projects that do not meet the statutory R&D definition. For ERIS specifically: SMEs that are not loss-making, and SMEs whose R&D intensity is below 30% (they can still claim the merged 20% credit instead). You cannot claim both schemes for the same expenditure. Some overseas expenditure is restricted under both schemes - payments to overseas contractors and overseas externally provided workers are restricted (Northern Ireland SMEs claiming ERIS are NOT subject to those overseas restrictions). Costs consisting of a payment to a connected company are excluded from total relevant expenditure for the intensity test. Credit above the PAYE/NIC cap is restricted unless exempt; under the merged scheme any excess is carried forward to the next period. A claim with no valid claim notification form is invalid, and relief is lost entirely.
scope.from_when: Merged R&D expenditure credit and ERIS apply for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2024. The 86%/14.5% ERIS rates apply to expenditure incurred on or after 1 April 2023. Claim notification applies to accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2023.
scope.how_to_claim: Three steps, all mandatory. 1) Submit a claim notification form in advance, no later than six months after the end of the period of account, unless exempt as a recent claimant. 2) Submit the online additional information form before or at the same time as the claim. 3) Make the claim in the Company Tax Return (CT600) with the R&D figures. Northern Ireland companies that opt out of the NI-specific treatment must also complete the additional information form at the time of claiming.

notes: This is NOT the old SME enhanced deduction plus 10% payable credit, and it is NOT the old standalone RDEC - both were replaced by the merged scheme for accounting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2024. The two numbers most often confused: the intensity threshold is 30% for the new ERIS rules but was 40% under the old SME scheme, and the switch is by accounting period start date, not expenditure date. There is a one-year lookback route to ERIS: a company can still qualify if it met the intensity condition in its last 12-month accounting period and made a valid SME or ERIS claim on expenditure incurred on or after 1 April 2023. The claim notification trap is the big one - it is a pre-notification, so the deadline can fall before the company has even decided to claim, and missing it invalidates the claim outright with no late-claim route. Northern Ireland: NI SMEs claiming ERIS are not subject to the overseas contractor and overseas externally provided worker restrictions, and NI companies that opt out of that treatment must still file the additional information form at the time of claiming.

title: Structures And Buildings Allowance

figures.what: Annual SBA rate on qualifying expenditure, straight line, for a chargeable period of one year (CAA 2001 s270AA(5))
The allowance period over which the expenditure is relieved on the straight-line 3% basis, running from the later of first non-residential use and the date the qualifying expenditure is incurred
The original SBA rate, which applied before 1 April 2020 for Corporation Tax and before 6 April 2020 for Income Tax
All construction contracts must be signed on or after this date for the expenditure to qualify for SBA
The enhanced SBA rate available for qualifying expenditure in a designated special tax site
Where there is no allowance statement, the qualifying expenditure on which the current owner's allowance is based is treated as nil (CAA 2001 s270IA(1)-(3))

scope.who: Businesses within the charge to UK Corporation Tax or Income Tax that incur qualifying capital expenditure on constructing, renovating, converting or buying a non-residential structure or building, and use it for a qualifying activity taxable in the UK: a trade, profession or vocation; a UK or overseas property business; managing a company's investments; or mining, quarrying, fishing and other land-based trades such as running railways and toll roads. Qualifying expenditure includes construction costs, design fees, site preparation, construction works, renovation, repair and conversion costs, and fitting-out works.
scope.excluded: Any residence, and any structure in the grounds of a residence. Residential use is defined widely: a dwelling-house, residential accommodation for school pupils, student accommodation, residential accommodation for members of the armed forces, a home or other institution providing residential accommodation, and a prison or similar establishment - plus anything ancillary to those, with swimming pools in a dwelling's grounds and gyms, cinemas and car parks provided for a block of flats given as examples. Residential and furnished holiday lettings property businesses are excluded. Also excluded: the cost of land and of rights in or over land; fees, SDLT (or LBTT/LTT) and other incidental acquisition costs attributable to the land rather than the building; land reclamation, contaminated or derelict land remediation and landscaping (unless the landscaping creates a structure); planning permission costs; financing costs; public enquiry and legal costs; any cost that qualifies for plant and machinery allowances, and integral features or fixtures included in the price; any cost already used to claim another allowance; and any cost met by a grant or contribution. Site preparation costs are carved out of the land-alteration exclusion and do qualify.
scope.from_when: SBA applies where the earliest written construction contract was entered into on or after 29 October 2018. The rate is 3% from 1 April 2020 (Corporation Tax) or 6 April 2020 (Income Tax), and 2% before those dates.
scope.how_to_claim: Claim on your tax return. Before any claim you must hold a written allowance statement. If you are the first user you must create it; if you bought a used structure you must obtain a copy from a previous owner. It must contain: information identifying the building (such as address and description), the date of the earliest written construction contract, the amount of qualifying expenditure incurred on construction or purchase, the date the building was first brought into non-residential use, and the date each later qualifying construction cost was incurred.

notes: The allowance statement is the single biggest trap: it is a statutory condition, not paperwork. With no allowance statement the qualifying expenditure is nil, so a buyer who completes without getting a copy from the seller loses the whole remaining 33 1/3-year entitlement. A seller who is outside the UK tax charge must still prepare a statement for a later purchaser, and where part of a building is sold the relevant parts of the expenditure must be clearly identified on the statement. On sale there is no balancing allowance or balancing charge: the seller's allowances simply stop, and the total allowances claimed are added to the seller's disposal receipts, which increases the chargeable gain (Capital Gains Tax or Corporation Tax on the gain). The buyer picks up the remaining allowance period and, buying a used structure from a non-developer, claims the same amount the previous owner was entitled to - so SBA is a timing benefit on the building, clawed back through the gain, not a permanent deduction. SBA is also NOT an alternative to plant and machinery allowances: anything qualifying for P&M allowances, including integral features, is excluded from SBA, and the Annual Investment Allowance never applies to SBA expenditure. Claims also end if the structure is demolished or put to a non-qualifying purpose. The rules are UK-wide and identical in Northern Ireland; the only nation-specific point is which land transaction tax is excluded as a land acquisition cost (SDLT in England and Northern Ireland, LBTT in Scotland, LTT in Wales).

title: SEIS And EIS Investor Income Tax Relief

figures.what: SEIS income tax relief rate - a reduction in the individual's Income Tax liability equal to 50% of the amount subscribed, excluding incidental costs
EIS income tax relief rate - a reduction in the individual's Income Tax liability equal to 30% of the amount subscribed, excluding incidental costs (it was 20% for shares issued before 6 April 2011)
SEIS maximum annual investment on which an individual can claim relief, for shares issued on or after 6 April 2023 (it was £100,000 up to 5 April 2023)

EIS maximum annual investment for an individual, rising to £2 million per tax year provided at least £1 million of it goes into knowledge-intensive companies - no more than £1 million may go into non-knowledge-intensive companies
Minimum holding period for both SEIS and EIS shares - the investor must hold the shares for at least 3 years to keep the relief, and the company must keep meeting the scheme conditions for 3 years

SEIS company limit: total SEIS investment plus any other de minimis State aid received in the three years up to the latest SEIS investment must not exceed £250,000, for shares issued after 5 April 2023 (previously £150,000)
SEIS company gross assets limit - the company must have no more than £350,000 of gross assets at the time of the investment
SEIS company employee limit
SEIS company age limit - and the company must not have previously carried on a different trade
EIS lifetime limit on the amount a company can raise for most companies; higher limits may apply depending on the company's circumstances, such as research, development or innovation activity
EIS company gross assets limit at the time of the investment, reduced to £15 million for 'specified companies'
EIS company employee limit
EIS company age limit - no more than 7 years since the company's first commercial sale
The excluded-activities tolerance: a company may fail to qualify if more than 20% of its trade consists of non-qualifying (excluded) activities

scope.who: Individuals subscribing cash for new, full-risk ordinary shares in a qualifying unquoted company, who are within the charge to UK Income Tax. Relief reduces the investor's Income Tax liability for the year; the investor can elect to treat the shares as acquired in the preceding tax year, subject to that year's limit. The company must receive full payment in cash for newly issued full-risk ordinary shares and must not be listed on a recognised stock exchange.
scope.excluded: Relief cannot exceed the investor's Income Tax liability for the year - it reduces the liability to nil and any excess is simply lost, so there is nothing for an investor with no or low tax liability. Relief is withdrawn or restricted if the shares are disposed of within 3 years, if the investor receives value from the company, or if claims exceed the annual limit. Companies carrying on excluded activities (more than 20% of the trade) do not qualify, and the statutory list of excluded activities under ITA 2007 s192(1) and s303(1) is: dealing in land, commodities or futures or in shares, securities or other financial instruments; dealing in goods otherwise than in the course of an ordinary trade of wholesale or retail distribution; banking, insurance, money-lending, debt-factoring, hire-purchase financing or other financial activities; leasing, including letting ships on charter or other assets on hire; receiving royalties or licence fees; providing legal or accountancy services; property development; farming or market gardening; holding, managing or occupying woodlands, any other forestry activities or timber production; shipbuilding; producing coal; producing steel; operating or managing hotels or comparable establishments, and managing property used as such; operating or managing nursing homes or residential care homes, and managing property used as such; all energy generating activities; and activities excluded under ITA 2007 s199 (provision of services or facilities for another business). Listed companies are excluded. A company that has already received EIS or VCT investment cannot then qualify for SEIS.
scope.from_when: SEIS £200,000 investor limit and £250,000 company limit apply to shares issued on or after 6 April 2023 (the company limit to shares issued after 5 April 2023). The EIS £2 million investor limit including knowledge-intensive companies applies from 6 April 2018. The 30% EIS rate applies to shares issued on or after 6 April 2011.
scope.how_to_claim: The company first submits a compliance statement (SEIS1 or EIS1) confirming it met the conditions when the shares were issued; HMRC then issues an authority and the company gives each investor a SEIS3 or EIS3 certificate. The investor claims the relief on their Self Assessment tax return using the certificate. Where several reliefs apply, VCT relief is deducted first, then EIS, then SEIS.

notes: The two schemes are not interchangeable and the limits are routinely mixed up: SEIS gives 50% on up to £200,000 a year, EIS 30% on up to £1 million (£2 million only if at least £1 million goes to knowledge-intensive companies). The 3-year clock is two-sided - the investor must hold the shares for 3 years AND the company must keep meeting the conditions for 3 years, so a company breach claws back the investor's relief even though the investor did nothing. Relief is capped at the investor's actual Income Tax liability with no carry-forward of the excess, which is the most common disappointment. SEIS sits ahead of EIS in sequence: a company that has already taken EIS or VCT money can no longer use SEIS, so SEIS must come first. The SEIS £250,000 company limit counts other de minimis State aid received in the preceding three years, not just share subscriptions. 'Receiving royalties or licence fees' and 'property development' being excluded activities catches a lot of otherwise innovative businesses. These are UK-wide Income Tax reliefs with no Northern Ireland, Scotland or Wales variation - Scottish and Welsh rates of Income Tax do not change the 50% and 30% relief rates, which are set UK-wide. Figures here were read on 22 November 2026 and the EIS company limits in particular have been increased from their earlier levels, so recheck after the next Finance Act.

title: Patent Box Reduced Corporation Tax

figures.what: The effective rate of Corporation Tax on qualifying profits attributable to patented inventions and certain other qualifying IP ('relevant IP profits')
Election deadline - the election must be made within 2 years after the end of the accounting period in which the relevant profits arose
The date from which the full 10% reduced rate applied, after being phased in over the first four financial years from 1 April 2013
The nexus cut-off: companies electing into the Patent Box after 30 June 2016 are subject to the R&D fraction restriction and the streaming requirement
From this date all companies in the Patent Box must stream IP income separately from other income
The R&D fraction equals 1, and the Patent Box deduction is unrestricted, where there are no patent acquisition costs and all R&D is done in-house or by unconnected third-party subcontractors

scope.who: A qualifying company liable to UK Corporation Tax that makes a profit from exploiting patented inventions, owns the qualifying patents or holds them under an exclusive licence, and has undertaken qualifying development on them. The development condition requires that the company, or another company in the same group, made a significant contribution to creating or developing the patented invention, or to a product incorporating it. Qualifying patents must be granted by the UK Intellectual Property Office, the European Patent Office, or a listed EEA state such as Germany, Poland or Sweden. Group companies must also meet an active ownership condition: a group member must actively own the patented invention and play a significant role in managing the whole portfolio of eligible patents. Relief is delivered as an additional deduction in the Corporation Tax computation, which brings the effective rate on relevant IP profits down to 10%; relevant IP profits are calculated in four stages - identify relevant IP income, remove a routine return, remove profits attributable to other intangibles (the marketing assets return), then apply the R&D fraction.
scope.excluded: Companies not liable to UK Corporation Tax, and companies that make no profit from exploiting patents. Companies that neither own the qualifying patents nor hold them under a qualifying exclusive licence. Companies that have not undertaken qualifying development on the patents. Patents granted by an authority outside the eligible jurisdictions (UK IPO, EPO and the listed EEA states). Group companies that do not actively own the patents or do not play a significant role in managing the patent portfolio. Exclusive licensees that lack the required rights - the licensee must have rights to develop, exploit and defend the invention, with exclusivity across an entire national territory, and must be able to bring infringement proceedings or be entitled to most of any damages awarded. The R&D fraction restricts relief where the company paid acquisition costs for the patents or paid connected parties to do its R&D. Partnerships and other non-corporates are outside the regime, which applies only to companies within the charge to Corporation Tax.
scope.from_when: Part 8A CTA 2010, introduced by Finance Act 2012 and effective from 1 April 2013, with the full 10% rate from 1 April 2017. The R&D fraction (nexus) and streaming rules apply to elections made after 30 June 2016, and to all companies in the Patent Box from 1 July 2021.
scope.how_to_claim: Elect in writing under CTA 2010 s357A(1), within 2 years after the end of the accounting period in which the relevant profits arose. There is no box on the Company Tax Return and no special form of words: include the election in the computations accompanying the return, or make it separately in writing. If the company has more than one trade the election covers all of them. Once elected, the company must include a Patent Box computation in its original or amended CT computation for that period and for subsequent periods, until it revokes the election.

notes: The 10% is an effective rate, not a separate tax rate: it is delivered through an additional deduction in the CT computation, so the company still pays Corporation Tax at the main or small profits rate on everything else. The commonest misunderstanding is that owning a patent is enough - it is not. The company must have done qualifying development on the invention, and in a group a member must also actively own and manage the portfolio, so a passive holding company that simply registers the IP will not qualify. The election is easy to miss because there is no box on the CT600: it must be made in writing, usually in the computations, within 2 years of the end of the accounting period, and after that the period is simply lost. The R&D 'nexus' fraction is the teeth of the regime: it scales the benefit down where the company bought the patents in or paid connected parties to do the R&D, and it only equals 1 (full benefit) where there are no acquisition costs and the R&D was done in-house or by unconnected subcontractors. That nexus requirement forces streaming - IP income has to be tracked and traced separately from other income, per IP right or per product stream, which is the real compliance cost. Patent Box is a Corporation Tax regime that applies UK-wide, including Northern Ireland, with no devolved variation; note only that Northern Ireland companies may also be interacting with separate NI-specific R&D treatment on the R&D relief side, which does not change the Patent Box rules. Patent Box and R&D tax relief are complementary, not alternatives - the same company can claim both, and the R&D it does feeds the nexus fraction.

title: Lump Sum Allowance And Lump Sum And Death Benefit Allowance

figures.what: Standard individual lump sum allowance (LSA) for 2026 to 2027
Lump sum allowance stated in HMRC's Pensions Tax Manual: an individual is entitled to a lump sum allowance of £268,275 unless they hold a protected right to a higher amount
Standard individual lump sum and death benefit allowance (LSDBA) for 2026 to 2027
Lump sum and death benefit allowance stated in HMRC's Pensions Tax Manual, unless a protected higher amount applies

figures.value: Pension commencement lump sum; the 25% tax-free element of an uncrystallised funds pension lump sum; stand-alone lump sum
figures.what: The lump sums that count against the lump sum allowance (LSA)

figures.value: Everything that counts against the LSA, plus serious ill-health lump sums and most authorised lump sum death benefits paid where death is before age 75
figures.what: What counts against the lump sum and death benefit allowance (LSDBA). Charity lump sum death benefits and trivial commutation lump sum death benefits are not relevant lump sum death benefits.

figures.value: Income tax at the recipient's marginal rate
figures.what: Tax charge on any amount paid above the available LSA or LSDBA (there is no longer a separate lifetime allowance charge). The scheme administrator normally deducts the tax before payment; for a lump sum death benefit the legal personal representative reports the charge to HMRC.
Date the LSA and LSDBA took effect and the lifetime allowance was completely abolished

scope.who: Anyone taking a tax-free lump sum from a UK registered pension scheme (and, for the LSDBA, their beneficiaries on a lump sum death benefit). Same figures across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland because this is HMRC pensions tax law.
scope.excluded: Not everyone is held to the standard figures or caught by them at all: people with a protected right to a higher allowance (lifetime allowance protections or protected tax-free lump sum rights) have a higher LSA and/or LSDBA; trivial commutation lump sums and winding-up lump sums do not reduce available LSA; charity and trivial commutation lump sum death benefits are not relevant lump sum death benefits for the LSDBA; unauthorised payments are not relevant benefit crystallisation events and do not count against either allowance. Pension income (annuity, drawdown income, scheme pension) is taxed as income and is not measured against these lump sum allowances at all.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2024 onwards; figures above confirmed for the 2026 to 2027 tax year
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. The scheme administrator tests each lump sum against your available allowance and deducts any income tax due before paying. A higher protected allowance must be evidenced to the scheme (protection certificate or a transitional tax-free amount certificate applied for from a scheme administrator).

notes: This is NOT the lifetime allowance, which was abolished outright on 6 April 2024 — there is no longer a lifetime allowance charge, and the old 25%/55% excess rates are gone. The LSA caps tax-free lump sums only; it does not cap the total you can hold in a pension or the pension income you can draw. The LSA and LSDBA are two separate tests, and the same pension commencement lump sum uses up both. Common confusion: the LSDBA figure is the same number as the old lifetime allowance, but it does a different job. Excess amounts are taxed as income at the recipient's marginal rate, so where the recipient is a Scottish taxpayer the Scottish income tax rates and bands apply to non-savings income; pension tax relief on contributions likewise interacts with Scottish rates.

title: Money Purchase Annual Allowance

figures.what: Money purchase annual allowance for 2026 to 2027
MPAA for tax year 2023-24 onwards (it was £4,000 from 2017-18 to 2022-23)
The standard annual allowance the MPAA replaces for money purchase savings once triggered
Alternative annual allowance that applies to any defined benefit savings in a year the MPAA applies (reduced further if the tapered annual allowance also applies)

figures.value: Taking income from a newly designated flexi-access drawdown fund; converting a pre-6 April 2015 capped drawdown fund into flexi-access drawdown; having qualified for flexible drawdown before 6 April 2015; taking an uncrystallised funds pension lump sum (UFPLS); taking a stand-alone lump sum (where tax-free lump sum rights exceeded £375,000); taking a lifetime annuity that can reduce in amount; taking a scheme pension from a money purchase arrangement where fewer than 12 people are receiving a pension from the scheme; certain payments from overseas pension schemes
figures.what: The full list of MPAA trigger events

figures.value: A pension commencement lump sum (tax-free cash) on its own; a trivial commutation lump sum; a small pot lump sum from a money purchase arrangement; a scheme pension from a money purchase arrangement where at least 11 other people are receiving a scheme pension or dependants' scheme pension from the scheme; a lifetime annuity that cannot decrease except in prescribed circumstances; continuing to draw no more than the capped drawdown permitted maximum from a pre-6 April 2015 drawdown pension fund; payments from a beneficiary's flexi-access drawdown fund
figures.what: Payments and events that do NOT trigger the MPAA

Deadline for the member to pass on the flexible access statement, or tell the scheme they received one and the date of the relevant event, to every registered pension scheme under which they are an accruing member (money purchase or hybrid arrangement). If they become an accruing member later, 91 days run from that date. The scheme that issued the statement does not need to be told. The scheme administrator must issue the flexible access statement to the member in the first place.

scope.who: Anyone with a money purchase (defined contribution) pension who flexibly accesses their pension savings. The £10,000 cap then applies to their money purchase contributions, employer contributions included, for that tax year and every later year. HMRC pensions tax rules, so identical across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
scope.excluded: The MPAA is NOT triggered by taking tax-free cash (a pension commencement lump sum) on its own, by a trivial commutation lump sum, by a small pot lump sum, by a scheme pension from a money purchase arrangement where at least 11 other people are already receiving a scheme pension or dependants' scheme pension from that scheme, by a lifetime annuity that cannot decrease except in prescribed circumstances, by staying within the capped drawdown permitted maximum on a pre-6 April 2015 drawdown fund, or by payments from a beneficiary's (inherited) flexi-access drawdown fund. Defined benefit pension income does not trigger it either — the MPAA bites on money purchase arrangements, and defined benefit savings in the same year are measured against the alternative annual allowance of £30,000 instead. Once triggered, carry-forward of unused allowance cannot be used to lift money purchase savings above £10,000.
scope.from_when: MPAA regime from 6 April 2015; the £10,000 figure applies from tax year 2023-24 onwards and is confirmed for 2026 to 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — it is automatic from the date of the trigger event. The scheme administrator must give the member a flexible access statement; the member must then pass it on, or report that they received one and the date of the event, to every other registered pension scheme they are accruing benefits in, within 91 days.

notes: The commonest and most expensive mistake is assuming any touch of the pension triggers the MPAA. Taking the 25% tax-free cash and nothing else does not. Taking an UFPLS does, even though 25% of it is tax free. A single £1 of taxable drawdown income from a newly designated flexi-access fund triggers it permanently. It is NOT the tapered annual allowance (that is income-based) and NOT the annual allowance itself. The duty to tell the other schemes within 91 days sits on the member, not the provider. Where the member is a Scottish taxpayer, pension tax relief and any annual allowance charge interact with Scottish income tax rates and bands on non-savings income. Cross-reference for scheduling: the banked entry 'pension-annual-allowance' also carries the £10,000 MPAA figure among its figures, so these two subjects must not be published in the same week.

title: Carry Forward Of Unused Annual Allowance

figures.what: How far back unused annual allowance can be carried forward (for 2019-20 onwards; it was a four-year window for 2016-17 to 2018-19 because of the 2015-16 transitional split)
Standard annual allowance for 2026 to 2027, used first before any carry-forward

figures.value: Member of a registered pension scheme at some point in the tax year concerned
figures.what: The membership requirement: there is no unused allowance to carry forward from a year you were not a scheme member. Membership as an active, pensioner, deferred or pension credit member all count; non-UK scheme membership can qualify in certain circumstances (PTM113300).

figures.value: Current year's annual allowance first, then unused allowance from the earliest of the three carry-forward years first
figures.what: The order in which annual allowance is used

figures.value: The greater of £3,600 (the basic amount) and 100% of relevant UK earnings chargeable to income tax
figures.what: The limit on relievable member contributions in a tax year — carry-forward does not lift it

scope.who: Anyone who was a member of a registered pension scheme in the relevant earlier years and whose pension savings this year would otherwise exceed the annual allowance. HMRC pensions tax rules, identical across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
scope.excluded: You cannot carry forward from a tax year in which you were not a member of a registered pension scheme — that year yields nothing, however little was paid in. Carry-forward cannot be used to lift money purchase savings above the money purchase annual allowance once that has been triggered, and it cannot lift your own contributions above the tax-relief limit of the greater of £3,600 and 100% of your relevant UK earnings. Nothing carries forward from further back than the three preceding tax years, and once a year drops out of the window its unused allowance is lost.
scope.from_when: Three-year window applies for 2019-20 onwards; figures confirmed for 2026 to 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim and no form to file to use it. It applies automatically when working out whether you have an annual allowance charge. Keep pension input amount records for the three earlier years; HMRC's 'check if you have unused annual allowances' tool works it out, and any annual allowance charge is reported on a Self Assessment return.

notes: Carry-forward is about the annual allowance, NOT about tax relief. Two separate caps apply at once: the annual allowance (with carry-forward) and the earnings cap on relievable contributions. A person with £20,000 of relevant UK earnings and three years of unused allowance still only gets tax relief on £20,000 of their own contributions — employer contributions are not limited by the member's earnings, which is why carry-forward is most useful for employer or company contributions. You do not have to have had earnings in the earlier years, only scheme membership. Where the member is a Scottish taxpayer, relief above basic rate and any annual allowance charge follow the Scottish income tax rates and bands for non-savings income.

title: Automatic Enrolment Earnings Trigger And Qualifying Band

figures.what: Automatic enrolment earnings trigger for 2026/27 (£833 a month, £192 a week, £768 every four weeks)
Lower limit of the qualifying earnings band for 2026/27 (£480 every four weeks)
Upper limit of the qualifying earnings band for 2026/27 (£3,867 every four weeks)
The 2026/27 thresholds as set out in the DWP annual review laid before Parliament (unchanged from 2025/26)
Minimum total contribution, on qualifying earnings, from 6 April 2019 onwards
Minimum employer share of that 8% (the staff member makes up the remaining 5%, part of which is tax relief)
Age range for an eligible jobholder who must be automatically enrolled
How the minimum contribution is calculated: on the band of qualifying earnings, not on total pay

scope.who: Every employer with at least one member of staff, for each worker aged 22 to State Pension age who is working or ordinarily working in the UK under their contract and earning more than the £10,000 trigger in the pay reference period. These are 'eligible jobholders' and must be put into a qualifying pension scheme automatically. The Pensions Regulator oversees it in Great Britain; Northern Ireland has corresponding legislation with the same thresholds, so the figures hold UK-wide.
scope.excluded: Workers who do NOT have to be automatically enrolled: anyone under 22 or over State Pension age; anyone earning at or below the £10,000 trigger. These are 'non-eligible jobholders' (aged 16 to 74, earning above the £6,240 lower limit but not meeting the eligible jobholder test) who can opt in and must then receive employer contributions; and 'entitled workers' (aged 16 to 74 earning at or below £6,240) who can ask to join but get no statutory employer contribution. Also outside the duty: anyone not working or ordinarily working in the UK. Eligible jobholders who are enrolled can opt out within one month of enrolment and have their contributions refunded. Earnings above £50,270 attract no further statutory minimum contribution, because the band is capped there.
scope.from_when: Thresholds above apply for the 2026/27 tax year (review published 18 December 2025, unchanged from 2025/26); the 8% / 3% minimum contribution rates have applied since 6 April 2019
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing for the worker to claim: the employer must assess staff each pay period and enrol eligible jobholders without being asked, then re-enrol roughly every three years and file a declaration of compliance with The Pensions Regulator. Workers who are not caught by the duty have to ask the employer to put them in.

notes: The £10,000 trigger and the £6,240 lower limit are different numbers doing different jobs and are constantly mixed up: the £10,000 decides WHETHER someone is enrolled, the £6,240 to £50,270 band decides WHAT contributions are calculated on. So someone earning £12,000 is enrolled, but minimum contributions are 8% of £5,760, not 8% of £12,000. The band is also not the same as the National Insurance thresholds, even though £6,240 and £50,270 coincide with figures used elsewhere. An employer may use a different, certified basis (such as total pay or basic pay) with different percentages, but the qualifying-earnings basis above is the statutory default. Thresholds are reviewed by DWP every year, so the figures must be rechecked before April. Tax relief on the staff member's share interacts with Scottish income tax rates where the worker is a Scottish taxpayer and the scheme uses relief at source or net pay.

title: MTD For VAT: Digital Links And Digital Records

figures.what: VAT Notice 700/22 s1.2 — "Making Tax Digital for VAT requires all VAT-registered businesses to keep records digitally and file their VAT Returns using software." There is no longer any turnover threshold

The Value Added Tax (Amendment) Regulations 2021 (SI 2021/986) reg 1(1)-(2) — came into force 1 April 2022, and reg 2 omits paragraphs (2) to (5) of reg 32B of the VAT Regulations 1995, removing the turnover exemption so MTD covers all VAT-registered businesses; effective from the first prescribed accounting period beginning on or after 1 April 2022

figures.value: Copy and paste is not a digital link
figures.what: VAT Notice 700/22 s3.2.1 — "HMRC does not consider the use of 'cut and paste' or 'copy and paste' to select and move information, as a digital link." Same paragraph: "Manually transferring data within or between software programs, products or applications ... is not acceptable under Making Tax Digital"

figures.value: A transfer or exchange of data made (or capable of being made) electronically, with no manual intervention
figures.what: VAT Notice 700/22 s3.2.1 — "A digital link is where a transfer or exchange of data is made (or can be made) electronically between software programs, products or applications. A digital link does not need any manual intervention, such as the copying over of information by hand, or the manual relocation of data between 2 or more pieces of software." Linked cells in spreadsheets (a formula in one sheet mirroring a source cell) are a digital link

figures.value: Emailing a spreadsheet, portable device transfer, XML, CSV import/export, upload/download, automated data transfer, API transfer
figures.what: VAT Notice 700/22 s3.2.1 — HMRC's non-exhaustive list of what it accepts as digital links

figures.value: Designatory data; supplies made; supplies received; VAT Return summary data
figures.what: VAT Notice 700/22 s3.3 — "The records listed in the following paragraphs must be kept, maintained and preserved digitally" (the 'electronic account'): s3.3.1 designatory data (business name, address of principal place of business, VAT registration number, VAT accounting schemes used); s3.3.2 supplies made (time of supply/tax point, net value excluding VAT, rate of VAT charged); s3.3.3 supplies received; s3.3.5 VAT Return summary data. Retail scheme daily gross takings must also be kept digitally (s3.5)

figures.value: Invoices need not be kept digitally
figures.what: VAT Notice 700/22 s3.1 and s3.3 — "You'll need to keep additional records, such as invoices. You do not have to keep these digitally but you may choose to do so." Some documents must still be kept in their original form, e.g. a C79 import VAT certificate

VAT Notice 700/21 s2.4 — "Generally, you must keep all your business records for VAT purposes for at least 6 years." Records used for other taxes may need keeping longer; if the 6-year rule causes serious storage problems or undue expense you can ask HMRC. Notice 700/22 s3.1 says that if you deregister you no longer need digital records in software but "you must still retain your VAT records for the required period"

scope.who: Every VAT-registered business in the UK, whatever its turnover: it must keep the records specified in VAT Notice 700/22 s3.3 digitally within functional compatible software, keep each piece of that software digitally linked, and file VAT Returns through HMRC's API (Notice 700/22 s1.2, s3.1, s3.2).
scope.excluded: Businesses HMRC is satisfied are exempt under VAT Notice 700/22 s2.1: where it is not practical to use digital tools to keep records or submit returns, for reasons such as age, disability or location (s2.2 gives no internet access, or a disability preventing computer use, as examples); businesses subject to an insolvency procedure; businesses run entirely by practising members of a religious society or order whose beliefs are incompatible with electronic communications or electronic record-keeping; and businesses already exempt from filing VAT returns online. Also outside the digital requirement: records not specified in the notice and not needed to complete the VAT Return (s3.1), intra-group supplies for a VAT group (s3.3.2), original documents such as invoices (s3.1, s3.3), and data transferred from software that is not used to maintain the electronic account (s3.2.1).
scope.from_when: 1 April 2022 for all VAT-registered businesses regardless of turnover — SI 2021/986 reg 1(1)-(2) and reg 2, effective from the first prescribed accounting period beginning on or after that date.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — the digital record-keeping and digital link duties apply automatically. Exemption is the opposite: it must be claimed. Notice 700/22 s2.4 — "To make a claim for exemption, contact VAT: general enquiries"; HMRC decides and "You'll always receive our decision in writing." You must keep filing as usual while waiting for a decision or an appeal outcome (s2.4). HMRC's route for this is its 'Applying for an exemption from Making Tax Digital for VAT' guidance: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/apply-for-an-exemption-from-making-tax-digital-for-vat

notes: The usual trap is the spreadsheet. A spreadsheet is allowed and can be part of functional compatible software (Notice 700/22 s3.2), but once data is in the software that maintains your electronic account, every later transfer, recapture or modification of that data must travel by digital link (s3.2.1). Retyping figures, writing invoice details in a ledger and keying them in again, or copy-pasting a VAT total between two workbooks all break the chain. Linked cells (a formula in one sheet mirroring another) do not. Emailing a spreadsheet so it can be imported, or handing over a pen drive, are both accepted — the test is whether a human has to move the data by hand, not whether the internet is involved. Two further distinctions: MTD does not change what records you must keep for VAT generally (Notice 700/21), only which of them must be digital and linked, and it does not shorten the 6-year retention period, which still bites after deregistration. Note also that VAT Notice 700/22 was last updated 1 April 2022, so the notice itself does not state the commencement date — that is in SI 2021/986. MTD for VAT is UK-wide; it is a record-keeping and filing regime, not a goods rule, so the Windsor Framework does not bear on it.

title: VAT On Business Gifts And Samples

figures.what: VAT Notice 700/7 s2.3 — "You do not have to account for VAT on business gifts made to the same person so long as the total cost of all gifts you make to that person does not exceed £50, excluding VAT, in any 12-month period." The figure is the total cost of all gifts to that one person, VAT-exclusive, not the cost of a single gift

figures.value: Output tax on the total cost value of all the gifts
figures.what: VAT Notice 700/7 s2.3 — once the £50 limit is breached, output tax is due on the total cost value of all the gifts (not just the excess over £50), where you were entitled to claim the VAT on the purchase as input tax. Any 12-month period that includes the day the gift is made is acceptable for testing the limit

VAT Notice 700/7 s4.2 — "If you provide free samples of products to individuals for marketing purposes and they meet the definition in paragraph 4.1, they are not liable to VAT." s4.1 defines a sample as "A specimen of a product which is intended to promote the sales of that product and which allows the characteristics and qualities of that product to be assessed without resulting in final consumption, other than where final consumption is inherent in such promotional transactions." There is no monetary limit and no quantity limit on samples

figures.value: Free services: usually no supply, no VAT
figures.what: VAT Notice 700/7 s3.1 — "If you provide a service to a customer free of charge there is usually no supply, so no VAT is due." But where you bought in the services and reclaimed the VAT as input tax, "output tax is due on the services you pass on free of charge". If you simply pay a third party to supply services to someone else, the VAT is not your input tax because the supply is not to you

figures.value: Gifts of goods with no £50 shelter: VAT on cost value
figures.what: VAT Notice 700/7 s2.1 — if you give away goods, were entitled to recover the VAT on them as input tax, and receive no payment or other consideration, "you must account for VAT on their cost value. That is unless they can be treated as business gifts under paragraph 2.3"

scope.who: VAT-registered businesses in the UK that give away goods or services free of charge in the course of promoting the business. A 'business gift' is defined at VAT Notice 700/7 s2.2 as a gift of goods made in the course of promoting your business and for which you were entitled to reclaim the VAT on its purchase as input tax — 'a definite, voluntary and unconditional transfer of the goods for no consideration'. s2.2 lists long service awards and retirement gifts, goods supplied to employees under attendance or safety at work schemes, items distributed to trade customers, 'thank you' goods given to customers, and prizes of goods in free lotteries and competitions as business gifts.
scope.excluded: Not caught by the output tax charge: gifts to one person costing £50 or less in total, VAT-exclusive, in any 12-month period (s2.3); goods on which you were never entitled to reclaim input tax, since the deemed supply only arises where you were so entitled (s2.1, s2.3); goods never bought for business purposes, which "are not business assets and any VAT incurred on their purchase is not reclaimable as input tax" (s2.5); free samples meeting the s4.1 definition, which are not liable to VAT however many you give (s4.2); a prize or trophy given at an awards ceremony where attendees pay an admission fee and the s2.6 conditions are met; point of sale material given free to business customers that gives direct promotional support (s2.12); goods withdrawn from sale and donated or destroyed (s2.14); and services provided free of charge where you did not buy them in and reclaim input tax (s3.1). Gifts of goods to a charity may be zero-rated where the charity sells, lets or exports them (s2.7). Explicitly outside this notice: business entertainment, which s1.1 says the notice "does not cover" and which is dealt with in Notice 700/65; s3.2 confirms input tax on goods or services bought for business entertainment is not normally deductible.
scope.from_when: The current HMRC notice (VAT Notice 700/7, Business promotions) states the £50 rule as the rule in force; the notice itself gives no commencement date for the limit, so no start date is asserted here.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim or apply for. The £50 shelter and the sample treatment apply automatically if the conditions are met — the duty is on the business to track the running total of gifts per recipient over a 12-month period and to account for output tax once it is exceeded. Where output tax is accounted for on a gift to a VAT-registered recipient who uses the goods in business, s2.4 says you cannot issue a VAT invoice but may use your normal invoicing documentation with the wording: 'Tax Certificate — No payment is necessary for these goods. Output tax of £XX.XX (insert amount) has been accounted for on the supply.'

notes: Three things get mixed up here. First, business gifts are not business entertainment: gifts of goods are covered by Notice 700/7 and can be sheltered by the £50 limit, while entertainment (hospitality of any kind) sits in Notice 700/65 and generally blocks input tax recovery outright. Second, the £50 is cumulative per recipient over any 12-month period and excludes VAT — it is not £50 per gift, and once you pass it output tax is due on the cost value of all the gifts in the period, not just the slice above £50. Third, samples are a separate relief with no monetary cap, but the definition is narrow: a discontinued line cannot be a sample because there is no product left to promote, and quantity matters — one bottle of wine to a prospective buyer is a sample, a case of twelve is not (s4.3). If you are given samples and then sell them, output tax is due on that sale (s4.4). Free services are the odd one out: giving your own labour away is usually no supply at all, but passing on bought-in services free of charge triggers output tax where you reclaimed the input tax. This is a UK-wide valuation and deemed-supply rule, so the Northern Ireland Protocol/Windsor Framework does not bear on it.

title: The VAT Retail Schemes

figures.what: VAT Notice 727 s3.2 — "If your annual turnover of all taxable retail sales, excluding VAT, is above £130 million, you cannot use the published standard schemes. If you think your annual turnover is about to exceed £130 million, you should contact HMRC as soon as possible to agree a bespoke retail scheme." A bespoke scheme is tailored to the business and is likely to be an adaptation of one of the published schemes

figures.value: Point of sale scheme, 2 apportionment schemes, 2 direct calculation schemes
figures.what: VAT Notice 727 s3.1 — "The standard schemes take their name from the principle on which they're based. They are: the point of sale scheme, 2 apportionment schemes, 2 direct calculation schemes. You can choose any of the published schemes for which you're eligible." Point of sale is detailed at s3.4, apportionment 1 at s3.5, apportionment 2 at s3.6, direct calculation 1 at s3.7, direct calculation 2 at s3.8

VAT Notice 727 s3.5.1 and s3.5.2 — apportionment scheme 1 is "the simpler scheme designed for smaller businesses with a tax exclusive retail turnover not exceeding £1 million"; you "can only use the scheme if your total tax exclusive turnover from retail sales does not exceed £1 million"

VAT Notice 727 s3.6.1 and s3.6.2 — apportionment scheme 2 "is available for businesses with a tax exclusive retail turnover not exceeding £130 million"; you "can only use the scheme if your total tax exclusive retail turnover from retail sales does not exceed £130 million"

VAT Notice 727 s3.7.1 and s3.7.3 — "Direct calculation scheme 1 is available to businesses with a tax exclusive retail turnover not exceeding £1 million"; "you cannot use direct calculation scheme 1 if your annual tax exclusive retail turnover exceeds £1 million"

VAT Notice 727 s3.8 — direct calculation scheme 2 works like scheme 1 but requires an annual stock adjustment: "You can use the scheme if your annual tax exclusive retail turnover does not exceed £130 million"

VAT Notice 727 s7.5 — the catering adaptation may be used only if you can satisfy HMRC you are unable to operate the Point of Sale Scheme, you have reasonable grounds for believing the tax-exclusive value of your taxable retail catering sales will not exceed £1 million in the next 12 months, and the adaptation produces a fair and reasonable result. You must notify HMRC and may start on receiving HMRC's acknowledgement

scope.who: VAT-registered businesses making retail sales that cannot account for VAT using normal accounting. VAT Notice 727 s2.1 — "Retail is the selling of goods or services to consumers and the retail schemes are aimed at retailers that cannot account for VAT using normal accounting." Normal accounting requires you to identify, for each sale, the tax-exclusive value and the VAT, and to produce periodic totals (s2.2). Under s3.1 you can choose any published scheme for which you are eligible; where you qualify for more than one, s2.4 says you choose the one best suited to the business.
scope.excluded: Cannot use a published standard scheme: any business whose annual turnover of all taxable retail sales, excluding VAT, is above £130 million — it must agree a bespoke retail scheme with HMRC instead (s3.2). HMRC may also refuse use of a retail scheme "if you can reasonably be expected to account for VAT in the normal way", if the chosen scheme does not produce a fair and reasonable result, or for the protection of the revenue (s3.3). Non-retail sales can never go through a retail scheme — "you can only use the retail schemes to account for retail sales" and non-retail sales must use normal accounting (s2.3). Scheme-specific bars: apportionment scheme 1 is unavailable above £1 million tax-exclusive retail turnover and "cannot be used for supplies of services, for supplies of goods which you have made or grown yourself" (s3.5.2); apportionment scheme 2 is unavailable above £130 million and cannot be used "for supplies of services or catering" (s3.6.2); direct calculation scheme 1 is unavailable above £1 million (s3.7.3); catering sales "must normally be accounted for using the Point of Sale Scheme" (s7.1); and the Retail Chemist Adjustment "cannot be used with Apportionment Scheme 2" (s8.3).
scope.from_when: The schemes are a standing feature of the VAT Regulations; VAT Notice 727 states the current limits. Timing rules on moving between schemes: s4.2 — changes are normally made at the end of a complete scheme year, an earlier change needs HMRC approval, and you must stop using a scheme once you become ineligible. s4.3 — retrospective changes are "not normally allowed" but HMRC may allow them in exceptional cases.
scope.how_to_claim: For a published standard scheme there is no application and no HMRC permission: s3.1 — "You can choose any of the published schemes for which you're eligible." The published scheme notices (727/3 point of sale, 727/4 apportionment, 727/5 direct calculation) set out rules some of which have force of law, and you must keep the daily gross takings record and comply with the DGT checklist in your scheme's notice (s6). Permission or notification IS needed in specific cases: above £130 million you must contact HMRC to agree a bespoke retail scheme (s3.2); to use the catering adaptation "you must notify HMRC" and may start "as soon as you receive our acknowledgement" (s7.5); an early change of scheme needs HMRC approval (s4.2); adjustments for transfers between parts of the business must be agreed with HMRC (s4.1); and "You must always tell HMRC of changes to your business structure" (s5.2).

notes: The retail schemes are not a reduced rate or a saving — they are a way of working out output tax when you cannot identify the VAT on every individual sale, typically because you sell to the public at mixed rates. They are commonly confused with the Flat Rate Scheme (Notice 733), which is a different scheme with a much smaller turnover test and which you must apply to join; a retail scheme you simply adopt if eligible. The £130 million ceiling is on tax-exclusive taxable retail turnover and is the point at which the published schemes stop being available at all and a bespoke agreement with HMRC becomes compulsory; the £1 million figures are the separate, much lower ceilings on apportionment scheme 1 and direct calculation scheme 1. Two further traps: a scheme covers retail sales only, so a business with wholesale or trade sales alongside its shop must run normal accounting for that part, and catering normally has to go through the Point of Sale Scheme rather than apportionment. Retail scheme daily gross takings must also be kept digitally under Making Tax Digital (Notice 700/22 s3.5). UK-wide; a VAT accounting method rather than a goods rule, so the Windsor Framework does not bear on it.

title: VAT On Food, Catering And Hot Takeaway

figures.what: VATA 1994 Schedule 8 Group 1 — the supply of anything comprised in the general items (item 1: "Food of a kind used for human consumption") is zero-rated "except— (a) a supply in the course of catering; and (b) a supply of anything comprised in any of the excepted items set out below, unless it is also comprised in any of the items overriding the exceptions". Notice 701/14 s1.3 confirms VATA 1994 s30 and Sch 8 Group 1 as the law

figures.value: Consumption on the premises, and hot takeaway food
figures.what: VATA 1994 Sch 8 Group 1 Note (3) — "A supply of anything in the course of catering includes— (a) any supply of it for consumption on the premises on which it is supplied; and (b) any supply of hot food for consumption off those premises". Note (3A) — "the premises on which food is supplied include any area set aside for the consumption of food by that supplier's customers, whether or not the area may also be used by the customers of other suppliers"

figures.value: Hot at the time provided to the customer, plus any one of five tests
figures.what: VATA 1994 Sch 8 Group 1 Note (3B) — "'Hot food' means food which (or any part of which) is hot at the time it is provided to the customer and— (a) has been heated for the purposes of enabling it to be consumed hot, (b) has been heated to order, (c) has been kept hot after being heated, (d) is provided to a customer in packaging that retains heat (whether or not the packaging was primarily designed for that purpose) or in any other packaging that is specifically designed for hot food, or (e) is advertised or marketed in a way that indicates that it is supplied hot." The five tests are alternatives: meeting any one, together with being hot on provision, makes the food standard-rated. Notes (3B) to (3D) were inserted with effect from 1 October 2012 by Finance Act 2012 Sch 26 paras 2(4), 7(1)

VATA 1994 Sch 8 Group 1 Note (3C) — "(a) something is 'hot' if it is at a temperature above the ambient air temperature, and (b) something is 'kept hot' after being heated if the supplier stores it in an environment which provides, applies or retains heat, or takes other steps to ensure it remains hot or to slow down the natural cooling process." Note (3D) — references to food being heated include it being cooked or reheated. Notice 709/1 s4.3 states the same ambient-air test and adds that for test (a) "it's the purpose of the supplier (and not the customer)" that counts, and that 'freshly baked' marketing does not meet test (e)

VAT Notice 709/1 s3.1 — "You must always charge VAT at the standard rate if you make a supply of food and drink for consumption on the premises." s3.2 defines premises as the areas occupied by the food retailer or any area set aside for the consumption of food by its customers; general public seating such as benches in a shopping centre or a picnic area is not included. s2.1 — "Catering in its ordinary meaning includes the supply of prepared food and drink. It is characterised by a supply involving a significant element of service"; s2.2 — any food supplied under a contract for catering is standard-rated

VATA 1994 Sch 8 Group 1 excepted item 2 — "Confectionery, not including cakes or biscuits other than biscuits wholly or partly covered with chocolate or some product similar in taste and appearance." Note (5) — "for the purposes of item 2 of the excepted items 'confectionery' includes chocolates, sweets and biscuits; drained, glacé or crystallised fruits; and any item of sweetened prepared food which is normally eaten with the fingers." Items overriding the exceptions 2 and 3 (drained cherries, candied peels) are zero-rated. Notice 701/14 s3.6 adds that confectionery includes items that are inherently sweet, for example certain fruit and cereal bar products

figures.value: Crisps and savoury snacks — excepted item 5
figures.what: VATA 1994 Sch 8 Group 1 excepted item 5 — "Any of the following when packaged for human consumption without further preparation, namely, potato crisps, potato sticks, potato puffs, and similar products made from the potato, or from potato flour, or from potato starch, and savoury food products obtained by the swelling of cereals or cereal products; and salted or roasted nuts other than nuts in shell." Notice 701/14 s3.8 — "Savoury snacks not falling within one or other of these 3 categories are zero-rated", and gives tortilla chips, corn chips, bagel chips, Twiglets, savoury popcorn, prawn crackers made from cereals, and roasted pulses and legumes as standard-rated, against sliced and dried or roasted vegetables other than potatoes (beetroot, carrot) and tapioca prawn crackers as zero-rated. Roasted or salted nuts are standard-rated even when sold loose

figures.value: Ice cream (item 1), alcoholic drinks (item 3), other beverages (item 4), sports drinks (item 4A), pet food (item 6), home brewing products (item 7)
figures.what: VATA 1994 Sch 8 Group 1, remaining excepted items. Item 1 ice cream, ice lollies, frozen yogurt, water ices and similar frozen products and mixes; item 3 beverages chargeable with alcohol duty; item 4 other beverages including fruit juices and bottled waters, and preparations for making them; item 4A sports drinks advertised or marketed as designed to enhance physical performance, accelerate recovery after exercise or build bulk (inserted 1 October 2012 by Finance Act 2012 Sch 26 paras 2(2), 7(1)); item 6 pet foods; item 7 products for domestic brewing and wine making. Items overriding the exceptions 4 to 7 restore the zero rate to tea, maté, herbal teas, cocoa, coffee, chicory and roasted coffee substitutes, milk, and preparations and extracts of meat, yeast or egg

scope.who: Any UK business supplying food or drink: producers, manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers (Notice 701/14 s1.2), and caterers, restaurants, pubs, cafes and takeaways (Notice 709/1). Most food of a kind used for human consumption is zero-rated when it is not supplied in the course of catering (Notice 701/14 s2.2); a product is 'food of a kind used for human consumption' if the average person, knowing what it is and how it is used, would consider it food or drink, and it is fit for human consumption (s2.3).
scope.excluded: The zero rate does NOT reach: any supply in the course of catering, which Note (3) defines as including all food and drink supplied for consumption on the premises and all hot food supplied to take away — Notice 701/14 s2.1 says "You must always standard rate food supplied in the course of catering including hot take-away food"; and the excepted items — ice cream and similar frozen products, confectionery (apart from cakes and most biscuits), alcoholic drinks, other beverages and preparations for them, sports drinks, potato crisps and listed savoury snacks and salted or roasted nuts, pet food, and home brewing and wine-making products. Equally, the standard rate does NOT catch: cold takeaway food, since retail supplies of cold takeaway food are not catering (Notice 709/1 s2.1) and are zero-rated unless they are an excepted item such as crisps or sweets (s4.1); food that happens to be hot when sold but meets none of the five Note (3B) tests, which stays zero-rated (s4.4) — the notice's example is freshly baked bread and bakery products, and its worked Example 1 is a pasty still hot when sold but left to cool naturally, sold in a standard paper bag and not advertised as hot; food eaten on general public seating such as shopping centre benches or picnic areas, which is not 'premises' (s3.2); and catering in education (s2.6) and in hospitals and similar institutions (s2.7), which is not standard-rated under the s1.3 carve-out. Items overriding the exceptions put the zero rate back for yoghurt unsuitable for immediate consumption when frozen, drained cherries, candied peels, tea, maté, herbal teas, cocoa, coffee, chicory, milk, and preparations and extracts of meat, yeast or egg.
scope.from_when: The Group 1 zero rate and the excepted items are long-standing. The current statutory hot food definition in Notes (3B) to (3D), and excepted item 4A for sports drinks, took effect on 1 October 2012 (Finance Act 2012 Sch 26 paras 2(2), 2(4), 7(1)).
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim or apply for. Liability follows the statutory tests, and the supplier must apply them at the point of sale. Where a business sells both standard-rated food for consumption on the premises and zero-rated cold takeaway food, Notice 709/1 s3.3 requires a fair apportionment with evidence kept to support it. Retailers who cannot identify the VAT on each sale may use a VAT retail scheme (Notice 727); catering sales must normally go through the Point of Sale Scheme (Notice 727 s7.1).

notes: Food is zero-rated, which is why people assume all food is VAT-free, but Group 1 opens with two exceptions that do most of the damage: catering, and the excepted items. Catering is not just restaurant service — Note (3) makes it cover anything consumed on the premises and all hot takeaway food, and Note (3A) extends 'premises' to any area the supplier sets aside for customers to eat in, even shared seating in a food court. A takeaway counter and a few tables is therefore two different VAT answers on the same sandwich. The five hot food tests in Note (3B) are alternatives, not cumulative, and four of them are about how the trader behaves rather than the food: heating it so it can be eaten hot, heating it to order, keeping it hot, hot-retaining packaging, or marketing it as hot. 'Hot' is simply above ambient air temperature. So a pasty cooling on an open shelf in a paper bag can be zero-rated while the identical pasty in a foil bag, or under a heat lamp, or advertised as 'hot', is standard-rated — the supplier's purpose counts, not the customer's (Notice 709/1 s4.3). Confectionery and crisps are standard-rated regardless of temperature or location, which is why a cold sandwich takeaway with a packet of crisps and a chocolate bar is a three-rate transaction. Both notices carried a temporary reduced rate of VAT on certain supplies of children's meals from 25 June 2026 to 1 September 2026, which had ended before this entry was verified.
