This is a UK-wide liability rule based on the nature of the supply, so the Northern Ireland Protocol/Windsor Framework does not bear on it.

title: Boiler Upgrade Scheme Grant

figures.what: Grant for an air-to-water heat pump, or a ground source heat pump (including water source and shared ground loop systems)
Higher grant for an air-to-water or ground source heat pump in an eligible off-gas-grid property, available 21 July 2026 to 31 March 2027
Grant for a biomass boiler (rural off-gas-grid properties only)
Grant for an air-to-air heat pump (residential properties only)
Maximum period the system may have been commissioned before the grant application is properly made
Time the property owner has to confirm consent to Ofgem once Ofgem makes contact about the application

scope.who: Owners of property in England and Wales who replace an existing fossil fuel or electric heating system with an eligible low-carbon system fitted by an MCS-certified installer. The new system must meet the full space heating and hot water needs of the property.
scope.excluded: Social housing, including shared ownership. New build properties, except qualifying self-builds. Properties that have already had government or Energy Company Obligation funding towards the same heat pump or biomass boiler. Hybrid systems. Systems replacing an existing low-carbon system rather than a fossil fuel or electric one. Systems that do not meet the property's full space heating and hot water need. Biomass boilers outside rural properties not connected to the gas grid, biomass in eligible self-builds, and biomass that is not a standalone system providing both space heating and hot water. Air-to-air heat pumps in non-residential buildings. Systems commissioned more than 120 days before the application. Properties in Scotland and Northern Ireland are outside the scheme entirely.
scope.from_when: The scheme is open in England and Wales as at 22 November 2026. The higher £9,000 off-gas-grid rate runs from 21 July 2026 to 31 March 2027; the £7,500, £5,000 and £2,500 rates carry no published end date.
scope.how_to_claim: You do not apply yourself. Your chosen MCS-certified installer makes the application to Ofgem on your behalf and takes the grant off your quote as an upfront discount. Ofgem then contacts you and you must confirm your consent within 14 calendar days. Confirming consent does not commit you to that installer.

notes: England and Wales only - this is the nation trap on this subject. Scotland has its own separate support through Home Energy Scotland, and Northern Ireland has no equivalent scheme; do not present this as UK-wide. There is no EPC band condition and no loft or cavity wall insulation condition: Ofgem's property owner guidance sets no EPC requirement, and mentions EPCs only as advisory, noting that an EPC's 'changes you could make' section can suggest efficiency improvements and that heat pumps perform best in well-insulated homes. The grant is not cash to the householder - it is a discount the installer claims, so the saving appears on the quote. It is not a boiler grant despite the scheme name: a replacement gas or oil boiler gets nothing. Hybrid systems get nothing. The £9,000 off-gas-grid rate is time-limited and must be re-checked before 31 March 2027.

title: Flight Delay And Cancellation Compensation

figures.what: Compensation per passenger, flight under 1,500km, arriving more than 3 hours late
Compensation per passenger, flight between 1,500km and 3,500km, arriving more than 3 hours late
Compensation per passenger, flight over 3,500km, arriving between 3 and 4 hours late
Compensation per passenger, flight over 3,500km, arriving more than 4 hours late
Minimum late arrival at the destination airport before delay compensation is payable
Cancellation compensation is payable only where the airline gave less than 14 days' notice of the cancellation

Reduced cancellation compensation (half rate) for the under 1,500km, 1,500-3,500km and over 3,500km bands where notice was 7 to 14 days and the replacement flight arrived within the shorter delay window
Time limit to bring a court claim in England and Wales, running from the date of the incident
Time limit to bring a court claim in Scotland, running from the date of the incident
Period after a written complaint to the airline, with no reply or an unsatisfactory reply, after which you can escalate to the CAA's PACT service

scope.nation: UK-wide (UK261, retained in UK law), and the amounts are the same wherever in the UK the passenger lives
scope.who: Passengers on a flight that departs from a UK airport on any airline; or arrives at a UK airport on a UK or EU airline; or arrives at an EU airport on a UK airline. For delays, you must arrive more than 3 hours late at your destination airport. For cancellations, the airline must have given less than 14 days' notice. Compensation is a fixed sum per passenger and depends on the airline being at fault.
scope.excluded: Flights with no UK connection of the kind above - for example a flight arriving at a UK airport on a non-UK, non-EU airline, or a flight wholly outside the UK and EU. Delays where you arrive less than 3 hours late. Cancellations notified 14 days or more before departure. Any disruption caused by extraordinary circumstances outside the airline's responsibility, which the CAA gives as severe weather making the flight unsafe to operate, strikes by staff at other organisations such as airports, ground handlers, air traffic control or Border Force, terrorism or sabotage, security risks, political or civil unrest, and manufacturer recalls for hidden defects. Fixed compensation is also reduced or removed where the airline re-routes you close to the original times - no fixed compensation applies if the replacement flight departs up to two hours before, or any time after, the original departure and arrives less than four hours late. Court claims brought more than 6 years after the incident in England and Wales, or more than 5 years in Scotland.
scope.from_when: UK261 applies to affected flights now; claims can reach back 6 years in England and Wales and 5 years in Scotland from the date of the incident.
scope.how_to_claim: Claim in writing to the airline direct and free of charge. The airline must explain the cause of the disruption, and if it says extraordinary circumstances applied it must justify that. If you get no reply within 8 weeks, or you are dissatisfied with the reply, escalate to the airline's alternative dispute resolution scheme or to the CAA's Passenger Advice and Complaints Team. Otherwise you can go to court within 6 years (5 in Scotland).

notes: This is UK261 - the EU regulation as retained in UK law - not EU261, though the structure is the same. The compensation amounts are fixed sums in sterling per passenger and are entirely separate from, and on top of, your right to a refund or re-routing and the airline's duty of care (meals, refreshments, accommodation and transport while you wait). An ordinary technical fault is NOT an extraordinary circumstance: the CAA cites Jet2 v Huzar (England, 2014), while KLM v van der Lans (2015) left room for a hidden manufacturing defect or damage from sabotage or terrorism to qualify. Distance is measured for the flight, and the delay that counts is arrival at the destination, not departure. Claim direct - claims companies take a cut of money the airline must pay you anyway. One practical trap: the CAA's PACT service will not take a complaint where there is less than a year left to take legal action, so do not sit on a claim until year five.

title: Breathing Space Debt Respite Scheme

figures.what: Maximum length of a standard breathing space; it ends automatically at 60 days unless cancelled earlier
Length of a mental health crisis breathing space - it runs for as long as the crisis treatment lasts, plus a further 30 days
Window in which the debt adviser must carry out the mandatory midway review of a standard breathing space
Cost of applying - applying for breathing space is free, although some debt advisers charge a fee for their wider advice service
Date the Debt Respite Scheme regulations came into force

scope.nation: England and Wales only - the regulations expressly extend to England and Wales only and apply to debtors domiciled or ordinarily resident in England or Wales
scope.who: An individual with problem debt who lives or is ordinarily resident in England or Wales. The application must go through a debt adviser who is authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority to offer debt counselling, or a local authority providing debt advice to its residents. A representative, for example someone with power of attorney, can apply on the person's behalf. Where someone is receiving mental health crisis treatment and cannot speak to an adviser themselves, another person can do so for them.
scope.excluded: People who live outside England and Wales - advisers must not start a breathing space for a client living elsewhere, and Scotland has its own separate statutory solution. On debts, the following are excluded from the protections: secured debts such as a mortgage, hire purchase or conditional sale (only the arrears existing when the application is made are included); debts incurred through fraud; court-imposed fines, including interest, penalties and charges on them; obligations under a confiscation order; child maintenance and obligations under family court orders; social fund crisis loans and budgeting loans; student loans; damages for death or personal injury caused to someone else; advance Universal Credit payments; and council tax not yet fallen due. Some business debts are also excluded where the client is VAT registered or is a partner in a business with someone else.
scope.from_when: In force since 4 May 2021 and running now.
scope.how_to_claim: You cannot apply yourself and you cannot apply direct to the government. You must speak to a debt adviser who is FCA-authorised for debt counselling, or a local authority debt advice service; the adviser submits the application for you if breathing space is appropriate. Applying is free.

notes: England and Wales only - this is the nation trap. The regulations state in terms that they extend to England and Wales only and apply to debtors domiciled or ordinarily resident in England or Wales. Scotland has a separate statutory debt solution and is not covered by breathing space; Northern Ireland has no equivalent. Do not present this as UK-wide. What it does: for up to 60 days it pauses most enforcement action, stops creditors contacting you about enforcing an included debt, and requires creditors to stop applying interest, fees, penalties and charges on included debts. What it is NOT: it is not a payment holiday and it is not debt write-off. Ongoing liabilities and priority bills must still be paid during the breathing space, and some creditor actions, such as court-approved enforcement, can continue. Two common confusions worth naming: council tax is included once all the year's instalments have fallen due or a reminder notice has been served, and parking tickets are NOT treated as court-imposed fines, so they are not excluded. There is no self-service route - the gate is the FCA-authorised debt adviser or the council's debt advice service, and going through one is free.

title: Tax Adviser Registration Opens For Payroll-Only Agents

figures.what: Date the registration window opened for businesses providing only third-party payroll services on behalf of clients with no other HMRC interaction
Deadline for payroll-only advisers to apply (3 months from the window opening)
Length of the registration window from the date it opens, during which you can keep interacting with HMRC
Window opening date for the next phase: financial services organisations without an agent services account
Cost of registration; it is an online application for an agent services account (ASA)

scope.who: Businesses paid to interact with HMRC on someone else's behalf about their tax affairs. The window that opened on 18 November 2026 is for businesses providing only third-party payroll services for clients, with no other HMRC interaction, that do not already hold an agent services account. HMRC states you must register even if you act for only one client, are a registered sole trader, or do not think of yourself as a tax adviser. Businesses based outside the UK must use a separate registration route.
scope.excluded: HMRC lists these as not needing to register: acting as an employer or as part of an in-house tax team, for example running payroll for your own staff; dealing with your own company group's tax affairs; giving tax advice for free, for example through a charity or helping friends or family; acting where the law requires it even if paid, for example insolvency practitioners or some pension or investment firms; responding to an HMRC request for information; developing or providing accounting or tax software, including payroll software; interacting with HMRC only on customs or import VAT; acting as a VAT representative; acting as a Northern Ireland tax representative; acting as a UK representative for Vaping Duty; acting as an intermediary for the Import One Stop Shop scheme; representing a client in appeals to a court or tribunal; dealing with business rates, council tax or property valuation. Advisers who already hold an agent services account do not register again, though HMRC may contact them between April 2027 and March 2028 to check conditions.
scope.from_when: Window opened 18 November 2026; applications must be made by midnight on 17 February 2027. In force now, not merely announced.
scope.how_to_claim: Use HMRC's online checker to confirm whether and when you must register, check you meet HMRC's registration conditions, then apply online for an agent services account. Once you have a registration number you can continue dealing with HMRC while the application is considered.

notes: This is the payroll phase of HMRC's Modernising and Mandating Tax Adviser Registration (MMTAR). It is a phased rollout: 18 May 2026 for unregistered advisers without an ASA, 18 August 2026 for those with a Self Assessment or Corporation Tax account but no ASA, 18 November 2026 for payroll-only advisers, and 31 December 2026 for financial services organisations. Common confusion: this is NOT the same as professional body membership, and it is NOT a replacement for client authorisation (64-8 or digital). It also does NOT re-register existing ASA holders. If you do not register, HMRC says it may limit your ability to act for clients and may take enforcement action including financial penalties. Anyone who has missed a window, or is new to the market, should register now. Reported on the HMRC organisation page on 18 November 2026 and covered in Agent Update issue 149 (19 November 2026). Applies UK-wide because it is an HMRC requirement, with no separate England, Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland variants, though some Northern Ireland representative roles are among the listed exemptions.

scope.who: UK financial institutions, and UK branches of non-resident financial institutions. Reporting Financial Institutions and Trustee-Documented Trusts must report whether or not they have anything to report. Covers both FATCA and CRS. Agents and group members who file on behalf of an institution are affected too.
scope.excluded: anyone who is not a financial institution — ordinary trading companies, individual taxpayers and non-financial entities have nothing to do here. Among financial institutions: Non-Reporting Financial Institutions are out of scope, meaning those in Annex II of the UK-US agreement for FATCA, and for CRS only those defined in Section VIII Paragraph B of the Standard plus Qualified Non-Profit Entities from 1 January 2026. The UK has defined no institutions under the CRS low-risk category, so that exemption route is not available here. Accounts held outside the UK are not reported to HMRC and nil returns are usually unnecessary.
scope.from_when: service closes 3pm on 15 December 2026; new service phases in from January 2027
scope.how_to_claim: the reporting obligation is mandatory, not a claim. Submit all outstanding reports, corrections and amendments before 3pm on 15 December 2026. Existing users do NOT need to register again — the migration is automatic.

notes: The practical trap is a reporting blackout: the old service dies on 15 December 2026 and the new one cannot accept reports until later in 2027, with only account management arriving in January. Corrections and amendments to earlier years must go in before the deadline or they wait. Do not tell anyone to re-register — the separate registration guidance page has not been updated for the closure and still shows a 31 December 2025 deadline, so a reader landing there gets no warning at all. The AEOI service availability page is also stale and must not be cited for the closure. HMRC may charge a penalty for late returns.

scope.who: the importer — the person in whose name, or on whose behalf, the customs declaration is made — who meets or exceeds the threshold on either test. Tax agents can submit returns but cannot register on the liable person's behalf and carry no liability.
scope.excluded: importers below £50,000 on both tests. Goods originating in the EU, EEA and Switzerland are intended to be exempt from 1 January 2027 and not to count toward the threshold, judged on origin rather than country of export — but that exemption is still only draft legislation, so keep origin evidence and keep complying meanwhile. Also out: imported scrap in the aluminium and iron and steel sectors from 1 January 2027; private individuals importing for non-commercial purposes; UK-origin goods; returned goods relief cases; temporary admission with full customs duty relief; and goods under special procedures exported before the tax point. Glass and ceramics are not among the five sectors.
scope.from_when: liability from 1 January 2027; registration due by 31 January 2028 for 2027 triggers
scope.how_to_claim: register with HMRC once a test is met, by 31 January 2028 for 2027. Keep records and origin evidence from 1 January 2027 whether or not you are liable.

notes: The old id said 'january-2027', which the legislation contradicts: SI 2026/830 substitutes 31 January 2028 for the usual 30-day registration deadline for anyone triggering in 2027. Saying 'register in January 2027' is wrong. Do not source the threshold or the exemptions from the 'work out the date' guidance page — it gives no deadline and lists no exemptions; the deadline is in the SI and the exemptions in the policy summary. Failure to notify when required attracts penalties.

title: Inheritance Tax: Business and Agricultural Property Relief from April 2026

figures.what: Individual relief allowance for 100% Agricultural Property Relief and Business Property Relief combined, on a chargeable transfer including death, from 6 April 2026. Reduced by amounts already used by chargeable transfers in the previous 7 years. Raised from the £1 million originally announced at Autumn Budget 2024.

Relief rate on qualifying agricultural or business property above the available allowance. Shares not 'listed' under HMRC's definition, such as AIM shares, get 50% only and do not use the 100% allowance.

figures.value: Transferable to a surviving spouse or civil partner
figures.what: Unused relief allowance from a late spouse or civil partner may be transferred to the deceased's estate, on death, provided a claim is made within 4 years of the survivor's death or within 6 months of the personal representatives starting their role.

Trust allowances: pre-commencement settlements get £2.5m for future relevant property charges; other relevant property settlements get an allowance when the settlor makes a qualifying chargeable transfer, capped at £2.5m across all that settlor's settlements in lifetime; special trusts £2.5m reduced by the amount used on each charge; 18-25 trusts £2.5m per qualifying beneficiary; qualifying interest in possession settlements use the life tenant's own allowance.

Gifts made before this date get unlimited 100% relief and do not use the allowance. Gifts from 30 October 2024 to 5 April 2026 fall under transitional rules; the 50% rate applies to them only if death occurs within 7 years of the gift.

scope.nation: UK (Inheritance Tax is a UK-wide tax; the manual page does not state nations separately)
scope.who: Estates and trusts holding qualifying agricultural property or business property, including unquoted shares, where relief is claimed on death, on a failed potentially exempt transfer, or on a chargeable lifetime transfer.
scope.excluded: Property that only ever qualified for 50% relief is unaffected by the allowance. AIM and other not-listed shares never use the 100% allowance and always get 50%. Value above the available allowance gets 50% only. Unused allowance cannot be passed to anyone other than a surviving spouse or civil partner. Property not meeting the relief conditions, for example an investment business, gets no relief at all.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 (transitional rules from 30 October 2024)
scope.how_to_claim: Personal representatives or trustees claim the relief on the IHT return (IHT400 and the relevant schedules). A transferred spouse allowance must be claimed within 4 years of the survivor's death or within 6 months of the personal representatives starting their role.

notes: WARNING FOR THE EVENING RUN: the gov.uk 'Summary of reforms to agricultural property relief and business property relief' guidance page still shows the original £1 million allowance and is out of date. Do NOT write £1m. The £2.5m figure comes from HMRC's Inheritance Tax Manual IHTM25510, which was read twice independently on 23 November 2026 by two researchers and shows 'Updated: 7 April 2026'. The nil-rate band, residence nil-rate band and spouse exemption are unaffected and are separate banked subjects. Not the same as the 50% relief that already applied to some shares before April 2026.

title: Double Cab Pickups: Now Treated as Cars for Benefit in Kind and Capital Allowances

figures.what: Date from which double cab pickups are assessed for income tax benefit in kind against the primary suitability test, so most are expected to be classed as cars rather than vans. The old VAT definitions of car and van are no longer used for this.

Latest date van treatment can continue for an employer who bought, leased or ordered a double cab pickup before 6 April 2025. It ends earlier on disposal or lease expiry. Reallocation to another employee of the same employer is allowed until then.

figures.value: 1 April 2025 for corporation tax, 6 April 2025 for income tax
figures.what: Capital allowances: HMRC treats double cab pickups with a payload of one tonne or more as cars from these dates, so they are not eligible for annual investment allowance or full expensing.

Capital allowances transitional rule: expenditure incurred on or after the start date but before 1 October 2025, under a contract made before the start date, keeps the old not-a-car treatment, so AIA or full expensing may still apply to it.

scope.nation: UK (HMRC income tax and corporation tax rules; the manual pages do not state nations separately)
scope.who: Employers providing double cab pickups to employees, and businesses claiming capital allowances on double cab pickups with a payload of 1 tonne or more.
scope.excluded: Vehicles bought, leased or ordered before 6 April 2025 keep van treatment for benefit in kind until disposal, lease expiry or 5 April 2029, whichever is earliest. Contracts made before 1 April or 6 April 2025 with expenditure before 1 October 2025 keep the old capital allowances treatment. A lease renewed after expiry, or a replacement vehicle, is treated as a car. Vehicle Excise Duty is not affected by this change.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2025 for benefit in kind; 1 April 2025 corporation tax and 6 April 2025 income tax for capital allowances
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. The employer reports the car benefit on P11D, or payrolls it, from the relevant date. For capital allowances the business must follow the car rules.

notes: Double cab pickups with a payload under 1 tonne were already treated as cars. Vehicle Excise Duty is unchanged by this. The VAT definition of a car no longer decides the income tax question. Nation scope is inferred from the taxes concerned, not stated on the pages read.

title: Van Benefit Charge and Van Fuel Benefit Charge 2026-27

figures.what: Flat-rate van benefit charge for 2026-27, up from £4,020 in 2025-26.
Flat-rate van fuel benefit charge for 2026-27, up from £769 in 2025-26.
Zero-emission vans have had a nil rate within the van benefit charge since 6 April 2021.

scope.nation: UK (the charge is under the Income Tax (Earnings and Pensions) Act 2003; the page does not state nations separately)
scope.who: Employees and directors with a company van available for private use, taxed through payroll or P11D, and the employers who report it.
scope.excluded: Zero-emission vans have a nil van benefit charge. Vans with no private use beyond ordinary commuting attract no charge. The van fuel charge applies only where the employer provides fuel for private use. The flat charge is not reduced for the employee's own tax band. Cars are taxed on an entirely different basis, with a separate car fuel benefit multiplier of £29,200 for 2026-27.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 (tax year 2026-27)
scope.how_to_claim: The employer reports it on P11D or payrolls the benefit; the employee claims nothing.

notes: The zero-emission nil rate is stated at source for the van benefit charge only. Do NOT state that the van FUEL charge is nil for electric vans - that was not verified. Do not confuse the van fuel charge (£798) with the car fuel benefit multiplier (£29,200). Nation scope is inferred from the Act, not stated on the page read.

title: Statutory Sick Pay Reform: No Waiting Days and No Lower Earnings Limit

figures.what: Date the Employment Rights Act 2025 SSP changes came into force - removal of the waiting period and of the lower earnings limit - for both Great Britain (ss.10, 11) and Northern Ireland (ss.12, 13). S.I. 2026/373 reg. 2 says the provisions 'come into force on 6th April 2026'. This is in force now, not announced.

figures.value: From the first full day of sickness absence
figures.what: SSP is now payable from the first day of incapacity instead of the fourth, the three waiting days having been removed. gov.uk guidance: 'No SSP is paid for waiting days before 6 April 2026'.

SSP is available to all eligible employees regardless of earnings. The lower earnings limit condition (para 2(c), Sch 11) is omitted from the Act text. gov.uk guidance: 'available to all eligible employees regardless of their earnings'.

figures.value: 80% of normal weekly earnings, or the flat rate, whichever is lower
figures.what: The weekly SSP amount is the lower of the flat rate and 80% of the employee's normal weekly earnings. The £118.75 appearing in the Act's amending text is a superseded rate and must not be quoted as current.
Flat weekly SSP rate that caps the 80% calculation, per gov.uk guidance. The regulations also use £123.25 for the transitional group.

scope.nation: Great Britain and Northern Ireland - parallel provisions, ss.10-11 for GB and ss.12-13 for NI, both commenced on 6 April 2026 by S.I. 2026/373
scope.who: Eligible employees who are incapable of work because of sickness, now with no earnings floor and no waiting days.
scope.excluded: Employees who received Employment and Support Allowance in the last 85 days are not eligible for SSP, per the gov.uk guidance. Only 'eligible employees' qualify and the Act refers to employees, so the self-employed are not covered. Some absences that began before 6 April 2026 remain under transitional rules: an absence starting on or before 21 September 2025 that ran unbroken to 5 April 2026 stays ineligible until the employee has returned to work for at least 8 weeks.
scope.from_when: in force now, since 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: The employee tells the employer, who pays SSP through payroll if the employee is eligible. Waiting days are no longer unpaid.

notes: Do NOT describe this as announced or upcoming - it has been in force since 6 April 2026. The 80% figure is a ceiling: pay is the LOWER of 80% of normal weekly earnings and the flat rate, so higher earners still get only the flat rate. Transitional rule per gov.uk: existing SSP recipients earning between £125 and £154.05 a week keep the flat rate where 80% of average weekly earnings would reduce it, until they return to work or entitlement ends. The 2025 SSP factsheet called 6 April 2026 'expected' and is superseded by the S.I. The gov.uk guidance page does not itself state nations; the GB and NI scope comes from S.I. 2026/373 and the Act. Cross-check the £123.25 against the existing statutory-sick-pay entry before publishing both.

scope.excluded: Businesses that have manufactured or imported under 10 tonnes in the last 12 months, and do not expect to reach 10 tonnes in the next 30 days, do not need to register. Packaging components containing 30% or more recycled plastic are not taxed.

title: How Long HMRC Can Open An Enquiry Into Your Self Assessment Return

figures.what: the enquiry window where the return is filed on or before the filing date: HMRC's written notice of enquiry must be given within 12 months of the date the return was actually delivered (for 2007-08 and later years), not 12 months from the 31 January filing date

figures.value: quarter day after the first anniversary of filing
figures.what: the enquiry window where the return is filed late, after the filing date - HMRC gets until the next quarter day following the first anniversary of the day the return was delivered
the four statutory quarter days used to set the end of the enquiry window on a late-filed return
under section 9A(3) TMA 1970 only one notice of enquiry may be issued in respect of any one tax return or amendment

the only condition HMRC must satisfy before opening an enquiry is giving the taxpayer written notice of the intention to enquire; HMRC needs no reason or suspicion, and the right applies to any return

scope.who: Anyone who delivers a Self Assessment tax return under section 8 TMA 1970 - the self-employed, landlords, company directors who file, partners, and anyone filing for capital gains or the High Income Child Benefit Charge. The window applies to the original return and to any later amendment the taxpayer makes, and it applies even where HMRC rather than the taxpayer calculated the tax.
scope.excluded: Taxpayers who file LATE do not get the clean 12-month window - theirs runs on to the next quarter day after the first anniversary of filing, which can give HMRC up to roughly 15 months. Someone who never files at all gets no enquiry window, because there is no return to enquire into: HMRC uses a determination instead. And closing the window does NOT make anyone safe - it is not a 12-month amnesty. Where the window has elapsed HMRC can still raise a discovery assessment outside it, and a taxpayer who amends a return re-opens a window on that amendment. Partnerships are outside section 9A itself: a partnership return is enquired into under section 12AC, not section 9A.
scope.from_when: Rules for 2007-08 and later tax years. Earlier years (up to and including 2006-07) ran the 12 months from the filing date rather than the date of delivery.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim - the window runs automatically. The practical consequence for the taxpayer is a date to diary: file the 2025-26 return early, say in June 2026, and HMRC's right to enquire expires 12 months later; file it on 31 January 2027 and HMRC has until 31 January 2028. HMRC must notify any enquiry in writing, so a return is final once the window passes and no written notice has arrived. HMRC is under no obligation to confirm a return has been accepted.

notes: SUBSTITUTED SUBJECT - the five Self Assessment subjects requested for this run were all already in the bank (see report). This one is genuinely absent and is the most useful adjacent point for the 31 January 2027 deadline, because it is the one real reward for filing early: filing in June rather than on 31 January shortens HMRC's enquiry window by about seven months. UK-wide and reserved - identical in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Two confusions to avoid. (1) The 12 months runs from the date the return was DELIVERED, not from 31 January - this changed for 2007-08 onwards and older guidance still gets it wrong. (2) An enquiry window is not the same as the record-keeping period, the four-year overpayment relief limit, or the discovery assessment time limits, which are longer and are what applies once the enquiry window has shut. Source is the HMRC Self Assessment Manual and the Self Assessment legal framework manual rather than a public guidance page, because the public pages do not state the quarter-day rule; SAM31100 was last updated 2 November 2026 and SALF403 on 13 October 2026. recheck_after is set to the start of the next tax year because the rule is statutory and only moves with legislation.

title: Reporting PAYE When You Pay Staff Early At Christmas

figures.value: the normal or contractual payment date
figures.what: the date an employer must enter as the payment date on the Full Payment Submission when staff are paid early over Christmas - NOT the earlier date the money actually left the account
HMRC's own worked example: pay run made on 19 December but contractual pay date 31 December must be reported as 31 December

figures.value: on or before the contractual payment date
figures.what: when the FPS itself must be sent - so an FPS showing 31 December must be filed on or before 31 December

scope.who: Employers operating PAYE who bring the December pay date forward - typically because the business closes over the festive period
scope.excluded: Employers who pay on their normal contractual date in December have nothing to change - the easement only applies where the pay date is brought forward. It does not apply to a permanent change of pay date (if the contractual pay date itself has changed, the new date is reported). It is not a relief from any tax or NIC: the amounts reported are unchanged, only the date field.
scope.from_when: A permanent easement on Real Time Information reporting, restated in the October 2026 Employer Bulletin for the December 2026 pay runs
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim or apply for. The employer simply enters the normal contractual payment date in the payment date field of the FPS and submits on or before that date.

notes: This is the single most common December payroll error and it costs employees money, not the employer. Reporting the early actual date can push two months' pay into one Universal Credit assessment period, cutting or wiping out that month's award and affecting future entitlement. HMRC's reason for the easement is expressly to protect eligibility for income-based benefits such as Universal Credit. It is NOT an extension of the PAYE payment deadline - the tax and NIC are still due by the normal 22nd (electronic) date for the tax month. UK-wide: PAYE and Universal Credit both operate across all four nations, so there is no Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland variation here.

title: VAT Payments On Account For Large Businesses

figures.what: the VAT owed in any period of 12 months or less that forces a quarterly-return business into the payments on account regime
the size of each interim payment on account

figures.value: last working day of the second and third months of each VAT quarter
figures.what: the due dates for the two interim payments on account in each quarter, regardless of the business's own period end date
the usual 7 extra calendar days for electronic VAT payment does NOT apply to payments on account - cleared funds must reach HMRC by the due date
the total annual VAT liability for a completed year at which a business may write to HMRC asking to leave the regime
the delay before HMRC removes a business whose liability in the reference year has fallen below £2.3 million

scope.who: VAT-registered businesses filing quarterly returns whose VAT liability exceeds £2.3 million in any 12 months or less. HMRC sets the amount from a reference year ending in September, October or November depending on the return stagger.
scope.excluded: Businesses whose VAT liability is £2.3 million or less are not in the regime. Businesses that file monthly VAT returns are outside it, and a business in the regime can switch to monthly returns or to paying its actual monthly liability instead. Businesses whose completed-year liability falls below £1.8 million can apply to be removed, but removal is not automatic - they must write to HMRC.
scope.from_when: Long-standing regime; the £2.3 million entry and £1.8 million exit figures are those on the guidance as read on 24 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim - HMRC writes to the business telling it the regime applies and the amount of each interim payment. To leave the regime below £1.8 million, or to switch to actual monthly payments or monthly returns, the business must write to HMRC.

notes: Matters right now because the reference year for the 2026 recalculation ends in September, October or November, so businesses on a November stagger have their interim payments reset off the year just ending. The trap is the loss of the usual seven extra days for electronic payment: a payment on account is late if cleared funds do not reach HMRC by the last working day of the month, even though the balancing payment on the same VAT account still follows the normal return due date. 'Last working day' means the payment must be initiated earlier still - Faster Payments aside, Bacs takes three working days. This is NOT the same thing as Self Assessment payments on account (banked separately) and not the VAT Annual Accounting Scheme, which is for small businesses. UK-wide, as VAT is reserved to Westminster; no Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland variation.

title: Plastic Packaging Tax Return And Payment Deadlines

figures.value: last working day of the month following the end of the accounting period
figures.what: the deadline for both submitting the Plastic Packaging Tax return and paying the tax due

figures.value: 1 April to 30 June, 1 July to 30 September, 1 October to 31 December, 1 January to 31 March
figures.what: the four fixed Plastic Packaging Tax accounting periods - returns are filed four times a year
the amount of finished plastic packaging components manufactured in or imported into the UK that creates a liability to register, measured over the next 30 days or the last 12 months
the time allowed to register from the date the 10-tonne threshold was met or exceeded

scope.who: Businesses registered for Plastic Packaging Tax because they manufacture in or import into the UK 10 tonnes or more of finished plastic packaging components in a 12-month period, or expect to within the next 30 days. A group representative member files one return and one payment covering group totals.
scope.excluded: Businesses manufacturing or importing less than 10 tonnes of finished plastic packaging components a year do not have to register and file no returns - but they should keep records evidencing that they are under the threshold. Individual members of a registered group do not file their own returns; the appointed representative member files for all of them. Note that packaging which is itself exempt from the charge still counts towards the 10-tonne registration threshold, so being under the charge is not the same as being under the threshold.
scope.from_when: Accounting periods and deadline as on the guidance read 24 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: File online through the Plastic Packaging Tax service and pay by the same deadline. Registration must be done within 30 days of meeting the threshold.

notes: In the current window this bites on the 1 October to 31 December 2026 period: the return and payment fall due on the last working day of January 2027, which lands in the same week as the Self Assessment deadline. 'Last working day' is not 'last day of the month' - where the month end falls on a weekend the deadline moves BACKWARD to the preceding working day, not forward, so the practical date in January 2027 is earlier than the 31st. The 10-tonne test is a registration threshold, not a charging threshold: packaging containing 30% or more recycled plastic and other exempt categories are not charged but must still be counted when testing the 10 tonnes, which is the usual reason a business discovers late that it should have registered. UK-wide - Plastic Packaging Tax is a UK tax with no Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland variation, though imports into Northern Ireland follow the same UK rules.

title: Re-Enrolment And The Re-Declaration Of Compliance

figures.what: how often an employer must run automatic enrolment re-enrolment and complete a re-declaration of compliance

figures.value: within 5 months of the third anniversary
figures.what: the re-declaration of compliance deadline - five calendar months from the third anniversary of the employer's duties start date (or, for later cycles, of the previous re-enrolment date)

figures.value: 6-month window: 3 months before to 3 months after
figures.what: the period around the third anniversary within which the employer may choose its own re-enrolment date

figures.value: duties start date of 1 June 2020 gives a deadline of 31 October 2023
figures.what: The Pensions Regulator's own worked example of the five-month re-declaration deadline

scope.who: Every employer with automatic enrolment duties, on each three-year cycle. The re-declaration must be completed even by employers who find they have no staff to put back into the scheme.
scope.excluded: Staff who do not meet the age and earnings criteria at the re-enrolment date are not put back in and the employer does nothing further with them until the next cycle. For a director who meets the criteria, and for a worker who leaves before the process is finished, re-enrolment is the employer's choice, not a duty. Employers whose duties start date (or last re-enrolment date) is less than three years ago have no re-declaration due yet. The deadline is not altered by the employer having chosen a different date to assess its staff.
scope.from_when: Deadline rule as on The Pensions Regulator's guidance read 24 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Complete the re-declaration of compliance online through The Pensions Regulator's service. Legal responsibility stays with the employer even where a payroll bureau or adviser files it.

notes: The re-declaration is a filing obligation in its own right and the one most often missed, because the employer has already done the pension work and assumes the paperwork follows automatically - it does not. The Pensions Regulator states that a late or inaccurate re-declaration may lead to fines; it does not publish the penalty amounts on this page, so no figure is given here. The two dates are different and both matter: the re-enrolment DATE can be chosen anywhere in a six-month window around the third anniversary, but the re-declaration DEADLINE always runs five months from the third anniversary itself and does not move with the chosen date. UK-wide: automatic enrolment duties are mirrored in Northern Ireland legislation and The Pensions Regulator covers all four nations, so there is no national variation. This is NOT the same as the original declaration of compliance made when duties first started.

title: Charity Annual Return Deadline

figures.value: within 10 months of the end of your financial year
figures.what: the deadline for sending a registered charity's annual return to the Charity Commission
the annual income above which a registered charity must send a full annual return

scope.who: Charities registered with the Charity Commission for England and Wales: those with income over £10,000, and every charitable incorporated organisation (CIO) whatever its income
scope.excluded: Registered charities with income of £10,000 or less that are NOT charitable incorporated organisations do not have to send a full annual return - but they must still report their total income and expenditure through the same service. Charities registered in Scotland follow OSCR's rules and charities registered in Northern Ireland follow those of the Charity Commission for Northern Ireland; neither files this return.

Trustees routinely assume the charity deadline follows the Companies House nine-month rule or the Corporation Tax twelve-month rule; it does neither. A charitable company must file BOTH its accounts at Companies House and its annual return at the Charity Commission, to two different deadlines. The annual return is separate from the trustees' annual report and accounts, which charities over the audit or examination thresholds must also attach. Nation differences are real and complete: Scotland's regulator is OSCR and Northern Ireland's is CCNI, each with its own return and its own deadline, and a charity registered in Scotland or Northern Ireland does not use this service at all.

title: Inheritance Tax Payment And IHT400 Deadlines

figures.value: within 12 months of the person dying
figures.what: the deadline for submitting form IHT400, the Inheritance Tax account
excepted estate limit where the unused Inheritance Tax threshold of a spouse or civil partner who died first is transferred
excepted estate limit where everything is left to a UK-resident spouse or civil partner, or to a qualifying charity
excepted estate limit for UK assets where the person was living permanently outside the UK (foreign domiciliary)

figures.value: over £250,000 given away in the 7 years before death
figures.what: one of the triggers that forces full details (IHT400) even where the estate would otherwise be excepted
another trigger that forces full details even where the estate would otherwise be excepted

scope.who: Personal representatives - the executors or administrators - of an estate where Inheritance Tax is due or where HMRC requires full details of the estate
scope.excluded: Personal representatives of an excepted estate need not send full details at all. An estate is usually excepted where its value is below the current Inheritance Tax threshold; or is £650,000 or less with a transferred unused threshold from a spouse or civil partner who died first; or everything passes to a UK-resident spouse or civil partner or a qualifying charity and the estate is worth less than £3 million; or the person was a foreign domiciliary with UK assets of £150,000 or less. Even then full details ARE required if any trigger applies - more than £250,000 given away in the 7 years before death, foreign assets over £100,000, or an estate over £3 million. scope.from_when: Deadlines and excepted estate limits as on GOV.UK read 24 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Submit form IHT400 to HMRC within 12 months of death, and before applying for probate if probate is needed. Pay the tax by the end of the sixth month after death; interest runs from that point. HMRC calculates any interest once the IHT400 is processed.

notes: The two deadlines are six months apart and that gap is the whole problem: the tax is due at six months but the account that works out how much is not due until twelve, so personal representatives must pay on an estimate or accrue interest. HMRC says a financial penalty may apply for missing the deadline without a reasonable excuse; no penalty figure is published on this page so none is given here. Interest rates are not on this page either - they follow HMRC's published late payment rate. Note the practical sequencing: IHT400 must normally be submitted before a probate application, and tax on non-instalment assets generally has to be paid before probate issues, which is why grants on credit and the ten-year instalment option exist. Nation difference to state: in Scotland the grant is confirmation rather than probate and is obtained through the sheriff court, and Northern Ireland has its own probate office - but the Inheritance Tax deadlines themselves are identical across all four nations, as IHT is a UK-wide tax. These deadlines are separate from the banked nil-rate-band and seven-year-gift subjects.

title: Pension Tax Allowance: Income Tax Reduction For Eligible Pensioners From April 2027

figures.what: the rate applied to the amount by which the full new State Pension for the tax year exceeds the Personal Allowance, to give the Pension Tax Allowance (a tax reduction, not an allowance against income)
rate at which the reduction is tapered away where total income exceeds the full new State Pension amount, until it reaches nil
date the reduction takes effect; it is legislated for tax years 2027-28, 2028-29 and 2029-30
the step of the Income Tax calculation at which the reduction is applied

scope.who: Individuals above State Pension age. Full reduction where total income is up to the full new State Pension amount. Eligibility turns on age and total income from any source, so a person who does not actually receive the State Pension (private pension, employment or self-employment income only) can still qualify.
scope.excluded: Anyone below State Pension age; anyone whose total income is above the full new State Pension plus the taper range, where the reduction is fully withdrawn; and anyone with no Income Tax liability to set it against, because the reduction cannot exceed total tax liability and so never produces a repayment or cash payment.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2027 (tax year 2027-28)
scope.how_to_claim: No claim. HMRC applies it automatically each year. For PAYE pensioners it comes through a tax code change; Self Assessment filers get it in their usual return. gov.uk states eligible individuals will not need to contact HMRC or make a claim.

notes: Announced at Budget 2026 (28 October 2026); policy paper published 28 October 2026, updated 29 October 2026. It is a TAX REDUCER at step 6 of the Income Tax calculation, NOT an increase in the Personal Allowance and NOT a benefit payment - it cannot create a refund. The cash value depends on the full new State Pension figure for the year, which gov.uk does not state on this page, so do not quote a pounds figure. The government has said it will uprate the allowance in line with the new State Pension across this Parliament. Applies across the UK: Scottish and Welsh taxpayers are in scope because this is a reduction in the UK Income Tax calculation, but Scottish rates and bands still apply to their income. To be legislated in Finance Bill 2026, so detail can still move.

title: CGT Founders' Relief — proposed, not yet law

figures.what: proposed CGT rate under Founders' Relief, against 18% and 24% on share gains now
proposed lifetime limit of eligible gains per individual, reduced by any BADR and Investors' Relief claimed from 6 April 2027
ordinary share capital the founder must have held when the trade, or preparation for it, began
minimum period the shares must be held before disposal
minimum UK residence before disposal, under the Statutory Residence Test
company scale test for the accounting period ending in the year before disposal
25% compound turnover growth, 25% compound employee growth, or at least £1.5m qualifying R&D with relief claimed
proposed commencement, for qualifying disposals on or after that date
closing date of the technical consultation
HMRC's own estimate of how many will be eligible, across about 400 businesses
BADR lifetime limit from 6 April 2027, cut from £1,000,000 on the same date

scope.who: proposed for individuals only who founded the company: held 25% of ordinary share capital when the trade began, held the shares at least 5 years, UK resident at least 5 continuous tax years, with the company a trading company within UK Corporation Tax meeting the scale and growth tests. More than one founder of the same company could claim.
scope.excluded: anyone who is not an individual, so no companies, trusts or personal representatives; anyone below 25% when the trade began, which rules out later investors and most employee shareholders; anyone holding under 5 years; anyone not UK resident for 5 continuous tax years; companies in the trades excluded from EIS, such as dealing in land, financial services and property development; companies with substantial non-trading activity; companies that have changed the nature of their trade; companies below £10m turnover or below 15 qualifying employees, where directors, contract workers and agency workers do not count toward the employee test; companies meeting fewer than 2 of the 3 growth tests. Above all: nobody gets it yet, because it is not law.
scope.from_when: proposed for disposals on or after 6 April 2027
scope.how_to_claim: would be claimed on the Self Assessment return using a supplementary form, if enacted

notes: NOT LAW. This is a Budget 2026 announcement under technical consultation that does not even close until 30 November 2026, to be legislated by amendments to Finance Bill 2026-27. No draft clauses are published and the rules can still change. Any post treating it as settled April 2027 law is wrong — say 'proposed'. It is also far narrower than readers will assume: HMRC expects about 600 people a year. And it does not stack cleanly on the existing reliefs: the £10m limit is reduced by BADR and Investors' Relief claims, while BADR's own lifetime limit falls from £1m to £500,000 on the very same date.

title: HMRC Agent Authorisation: ARN Required From 19 November 2026 And Six-Month Rule For Paper 64-8

figures.what: date from which HMRC may not be able to discuss a client's record with an agent who does not give their agent reference number (ARN) or application reference - applies by phone, post, online and email
date from which paper form 64-8 must include the date of the client's signature
maximum period between the client's signature date and HMRC receiving the paper 64-8; forms outside it are rejected with a letter explaining why
the period within which HMRC targets clearing 80% of correspondence (the 'Where's my reply' tool target)

scope.who: Tax agents and accountants contacting HMRC about a client's record, and anyone submitting a paper form 64-8 to authorise an agent. Both changes are HMRC-wide and cover contact by phone, post, online and email.
scope.excluded: Taxpayers dealing with HMRC on their own behalf, with no agent - they do not need an ARN and do not file a 64-8. The six-month rule bites on PAPER 64-8 forms, not on digital authorisation through the agent services account. Agents who have not yet been issued an ARN use their application reference instead.
scope.from_when: ARN requirement from 19 November 2026; dated-signature and six-month receipt rule for paper 64-8 from 2 December 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Quote the ARN or application reference on every contact with HMRC about a client. For paper 64-8, have the client date their signature and get the form to HMRC within six months of that date, or use digital authorisation via the agent services account instead.

notes: Source is HMRC Agent Update issue 149, published 19 November 2026 - the current issue as at 24 November 2026. The six-month rule is a NEW hard stop: a 64-8 signed in, say, March and posted in October will be rejected outright, not just queried. The ARN change is already live. This is an administrative change only - it does not alter what an authorised agent can do once authorisation is in place. Recheck when Agent Update 150 is published, and after the 2 December 2026 start date in case HMRC amends the guidance.

title: Making Tax Digital For Income Tax: What You Owe Can Be Split Across Two Accounts For 31 January 2027

figures.what: date HMRC began writing to customers required to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax in 2026-27
the payment date for which amounts may appear in two separate places: the 2025-26 balancing payment and the first payment on account for 2026-27
number of accounts that must both be checked - the Self Assessment statement (for amounts marked 'transferred to digital') and the MTD account under 'what you owe'
date from which Making Tax Digital for Income Tax applied

scope.who: Individuals who moved onto Making Tax Digital for Income Tax from 6 April 2026, and their agents. HMRC states that for payments due by 31 January 2027 the figures can be split between the Self Assessment statement and the MTD account, so both must be checked and the amounts added together.
scope.excluded: Anyone not yet within Making Tax Digital for Income Tax - their 31 January 2027 position shows on the Self Assessment statement alone. Also excluded: companies (Corporation Tax is not in MTD for Income Tax), and anyone whose income is taxed only through PAYE with no Self Assessment requirement.
scope.from_when: HMRC letters from 9 November 2026; the split affects the payment due by 31 January 2027
scope.how_to_claim: No claim. Check the client's Self Assessment statement for amounts marked 'transferred to digital', then check the MTD account under 'what you owe', and confirm every amount has been found before paying.

notes: Source is HMRC Agent Update issue 149, published 19 November 2026. This is a PRESENTATION problem, not a tax change: HMRC says moving to MTD for Income Tax does not change how much is owed or when it must be paid. The risk is underpaying on 31 January 2027 because only one of the two accounts was checked, which would then attract late-payment interest and penalties. Distinct from the MTD qualifying-income thresholds and from the MTD penalty regime. Recheck straight after 31 January 2027, when HMRC's dual-account display is expected to be resolved.

title: Putting The Winter Fuel Payment On A Self Assessment Return When Income Is Over £35,000

figures.what: the level of total income above which the Winter Fuel Payment or Pension Age Winter Heating Payment must be included on the Self Assessment return for the year in which it was received
the return on which a payment received in winter 2025 belongs - the year of receipt, not the year of claim

scope.who: Self Assessment filers who received a Winter Fuel Payment or, in Scotland, a Pension Age Winter Heating Payment, and whose total income for that tax year was over £35,000. The payment goes on the return for the tax year in which it was received.
scope.excluded: Anyone whose total income for the year was £35,000 or less - they keep the payment in full and nothing goes on a return. Anyone who did not receive the payment at all. Anyone outside Self Assessment, whose recovery is handled through PAYE rather than a return.
scope.from_when: Applies to the 2025-26 return, due 31 January 2027, for payments received in winter 2025
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim - a reporting duty. In HMRC's online service the payment may be pre-populated as a charge; HMRC says you must check whether it is showing and include it if it is not.
scope.nation_note: Scotland pays the Pension Age Winter Heating Payment instead of the Winter Fuel Payment; HMRC treats both the same way for this purpose.

notes: Source is HMRC Agent Update issue 149, published 19 November 2026. This is the REPORTING side, not the payment itself: the payment is made automatically by DWP or Social Security Scotland, and this entry is about getting it onto the tax return where income exceeded £35,000. The trap HMRC flags is that the pre-population is not reliable - if the charge is missing from the online return the filer must add it, and an omission is an inaccurate return. The £35,000 is tested on TOTAL income for the year, from all sources, not on pension income alone. Recheck after 31 January 2027 and again for the 2026-27 return, when the £35,000 threshold could be uprated.

title: Companies House Identity Verification: Enforcement And The End Of March 2027 Compliance Deadline

figures.what: Companies House target date by which all companies must either meet the identity verification requirements or be on a compliance or enforcement pathway
number of enforcement and compliance actions Companies House is targeting by 31 March 2027
actions already taken between 1 April and 31 October 2026, affecting 73,000 corporate bodies
the aggravated fine increase recorded where identity verification failure was an aggravating factor in prosecutions for failure to file a confirmation statement (131 convictions)
appointments verified as at 11 November 2026 - 7.32 million director, 4.54 million PSC and 135,000 LLP member appointments; 85.55% of appointments due
share of companies that have met the requirements linked to their confirmation statement; 11.4% are on a compliance or enforcement pathway

the window for existing PSCs who are not directors to verify - within 14 days of the start of their birth month; existing PSCs who are also directors verify within 14 days of the confirmation statement due date; new PSCs within 14 days of incorporation or of notification
suspicious filings prevented, including over 2,700 suspicious incorporations

scope.who: UK companies and LLPs on the Companies House register, their directors, LLP members and people with significant control. Mandatory identity verification began 18 November 2025 and was phased in over 12 months, with existing directors verifying alongside confirmation statements due between 18 November 2025 and 17 November 2026. Enforcement now in use includes financial penalty warning letters (started July 2026), prosecution, director disqualification, and defaulting or redacting register addresses.
scope.excluded: Entities not on the Companies House register - sole traders and unincorporated partnerships have no company, no directors and no PSCs, so no verification duty. Shareholders who are not directors and do not meet a PSC test are not required to verify. Companies that have already completed verification for all appointments are outside the enforcement pathway. Registered overseas entities are dealt with under the separate Register of Overseas Entities regime.
scope.from_when: Duty live since 18 November 2025; compliance or enforcement pathway for every company targeted by the end of March 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Verify identity directly with Companies House or through an authorised corporate service provider, then connect the verified identity to each appointment. Verification is not done for you.

notes: News story published 18 November 2026, with data correct as at 11 November 2026 - this is the enforcement and progress position, distinct from the underlying verification duty itself. The headline for clients is that the voluntary phase is over: around 90% of live companies have verified, warning letters for financial penalties are already going out, the Insolvency Service secured its first convictions and disqualifications in September 2026, and Companies House intends every remaining company to be on a compliance or enforcement pathway by the end of March 2027. The PSC birth-month rule catches non-director PSCs who assume the confirmation statement date covers them - it does not. Companies House also reported 185,900 registered office addresses, 147,800 officer addresses and 117,500 PSC addresses defaulted, 113,800 pieces of information redacted from incorporation documents, over 75,000 personal data corrections and 14,000 PSC address inaccuracies identified, and put the measure's value at £210 million to £400 million a year.

title: VAT E-Invoicing Becomes Mandatory On 1 April 2029

figures.what: date from which VAT-registered persons must be able to issue and receive VAT invoices as e-invoices, unless an exemption applies
the consultation on technical standards; primary legislation in Finance Bill 2026 is also expected to become law in Spring 2027
window in which key requirements are confirmed and published - scope, exclusions, standards, guidance, business identifiers and service-provider requirements
date by which the detail of the digitally excluded exemption, and VAT guidance, are due; guidance for specific groups is due by the end of 2027

the preparation window - government communications campaign, business and software testing and onboarding; readiness testing Summer 2028, infrastructure operational Winter 2028, software provider accreditation complete by 1 April 2029

scope.who: VAT-registered persons - companies, sole traders, partnerships, Scottish partnerships, charities and public or government bodies registered for VAT. The obligation bites when making a taxable supply to another VAT-registered person in the UK. Non-established taxable persons are treated the same as UK-based entities.
scope.excluded: Businesses and other entities NOT registered for VAT, including those below the registration threshold who choose not to register - they may adopt e-invoicing voluntarily but are not obliged to. Sales to consumers (B2C), where no VAT invoice is required. Exempt, zero-rated and out-of-scope transactions where no VAT invoice is required. Cross-border transactions, where e-invoices are not required though they may be agreed with overseas customers. Digitally excluded VAT-registered persons, for whom an exemption is being developed modelled on the MTD for VAT criteria, with detail due by April 2028.
scope.from_when: 1 April 2029
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim. Affected businesses must have software and processes able to issue and receive e-invoices to the mandated standard by 1 April 2029. The digitally excluded exemption route is not yet defined.
scope.nation_note: VAT is a UK-wide tax, so this applies identically in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

notes: Roadmap published 28 October 2026 alongside Budget 2026 and updated 11 November 2026. The mandate date firmed up from the earlier 'from 2029' in the November 2025 consultation response to a specific 1 April 2029. Real-time reporting is NOT part of the 2029 mandate - the government will consider it separately once e-invoicing is established. There is NO turnover or invoice-volume threshold: the test is VAT registration plus a taxable supply to another VAT-registered person. Much of the detail (standards, exclusions, the digitally excluded exemption) is still open and is only due to be confirmed between October 2027 and April 2028; secondary legislation may not conclude until Autumn 2028 or early 2029, so treat everything except the 1 April 2029 date as provisional. Recheck after the Spring 2027 technical standards consultation.

title: Tax Relief On Professional Fees And Subscriptions (HMRC List 3)

figures.value: current tax year + 4 previous tax years
figures.what: the window in which an employee can claim tax relief for professional membership fees and approved subscriptions
relief available on life membership subscriptions - HMRC states you cannot claim tax relief on life membership subscriptions

the published HMRC list of approved professional organisations and learned societies; only bodies on this list qualify, and a 'J' in brackets after a body's name means annual subscriptions to its journals also qualify

scope.who: Employees who pay professional membership fees they must pay to be able to do their job, or annual subscriptions to a professional body or learned society on HMRC's List 3 where membership is relevant to the job. Relief is given at the employee's marginal rate of Income Tax.
scope.excluded: Anyone whose employer paid the fee or subscription (you cannot claim for fees you have not paid yourself); anyone paying a life membership subscription; anyone whose body is NOT on HMRC's approved List 3; some List 3 entries carry their own restriction (e.g. relief restricted to a stated percentage of the annual subscription) or an end date, after which no relief is due.
scope.from_when: Ongoing. Each List 3 entry carries its own 'with effect from' date, and some carry an end date.
scope.how_to_claim: Check the body is on List 3, then use the 'Check if you can claim tax relief for job expenses' service on GOV.UK (tax.service.gov.uk). Evidence of payment (receipts or equivalent) must be sent. If you file a Self Assessment return you must claim through the return instead.

notes: The body must be on List 3 - membership of a trade union or a body that is merely useful is not enough. The List 3 page is updated through the year, so a body can be added or have relief withdrawn mid-year (the page's update log shows one body's relief available only up to 5 April 2026). Not the same as the flat rate expenses for uniforms and tools. Income tax rates differ for Scottish and Welsh taxpayers, so the cash value of the same subscription differs by nation even though the relief itself is UK-wide.

title: Reclaiming Overpaid Tax On Savings Interest And PPI Payouts (Form R40)

figures.what: maximum gross income from savings and investments for a tax year for which form R40 may be used (above this a tax return is required)
maximum net income from land and property for a tax year for which form R40 may be used (gross land and property income must also be £10,000 or less)

figures.value: current tax year + 4 previous tax years
figures.what: the period an R40 repayment claim can cover; a separate claim is needed for each tax year
the overpayment relief time limit - claims must be made within 4 years after the end of the relevant tax year or accounting period

scope.who: People who had Income Tax deducted at source from savings or investment income (including the interest element of a PPI or similar compensation payout) and whose income means some or all of that tax should not have been paid. Claim on form R40, started online.
scope.excluded: Anyone registered for Self Assessment, or whose income exceeds the R40 limits - they must claim on a tax return, not an R40; people living outside the UK (a different form applies); anyone claiming for another person, who must claim by post rather than online; any year more than 4 years after the end of the relevant tax year, which is out of time under the overpayment relief limit.
scope.from_when: Current rules; HMRC removed its separate PPI guidance in February 2025 and replaced it with guidance on claiming tax back on interest.
scope.how_to_claim: Start the claim online from the R40 page on GOV.UK. For interest claims you must show the tax paid with evidence from the paying company, posted to Pay As You Earn, HM Revenue and Customs, BX9 1AS. For other repayment types do not send evidence; HMRC will ask if needed.

notes: It is the interest element of a PPI payout that is taxed, not the refunded premiums - the lender's statement shows the tax deducted. The R40 is not a route for anyone in Self Assessment: those claims go on the return, or (for closed years) as a standalone overpayment relief claim within 4 years of the end of the tax year. UK-wide, but a Scottish or Welsh taxpayer's repayment is worked out on their own nation's income tax rates. Deadline to flag: claims for 2022-23 must be made by 5 April 2027.

title: Seafarers' Earnings Deduction: 100% Relief On Pay Earned At Sea

figures.value: 100% of earnings attributable to the eligible period
figures.what: the deduction allowed - ITEPA 2003 s.379(1) states the deduction 'is allowed from the amount of the earnings from the employment attributable to the eligible period' and 'is equal to that amount'

the eligible period required - ITEPA 2003 s.378(2) defines an eligible period as 'a period consisting of at least 365 days'; HMRC's guidance states that if the eligible period is under 365 days the deduction is not due

scope.who: Employees who perform their employment duties on a ship, who are resident in the UK (or resident for tax purposes in an EEA State other than the UK), and who have an eligible period of at least 365 days mainly made up of days of absence from the UK. Royal Fleet Auxiliary Service employees can qualify.
scope.excluded: Crown employees - ITEPA 2003 s.384(1) defines seafarer employment as 'an employment (other than Crown employment)', so a Royal Navy sailor cannot claim; anyone working on an offshore installation, because s.385 states that 'ship' does not include an offshore installation (fixed and floating production platforms, floating storage units, mobile offshore drilling units and flotels are excluded, including while the structure is moving, temporarily in other use or temporarily out of use); anyone who was not UK resident and not resident in an EEA State other than the UK; anyone whose eligible period is under 365 days; and anyone who was absent from the UK on a day but not absent at the end of that day (s.378(4)). Where UK duties are performed, s.380 can limit the deduction to a reasonable proportion of total earnings.
scope.from_when: Current law (ITEPA 2003 Part 5 Chapter 6). EEA residents who are not UK resident can claim on form R43M(SED) from the 2011-12 tax year.
scope.how_to_claim: UK residents: register for Self Assessment, use working sheet HS205 to establish the eligible period, enter the deduction in box 11 on page Ai 2 of the Additional information pages and the names of the ships in box 19 of the SA100. Keep the discharge book and supporting documents but do not send them. Non-UK EEA residents use form R43M(SED). HMRC publishes a per-year claim deadline table (e.g. 2018-19 claims by 5 April 2023).

notes: 'Ship' is not defined in tax law, but an offshore installation is expressly not a ship - this is what rules out most oil and gas rig workers, who often assume they qualify. The 365 days do not have to be one continuous voyage; a combined period can count, but the day-counting rules in s.378 are strict (absence is tested at the end of the day). UK-wide, and because it is a deduction from earnings the cash value follows the claimant's own nation's income tax rates (Scottish and Welsh taxpayers included).

title: Mileage Relief For Motorcycles, Bicycles And Carrying Passengers

figures.what: approved mileage allowance payment rate for motorcycles, 2026-27, with no reduction after 10,000 miles
approved mileage allowance payment rate for bicycles, 2026-27, with no reduction after 10,000 miles
the approved passenger payment rate an employer may pay tax free for carrying a fellow employee on a business journey
approved mileage allowance payment rates for cars and vans for 2026-27 (45p for the first 10,000 miles applied before 6 April 2026)

figures.value: current tax year + 4 previous tax years
figures.what: the window for claiming mileage allowance relief where the employer paid less than the approved amount

scope.who: Employees who use their own motorcycle or bicycle for business journeys can claim relief at 24p or 20p a mile, less anything the employer pays towards the cost. Employers may pay 5p per passenger per business mile tax free when an employee carries a fellow employee.
scope.excluded: Passenger payments carry NO tax relief for the employee: GOV.UK states 'there is no relief if you receive less than 5p or nothing at all', so an employee whose employer pays nothing for carrying colleagues cannot claim anything; ordinary commuting is excluded - the relief 'does not include travelling to and from your work, unless it's a temporary place of work'; an employee claiming the mileage rates for their own vehicle cannot also claim separately for fuel, electricity, vehicle tax, MOTs or repairs; anyone whose employer already pays at or above the approved rate has nothing left to claim; anyone in Self Assessment must claim on the tax return rather than separately.
scope.from_when: Rates shown apply for the 2026-27 tax year. The car and van rate rose from 45p to 55p for the first 10,000 miles from 6 April 2026; motorcycle (24p), bicycle (20p) and passenger (5p) rates are unchanged.
scope.how_to_claim: Claim the shortfall as mileage allowance relief using the GOV.UK job expenses service, or on the Self Assessment return if you file one. Mileage logs are required showing the reason for each journey and the start and end postcodes.

notes: The headline 45p figure is out of date for 2026-27 - cars and vans are 55p for the first 10,000 business miles from 6 April 2026, and 25p after that. Motorcycles and bicycles have a single flat rate with no 10,000-mile step. Passenger payments are the trap: 5p a mile is what an employer may pay tax free, but there is no employee relief if the employer pays less or nothing. Company car drivers claim on actual fuel and electricity spent on business trips, not these rates, and may claim relief on the difference if the employer reimburses only part. UK-wide; the cash value follows the claimant's nation's income tax rates.

title: Gift Aid: The Higher Rate Relief Donors Leave Unclaimed

figures.what: the extra the charity can claim from HMRC on a Gift Aid donation (25% of the donation)
the amount a 40% taxpayer can claim back on a £100 Gift Aid donation - the difference between the tax paid on the donation and what the charity got back (GOV.UK worked example)
the cap - donations in a tax year must not be more than 4 times what you have paid in tax in that tax year

scope.who: Individual taxpayers who pay Income Tax above the basic rate and make Gift Aid donations can claim back the difference between the rate they pay and the basic rate the charity has reclaimed. Claim on the Self Assessment return, or by asking HMRC to amend your tax code.
scope.excluded: Basic rate taxpayers get nothing extra - the charity's 25p already uses up the relief; anyone who has not paid enough tax to cover what the charity reclaims should not sign a Gift Aid declaration, and donations must not exceed 4 times the tax paid in the year; some payments do not qualify for Gift Aid at all; donations to a community amateur sports club cannot be made through Payroll Giving; and if you miss the Self Assessment deadline you cannot claim the earlier year's relief on current-year donations.
scope.from_when: Ongoing.
scope.how_to_claim: Include the donations on your Self Assessment tax return, or contact HMRC and ask for your tax code to be amended.

notes: Two different pots of money: the charity's 25p in the £1, which is automatic once the declaration is signed, and the donor's own higher rate relief, which is NOT automatic and is only paid if claimed. GOV.UK states the mechanism is 'the same if you live in Scotland' and links to Scottish income tax rates - because Scotland has more bands, the amount a Scottish taxpayer can reclaim differs from the rest of the UK at the same income. Welsh rates are currently set at the same level as England and Northern Ireland. Distinct from the Gift Aid carry-back election, which must be made on the original return by the filing deadline.

title: Venture Capital Trust Relief Cut From 30% To 20%

figures.what: the rate of Income Tax relief on a qualifying Venture Capital Trust subscription - HMRC's measure 'reduces the VCT (Venture Capital Trusts) income tax relief, from 30% to 20%' with effect from 6 April 2026
the maximum annual investment in Venture Capital Trusts on which Income Tax relief can be claimed
minimum holding period - you must keep the whole investment in the VCT for 5 years or lose the Income Tax relief
the period after the end of the tax year of investment in which the relief can be claimed

scope.who: Individuals who subscribe for newly issued shares in an approved Venture Capital Trust, up to £200,000 a tax year. Dividends from VCT shares are free of Income Tax and gains on disposal are free of Capital Gains Tax, for both newly issued and previously owned shares.
