scope.excluded: Anyone buying previously owned VCT shares - Income Tax relief needs shares that are 'newly issued and paid for in full (in cash)', though the dividend and CGT exemptions still apply; anyone with too little UK Income Tax liability, because relief is limited to the Income Tax you need to pay in the UK and unused relief cannot be carried forward; anyone trying to claim in a year other than the year of investment, since VCT relief can only be claimed for the year the shares were issued; and anyone who sells within 5 years, who loses the Income Tax relief on those shares.
scope.from_when: The 20% rate takes effect from 6 April 2026. Investments made before that date attracted 30%.
scope.how_to_claim: Claim in the Self Assessment return for the tax year the shares were issued. You can instead ask HMRC to adjust your tax code or make a repayment without waiting to file. The claim must be made within 4 years of the end of the tax year of investment.

notes: The rate change is the story: a VCT subscription made on or after 6 April 2026 attracts 20%, not the widely quoted 30%. Separate from EIS and SEIS, which keep their own rates (the same measure increased EIS investment and gross asset limits). Social Investment Tax Relief is closed - no new investments on or after 6 April 2023. Gaining a connection with the VCT or an investee company does not remove the Income Tax relief, unlike the connected-person rules in EIS and SEIS. UK-wide.

title: Maintenance Payments Relief For Couples Born Before 6 April 1935

figures.what: the maximum amount of maintenance payments on which relief is given for the 2025-26 tax year (HMRC SA101 Additional information notes 2026, maintenance payments box)
the rate at which maintenance payments relief reduces the tax bill (a tax reducer, not a deduction from income)

the minimum amount of Married Couple's Allowance for 2026-27 (£4,360 for 2025-26) - the figure the maintenance payments cap has historically matched; the 2026-27 maintenance payments cap itself was not stated on the pages read

scope.who: A person making maintenance payments to a former spouse or civil partner, where either they or their former spouse or civil partner was born before 6 April 1935, and the payments are made under a court order, a Child Support Agency assessment or a written agreement. Relief is 10% of the payments, capped at the published maximum.
scope.excluded: Anyone where BOTH parties were born on or after 6 April 1935 - HMRC states 'Only fill in this box if you or your former spouse or civil partner were born before 6 April 1935'; anyone whose former spouse has remarried or whose former civil partner has entered another civil partnership, from the date of that remarriage or new partnership (payments up to that date still qualify); anyone making voluntary payments not covered by a court order, CSA assessment or written agreement; and payments above the cap, which attract no further relief.
scope.from_when: Figures confirmed for the 2025-26 tax year (claimed on the return due 31 January 2027). The relief is only available to a shrinking group because of the fixed 1935 birth date test.
scope.how_to_claim: Enter the payments in the maintenance payments box on the SA101 Additional information pages of the Self Assessment return, or ask HMRC to include the relief in your PAYE code.

notes: This is NOT Married Couple's Allowance and NOT Marriage Allowance - it is a separate 10% tax reducer for maintenance paid to a FORMER spouse or civil partner, and it uses the same pre-6-April-1935 birth test as Married Couple's Allowance. Maintenance paid for children does not qualify in its own right. The cap for 2026-27 was not published on the GOV.UK income tax rates and allowances page or on the Budget 2026 Annex A pages read on 24 November 2026, so only the 2025-26 figure of £4,360 is reported as verified; recheck when the 2026-27 SA101 notes are published. UK-wide, but as a tax reducer its cash value is the same across all four nations.

title: Crisis And Resilience Fund (Replaces The Household Support Fund In England)

figures.what: total Crisis and Resilience Fund grant to local authorities in England for 2026-27, Annex A of grant determination 31/8363
Birmingham City Council's Crisis and Resilience Fund allocation for 2026-27
Luton Borough Council's Crisis and Resilience Fund allocation for 2026-27
the period the Crisis and Resilience Fund covers; the 2026-27 determination runs 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027 and is paid in 12 monthly instalments

scope.who: People in England on low incomes who hit a financial shock, plus 'Resilience Services' (advice, income maximisation, food and fuel support). Help with energy and water bills, food, essential items and housing costs. You do NOT have to be on benefits: DWP guidance states Crisis Payments are not limited to those receiving benefits, and each council sets its own definition of low income and its own eligibility rules. Separate 'Housing Payments' (the former Discretionary Housing Payments) are for people entitled to Housing Benefit or the Universal Credit housing element who face a shortfall in housing costs.
scope.excluded: People who have No Recourse to Public Funds cannot get a Crisis Payment where the council is relying on its general power under section 1 of the Localism Act 2011, because that payment counts as public funds under paragraph 6 of the Immigration Rules (councils may still help using other legal powers, e.g. the Care Act 2014, case by case). Housing Payments can never be paid to someone with NRPF, and are unavailable to owner-occupiers and to anyone not entitled to Housing Benefit or the UC housing element. Crisis Payments cannot be used as an alternative source of regular income. Money obtained by fraud is not eligible spend. The fund cannot be used for any economic undertaking. Residents of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are outside the scheme entirely. From Year 3 (financial year ending March 2029) district councils no longer receive an allocation; all funding goes to unitary and remaining county councils.
scope.from_when: 1 April 2026 (the Household Support Fund's last period ended 31 March 2026)
scope.how_to_claim: Apply to your own county council or unitary authority; each designs its own scheme. Councils must offer at least two application routes (for example online, telephone, face to face). Some councils distribute through charities and community groups, and some limit households to one application a year.

notes: This supersedes the Household Support Fund: gov.uk now says 'In England, this support is known as the Crisis and Resilience Fund'. Do not describe the HSF as current. It absorbs Discretionary Housing Payments into a single ringfenced grant made under section 31 of the Local Government Act 2003. Nation: England only. Scotland runs the Scottish Welfare Fund, Wales the Discretionary Assistance Fund, and Northern Ireland has its own Discretionary Support scheme; the Barnett consequentials are for the devolved governments to allocate as they choose. A payment from the fund does not affect the claimant's benefits. The 2027-28 determination and allocations are not yet published. Confirmed 25 November 2026: the Housing Payment strand of this fund REPLACED Discretionary Housing Payments in England from 1 April 2026, and councils are required to name their schemes Housing Payment. Many council webpages will still say DHP during the transition. Wales still runs Discretionary Housing Payments, Scotland's are devolved, and Northern Ireland's are run by the Housing Executive.

title: Council Tax Disregard For Severe Mental Impairment

figures.what: council tax discount where the person who qualifies as severely mentally impaired lives alone, or where every other adult in the home is also severely mentally impaired or a full-time student
discount where everyone in the household is disregarded (for example a severely mentally impaired person living only with other disregarded adults)
discount for someone who lives with a severely mentally impaired person where there are no other counted adults in the household

figures.value: severe impairment of intelligence and social functioning (however caused) which appears to be permanent
figures.what: the statutory definition of severe mental impairment, Local Government Finance Act 1992 Schedule 1 paragraph 2(2)

scope.who: An adult in England who has a severe impairment of intelligence and social functioning that appears to be permanent is disregarded for council tax discount purposes, which can cut the household bill by 25%, 50% or 100% depending on who else lives there. The impairment can have any cause, so it covers conditions such as dementia and stroke as well as lifelong conditions.
scope.excluded: A disregard is not given automatically and is lost if not applied for: gov.uk states you must apply even if you are disregarded. It requires BOTH a certificate from a registered medical practitioner (for example a GP) stating that the person has been, or is likely to be, severely mentally impaired AND proof of entitlement to one of certain qualifying benefits, which the council will specify - someone with the medical certificate but no qualifying benefit does not get it. A sole adult occupier who is severely mentally impaired but lives with another adult who is counted gets no 100% discount, only the household's 25%. It gives no discount at all where two or more other adults in the home are counted. It is a discount on the bill, not a reduction of the valuation band, and it is not the same as the Disabled Band Reduction Scheme. People in Northern Ireland are outside it entirely because there is no council tax there.
scope.from_when: Long-standing; Schedule 1 to the Local Government Finance Act 1992 was retitled 'Persons Disregarded for Purposes of Discount: England' with effect from 1 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Apply to your local billing authority (your council) for the discount, with the medical certificate and benefit evidence. Backdating is at the council's discretion. If a discount is given in error you must tell the council or you can be fined and asked to repay it.

notes: Nation is the trap here. From 1 April 2026 section 11 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 is headed 'Discounts: England' and applies only to a chargeable dwelling in England, and the word 'England' was inserted into the heading of Schedule 1, by sections 18(11)(a) and 23(7) of the Local Government Finance (Wales) Act 2024 (W.S.I. 2026/14). Wales's discounts and the list of disregarded persons are now prescribed by Welsh Ministers in regulations under the new sections 11E and 11F, so do not quote the Schedule 1 wording for a Welsh address. Scotland operates council tax under Part II of the same Act with its own discount rules. Northern Ireland has domestic rates, not council tax, and has a separate disability-related rates allowance. This is a DISREGARD, which affects the discount, and is distinct from Council Tax Reduction, which is a means-tested rebate.

title: Council Tax Student Disregard And Full-Student Household Exemption

figures.what: households in England where everyone is a full-time student do not have to pay council tax; if a bill is issued you apply for an exemption

figures.value: at least 1 year and at least 21 hours study per week
figures.what: the course test for counting as a full-time student for council tax

figures.value: at least 3 months and at least 12 hours study per week
figures.what: the course test instead if you are under 20 and studying for a qualification up to A level
discount where you pay council tax and everyone else in the home is disregarded, for example a sole non-student sharing with full-time students
the maximum pay an apprentice can receive and still be disregarded; the employer must declare this and that the training leads to an Ofqual- or SVEC-accredited qualification

scope.who: Full-time students at a college or university, student nurses, 18 and 19 year olds in full-time education, people under 25 funded by the Education and Skills Funding Agency, foreign language assistants registered with the British Council, and people on certain apprentice schemes are all disregarded when the council counts the adults in a dwelling. Statutory basis: paragraphs 4 and 5 of Schedule 1 to the Local Government Finance Act 1992 (students, student nurses, apprentices and youth training trainees).
scope.excluded: Part-time students, and full-time students whose course fails the duration or hours test, are not disregarded. A household is not exempt if even one resident is not a full-time student - a bill is issued, and at best a 25% discount applies. The disregard must be claimed: gov.uk states you need to apply for a discount or exemption even if you are disregarded. An apprentice paid more than £195 a week does not qualify, nor does one whose training does not lead to an accredited qualification. Students are not relieved of liability for a dwelling they own but do not occupy as their main home. Students in Northern Ireland are outside the scheme because there is no council tax there.
scope.from_when: Long-standing; Schedule 1 became England-only in its heading on 1 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Apply to your local council for the student discount or exemption, using a student certificate from the institution. Paragraph 5 of Schedule 1 requires an institution to supply a certificate on request, and it may refuse only if the request is made more than a year after the person stopped attending.

notes: Nation: stated for England. From 1 April 2026 the discount and disregard provisions in sections 11 and Schedule 1 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 apply only to dwellings in England, with Wales moving to Welsh Ministers' regulations under the new sections 11E and 11F (Local Government Finance (Wales) Act 2024, sections 18 and 23(7)). Scotland has its own student discount and exemption rules under Part II of the 1992 Act. Northern Ireland has domestic rates, and full-time students there deal with the Land and Property Services rate reliefs instead. This is not Council Tax Reduction and not a student loan matter.

title: Disabled Band Reduction Scheme For Council Tax

figures.what: the bill is charged at the rate for the band immediately below your property's band, for example a Band D home is billed at the Band C rate
the reduction given instead if the property is already in Band A, the lowest band

scope.who: Households in England living in a larger property than they would need if the disabled occupant were not disabled. You must show either an extra bathroom, kitchen or other room needed for the disabled person, or extra space inside the property for using a wheelchair. The property must be the main home of at least one disabled person, who may be an adult or a child and does not have to be the person liable for the council tax.
scope.excluded: A property with no qualifying extra room and no extra internal wheelchair space gets nothing, however severe the disability - the test is about the property, not the person's condition. It does not apply to a property that is not the disabled person's main home. It is not awarded automatically: you have to apply and show you qualify. A property already in Band A cannot be moved to a lower band and gets the 17% reduction instead. There is no equivalent for people in Northern Ireland under this scheme, because Northern Ireland charges domestic rates rather than council tax.
scope.from_when: Long-standing; the England position was checked on 24 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Apply to your local council and provide evidence of the extra room or wheelchair space and that the property is the disabled person's main home.

notes: Stated for England only, deliberately. This is a reduction in the band used to calculate the bill under the 'reduced amounts' power in section 13 of the Local Government Finance Act 1992, not a discount and not Council Tax Reduction, and it can be held alongside the single person discount or the severe mental impairment disregard. Wales and Scotland run equivalent disability reductions under their own rules, and the Welsh council tax discount and disregard regime moved to Welsh Ministers' regulations on 1 April 2026 (Local Government Finance (Wales) Act 2024, section 18), so the Welsh position should be confirmed separately before it is quoted. Northern Ireland has domestic rates with its own disabled person's allowance. Do not confuse this with challenging your council tax band at the Valuation Office Agency.

title: Council Tax Discounts In Wales Became Welsh Government Rules On 1 April 2026

figures.what: the date section 18 of the Local Government Finance (Wales) Act 2024 took effect, inserting new sections 11E and 11F into the Local Government Finance Act 1992 and adding 'England' to the heading of section 11 and of Schedule 1

the new provisions under which the amount of any council tax discount in Wales, and the descriptions of person who are disregarded for discount, are prescribed by the Welsh Ministers in regulations approved by Senedd Cymru

scope.nation: Wales (the change also narrows the England provisions)
scope.who: Anyone liable for council tax on a dwelling in Wales. The discount for a sole counted resident, and the list of people disregarded when the adults in a dwelling are counted, are now set by Welsh regulations rather than by the England provisions of the Local Government Finance Act 1992. A Welsh billing authority may also determine, for a prescribed class of dwelling, that a discount does not apply or applies at a reduced amount.
scope.excluded: Dwellings in England are outside the new Welsh provisions: section 11 and Schedule 1 of the 1992 Act now apply only to a chargeable dwelling in England, and paragraph 12 of Schedule 1 was omitted for Wales. Scotland is unaffected, as it has its own Part II regime. Northern Ireland is outside this entirely because it charges domestic rates, not council tax. Regulations under the new sections cannot be made at all unless a draft has been laid before and approved by Senedd Cymru, so no Welsh discount change can take effect without that approval.
scope.from_when: 1 April 2026 (commenced by W.S.I. 2026/14, article 2)
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim: this is the legal framework. Individual Welsh discounts, disregards and exemptions are applied for from the local billing authority as before.

notes: This exists to stop the single commonest nation error in council tax content: quoting the Local Government Finance Act 1992 section 11 25% and 50% discounts, or the Schedule 1 list of disregarded people including the severely mentally impaired and students, as if they still governed Wales. From 1 April 2026 they do not - they are expressly England provisions, and Wales's equivalents live in Welsh Ministers' regulations. Sections 6(4C) and 9(2A) of the 1992 Act were rewritten the same way for liability and spousal joint liability. Scotland's council tax discounts sit under Part II of the 1992 Act. Northern Ireland has domestic rates administered by Land and Property Services. The exact Welsh discount percentages for 2026-27 must be read from the Welsh regulations themselves and are not stated here.

title: School Essentials Grant (Wales)

figures.what: School Essentials Grant for an eligible learner in reception to year 11 in Wales, claimable once per child per school year, plus extra funding for the school
the higher School Essentials Grant for a learner entering year 7, to help with the costs of starting secondary school
the window in which the current School Essentials Grant round is open for applications

scope.who: Families on lower incomes receiving certain benefits, with a child in reception to year 11 at a school in Wales, where the learner is eligible for means-tested free school meals (eFSM). All children in local authority care qualify. It can be spent on school uniform including coats and shoes, school activities such as learning a musical instrument and sports kit, classroom essentials, specialist equipment for curriculum activities such as design and technology, laptops or tablets where the school cannot lend equipment, kit for out-of-school trips and outdoor learning, and uniform for enrichment activities such as scouts, guides, cadets, sports, performing arts or dance.
scope.excluded: Receiving Universal Primary Free School Meals does not of itself entitle a child to the grant - the learner must be eligible for means-tested free school meals. Learners who have free school meals only under transitional protection arrangements do not qualify. Children outside reception to year 11 are not covered. Only one claim per child per school year is allowed. Families not entitled to public funds have no entitlement, though the Welsh Government encourages local authorities to use discretion to pay them. Children at school in England, Scotland or Northern Ireland are outside the scheme. Applications outside the 1 July 2026 to 31 May 2027 window are not accepted.
scope.from_when: Current round opens 1 July 2026 and closes 31 May 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Apply to the local authority where your child goes to school; gov.wales lists all 22 Welsh local authorities and has a postcode lookup. Receiving the grant does not affect your tax or your other benefits.

notes: Wales only. This is the successor to the former Pupil Development Grant - Access school uniform grant; the Pupil Development Grant itself is money paid to the school, which is a different thing. There is no equivalent national uniform grant in England - help with uniform costs there is at the discretion of the individual local authority or school. Scotland and Northern Ireland run their own clothing or uniform grant schemes on their own rules and amounts, which must be checked on mygov.scot and the Northern Ireland Education Authority's own pages before being quoted. Note the trap that a Welsh primary pupil automatically gets a free school meal but must still be checked for means-tested free school meals eligibility to unlock this grant.

title: Universal Primary Free School Meals In Wales, And The Secondary Expansion

figures.what: every primary school child in Wales can now access a free school meal, with no income test
the Welsh Government is expanding free school meals to all secondary learners in households claiming Universal Credit with no income limit, starting with years 7 and 8

scope.who: All primary school pupils in Wales, regardless of household income or benefits. Secondary learners in households claiming Universal Credit, with no income limit, are being brought in starting with years 7 and 8. Parents may be asked to register their child so the school can headcount meals.
scope.excluded: Secondary school learners outside the groups reached so far by the expansion do not get a universal meal and must qualify under the means-tested free school meals rules instead. The universal offer does not extend to a child at school outside Wales. Being given Universal Primary Free School Meals does not register a child for means-tested free school meals and does not by itself unlock the School Essentials Grant or the extra Pupil Development Grant funding for the school, so a family that stops checking eligibility loses that money.
scope.from_when: Rollout completed to all primary year groups; secondary expansion under way from years 7 and 8
scope.how_to_claim: The primary meal is provided by the school and no means test applies, though the school or local authority may ask you to register. Separately, you should still check means-tested free school meals eligibility with your local authority to access wider support.

notes: Wales only, and quite different from England, where the universal offer covers only infants (reception, year 1 and year 2) and older pupils need the means test. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own positions, which must be read on mygov.scot and the Northern Ireland Education Authority's pages before being quoted - do not assume they match Wales. The Welsh secondary expansion is being phased, so the year groups covered will move: check before quoting. Do not state a household income threshold for the Welsh secondary offer, because gov.wales says there is no income limit for Universal Credit households.

title: Education Maintenance Allowance (Wales)

figures.what: Education Maintenance Allowance for an eligible 16 to 18 year old in Wales staying in education, paid every two weeks directly to the student

scope.who: A young person who is above compulsory school age, who will be 16, 17 or 18 on or before 31 August, who normally lives in Wales, and who is studying an eligible full-time academic or vocational course at school or college. It is paid to the student, not the parent, and is meant for costs such as travel, books and equipment.
scope.excluded: Anyone who does not normally live in Wales is excluded, as is anyone still of compulsory school age, anyone who will be 19 or older on 31 August, and anyone on a part-time or otherwise ineligible course. It is not paid automatically with a school place: it has to be applied for each year through Student Finance Wales. There is also a household income test applied by Student Finance Wales, so a young person on an eligible course in Wales can still be refused on income grounds.
scope.from_when: Current scheme; the £40 weekly rate was on gov.wales on 24 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Apply online through Student Finance Wales; gov.wales links to the application.

notes: Wales only. There is no Education Maintenance Allowance in England - 16 to 19 year olds there are directed to discretionary bursary help through their school or college instead, so do not offer EMA to an English household. Scotland and Northern Ireland run their own EMA schemes at their own rates and on their own eligibility rules, which must be checked on mygov.scot and the Northern Ireland Education Authority's pages. The household income thresholds for the Welsh scheme are set out by Student Finance Wales and are NOT verified in this entry - do not state an income figure without checking it there first.

title: Business Gifts: The £50 Advertising-Gift Rule And The Client Entertaining Disallowance

figures.what: Maximum total cost of gifts to any one recipient in the basis period (tax year for unincorporated businesses, accounting period for companies) for the advertising-gift exception to apply; if the cost of the gift together with other gifts to the same recipient exceeds £50, no deduction is allowed at all
The statutory exception for small gifts carrying a conspicuous advertisement for the business (e.g. diaries, pens, mouse mats) - the advertisement must be on the gift itself, not just the wrapping
The general rule denying any deduction for expenses of providing business entertainment or gifts, even where the expense is incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the trade
Statutory definition of 'entertainment' for the corporation tax disallowance; s1298(5)(a) also provides that 'employee' includes a director of the company and a person engaged in its management

scope.who: All businesses computing taxable trading profits - sole traders, partnerships and companies - that give gifts to customers, prospects or other third parties
scope.excluded: Gifts of food, drink, tobacco, or a token or voucher exchangeable for goods are never allowable, whatever their cost (BIM45070). Gifts whose cost, together with other gifts to the same recipient in the same basis period, exceeds £50 get no deduction at all. Gifts that do not carry a conspicuous advertisement for the business on the gift itself get no deduction. All client and third-party entertaining - hospitality of any kind, including entertaining by employees and by directors or managers - is disallowed outright under s45 ITTOIA 2005 / s1298 CTA 2009 however commercial the purpose.
scope.from_when: In force; s45-s47 ITTOIA 2005 and s1298-s1300 CTA 2009
scope.how_to_claim: No claim. Allowable advertising gifts are simply deducted in the accounts and tax computation; disallowable entertaining and gifts must be added back in the tax computation (box for disallowable expenses on the CT600 computation or the Self Assessment self-employment pages)

notes: Not the VAT rule. The VAT treatment of business gifts (a separate £50 limit, VAT-exclusive, per person per 12 months) is a different subject with different conditions. Not staff gifts or staff entertaining either: gifts to employees and staff functions sit under separate exceptions and under the trivial benefits and annual function exemptions. The £50 is a cliff edge, not a deductible first slice - exceed it and the whole cost is disallowed. The limit is per recipient per basis period, not per gift. BIM45070 read 24 November 2026.

title: VAT On Deregistration: The Deemed Supply Of Assets On Hand

figures.what: De minimis: no VAT is due on the deemed supply if the total VAT on the business assets and stock on hand at cancellation is £1,000 or less (VAT Act 1994 Schedule 4 paragraph 8(1)(c))
Same de minimis stated in VAT Notice 700/11, section 7 (business assets and stock on hand): if the total VAT on the assets to be included is £1,000 or less, no VAT is due
The equivalent gross (VAT-inclusive) value where all the assets on hand are standard-rated - no VAT need be accounted for if their total gross value is £6,000 or less (VAT Notice 700/11 section 7)

scope.who: Any business cancelling its VAT registration that still holds goods forming part of its business assets - unsold stock, plant, furniture, computers, commercial vehicles, and opted-to-tax land or buildings - on which input tax was claimed; the goods are deemed to be supplied by the business on the day it ceases to be a taxable person
scope.excluded: No deemed supply arises where the business is transferred as a going concern to another taxable person (Sch 4 para 8(1)(a)), where the business is carried on by someone treated as a taxable person under regulations under s46(4), where the VAT on the deemed supply would be £1,000 or less, or where the person ceases to be taxable because of certification under s54 (Agricultural Flat Rate Scheme). Particular goods are excluded if no input tax credit was allowed on them - including goods bought from unregistered businesses or private individuals, goods bought under a VAT margin scheme, cars (except private taxis, self-drive hire cars and driving school cars where input tax was claimed), goods used wholly for business entertainment, goods directly attributable to an exempt activity, land or buildings obtained free of VAT, and goods not bought for business purposes. Intangibles - patents, copyrights, goodwill - are outside the charge.
scope.from_when: In force; VAT Act 1994 Schedule 4 paragraph 8, the £1,000 figure substituted with effect from 1 April 2000
scope.how_to_claim: Self-accounted: include any VAT due on stocks and assets in the final VAT Return (enter a nil figure if none is due), and keep a list of all business assets on hand at cancellation with their values even where no VAT is payable. Value the goods at the price you would expect to pay for them, or similar items, in their present condition

notes: The test is on the VAT, not on the value: £1,000 of VAT, which only equals £6,000 of gross value when every asset is standard-rated. Separate from the deregistration turnover thresholds. A transfer of the business as a going concern blocks the deemed supply only if the new owner is VAT-registered - Notice 700/11 section 7.5 says that where the new owner is not registered you must account for VAT on the assets on hand in the normal way. Where opted land or buildings are kept and input tax was claimed, the deemed supply is at current market value. Notice read 24 November 2026.

title: Reclaiming Statutory Parental Payments: 92%, Or 109% With Small Employers' Relief

figures.what: Percentage of statutory parental payments an employer can usually reclaim from HMRC - payable where total Class 1 National Insurance for the previous tax year is above £45,000
Percentage reclaimable under Small Employers' Relief - 100% of the statutory payments plus 9% NIC compensation

Total Class 1 National Insurance (employee and employer contributions) in the last complete tax year before the qualifying or matching week at or below which an employer qualifies for Small Employers' Relief; reductions such as Employment Allowance are ignored for this test
Confirmed in the 2026 to 2027 employer rates guidance: 109% if total Class 1 National Insurance for the previous tax year is £45,000 or lower, 92% if it is above £45,000
The NIC compensation element added to the 100% recovery for small employers - increased from 8.5% to 9% on 6 April 2026

scope.who: Employers paying Statutory Maternity Pay, Statutory Paternity Pay, Statutory Adoption Pay, Statutory Shared Parental Pay, Statutory Parental Bereavement Pay or Statutory Neonatal Care Pay
scope.excluded: Statutory Sick Pay cannot be reclaimed at all - the April 2026 Employer Bulletin states it is the one statutory payment outside the scheme. Employers whose total Class 1 National Insurance for the last complete tax year before the qualifying or matching week exceeded £45,000 get only 92%, not 109%. Employment Allowance and other reductions are ignored when applying the £45,000 test, so a company that paid no NIC after Employment Allowance can still fail it. A repayment cannot be requested from the PAYE Employer Office until the start of the next tax year.
scope.from_when: 109% applies to statutory payments from 6 April 2026 (compensation rate raised from 8.5% to 9% on that date)
scope.how_to_claim: Calculate the recovery and compensation in payroll software and report it on an Employer Payment Summary (EPS) to HMRC, setting the amount off against the PAYE and NIC otherwise payable; if it cannot be set off against the current year's liabilities, write to the National Insurance Contributions and Employers Office, HM Revenue and Customs, BX9 1BX from the start of the next tax year to ask for a repayment

notes: The widely quoted 103% is out of date and should not be used: the small employers' figure was 103% for many years, became 108.5%, and is 109% from 6 April 2026. The £45,000 test looks at the previous complete tax year, not the current one, and uses NIC before Employment Allowance. UK-wide; same rates in Northern Ireland. Pages read 24 November 2026.

title: Cheap Or Interest-Free Loans To Directors And Employees: The £10,000 Exemption

figures.what: No taxable benefit arises where the total balance outstanding on all the employee's or director's beneficial loans does not exceed £10,000 throughout the tax year (booklet 480 paragraph 17.16, section 180(1) ITEPA 2003)

figures.value: less than £10,000 throughout the whole tax year
figures.what: How the gov.uk employer guidance words the same exemption - loans with a combined outstanding value to an employee below £10,000 for the whole tax year do not have to be reported
HMRC official rate of interest for beneficial loans from 6 April 2026 (also 3.75% for 2025 to 2026) - the rate used to measure the benefit where the exemption does not apply

scope.who: Directors and employees (and their relatives) who have a cheap or interest-free loan by reason of their employment - including an overdrawn director's loan account
scope.excluded: The £10,000 exemption does not apply to loans made under optional remuneration (salary sacrifice) arrangements - those must be reported (booklet 480 paragraph 17.16; gov.uk employer guidance). It is lost entirely if the total outstanding balance on all beneficial loans exceeds £10,000 at any time in the tax year, in which case the benefit on the whole loan, not just the excess, is chargeable. It is not needed for loans already exempt on other grounds: qualifying loans where the whole of the interest would attract tax relief (partial relief does not count), loans made in the ordinary course of a lending business on the same terms as to the general public, fixed-period fixed-rate loans meeting the strict conditions in paragraph 17.19, and loans made in the normal course of a domestic, family or personal relationship by an individual employer.
scope.from_when: In force; section 180 ITEPA 2003 (£10,000 since 6 April 2014, £5,000 for 2013 to 2014). Official rate of 3.75% applies from 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: No claim - the exemption applies automatically and the loan is not reported. Where it does not apply, report the cash equivalent on form P11D (working sheet 4) and pay Class 1A National Insurance on it, or payroll the benefit

notes: Separate from the section 455 corporation tax charge on a loan to a participator, which has its own rate and nine-month repayment rule: a director's overdrawn loan account can trigger both, and the £10,000 benefit-in-kind threshold has nothing to do with the s455 charge. The £10,000 is tested across all the individual's employment-related loans combined, including loans to a relative, and at any point in the year - not on the year-end balance. Booklet 480 notes that accrued interest is not added to the balance until it falls due for payment. Pages read 24 November 2026.

title: Annual Tax On Enveloped Dwellings: 2026 To 2027 Charges And The 30 April Return

figures.what: Value threshold: a UK dwelling is within ATED only if valued above £500,000 (for returns from 2016 to 2017 onwards)
Annual chargeable amount for the chargeable period 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, property value more than £500,000 up to £1 million
Annual chargeable amount 2026 to 2027, value more than £1 million up to £2 million
Annual chargeable amount 2026 to 2027, value more than £2 million up to £5 million
Annual chargeable amount 2026 to 2027, value more than £5 million up to £10 million
Annual chargeable amount 2026 to 2027, value more than £10 million up to £20 million
Annual chargeable amount 2026 to 2027, value more than £20 million

Return deadline where the property is within the scope of ATED on 1 April; 30 days from acquisition if it comes into scope later; 90 days for a newly built dwelling from the earliest of the date it becomes a dwelling for council tax or is first occupied

scope.who: Non-natural persons owning a UK dwelling worth more than £500,000 - a company, a partnership with any corporate partner, or a collective investment scheme such as a unit trust or open-ended investment vehicle - whether the dwelling is owned wholly or partly
scope.excluded: Dwellings owned directly by individuals are outside ATED altogether, as is any partnership with no corporate partner. Dwellings valued at £500,000 or less are outside the charge. Property that is not a dwelling in the UK is outside it. GOV.UK states there are also reliefs and exemptions that may mean no tax is payable; the detailed relief conditions were not read at primary source in this run, so do not state them.
scope.from_when: Chargeable period 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Submit the ATED return through the ATED online service on or after 1 April for the chargeable period and by 30 April, and pay through the online service; where the same relief is claimed for more than one property a single Relief Declaration Return can be used

notes: The charge is for the whole chargeable period 1 April to 31 March and is based on the property's value at the relevant valuation date, not on rent or profit. A return is filed and paid at the start of the period, before the period it covers has run - unusual, and easy for a company to miss in its first year of ownership. The amounts above are the 2026 to 2027 figures and are indexed, so they change on 1 April 2027. Pages read 24 November 2026.

title: Alcohol Duty Rates From 1 February 2027

figures.what: RPI uprating applied to all Alcohol Duty rates from 1 February 2027
Standard duty per litre of alcohol in the product, all products below 3.5% ABV, from 1 February 2027 (was £9.96)
Standard duty per litre of alcohol: still cider 3.5% to under 8.5% ABV, and sparkling cider 3.5% to not exceeding 5.5% ABV, from 1 February 2027 (was £10.39)
Standard duty per litre of alcohol: beer 3.5% to under 8.5% ABV, from 1 February 2027 (was £22.58)
Standard duty per litre of alcohol: spirits, wine and other fermented products 3.5% to under 8.5% ABV, and sparkling cider over 5.5% to under 8.5% ABV, from 1 February 2027 (was £26.61)
Standard duty per litre of alcohol: all products 8.5% to not exceeding 22% ABV, from 1 February 2027 (was £30.62)
Standard duty per litre of alcohol: all products over 22% ABV, from 1 February 2027 (was £33.99)
Draught relief rate per litre of alcohol, qualifying draught products below 3.5% ABV, from 1 February 2027 (was £8.58)
Draught relief rate per litre of alcohol: draught still cider 3.5% to under 8.5% ABV and draught sparkling cider 3.5% to not exceeding 5.5% ABV, from 1 February 2027 (was £8.95)

Draught relief rate per litre of alcohol: draught beer, spirits, wine and other fermented products 3.5% to under 8.5% ABV, and draught sparkling cider over 5.5% to under 8.5% ABV, from 1 February 2027 (was £19.45)
Duty on products of 1.2% ABV or less — not liable to Alcohol Duty in any category (rates table in force to 31 January 2027)
Annual production of pure alcohol at or above which a producer cannot claim Small Producer Relief

scope.who: Businesses that produce, import, hold in duty suspense, warehouse or distribute alcoholic products — HMRC estimates up to 8,000 such businesses. Duty is paid by the producer or importer, not the retailer. Small Producer Relief discounts are also uprated: for products below 3.5% ABV a more generous taper applies, and for products 3.5% to 8.4% ABV the marginal discount is uprated by RPI plus a further 10%, so marginal and cumulative discount percentages increase. Simplified rates for alcohol brought into Great Britain for personal use also rise.
scope.excluded: Products of 1.2% ABV or less are not liable to Alcohol Duty at all (rate £0.00 in every category). Small Producer Relief is not available for products at or above 8.5% ABV, for products produced under licence, or to producers making 4,500 hectolitres or more of pure alcohol a year. Draught relief rates apply only to qualifying draught products — packaged (non-draught) products pay the standard rate. HMRC also says civil society organisations are not expected to be affected.
scope.from_when: 1 February 2027 (rates in the current table apply up to 31 January 2027)
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim for the rate change — the new rates apply automatically to duty on products released for consumption on or after 1 February 2027. Draught relief and Small Producer Relief are claimed by the approved producer or warehousekeeper on the alcohol duty return; producers must still work out their own SPR discount using HMRC's guidance.

notes: This is the Budget 2026 alcohol duty uprating, announced 28 October 2026 and taking effect 1 February 2027 — inside ten weeks of 24 November 2026, so copy written before 1 February 2027 must say 'from 1 February 2027' and not present these as current rates. Alcohol Duty is a UK-wide excise duty: it is not devolved, so the same rates apply in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland (Scotland's minimum unit pricing is a separate retail price floor, not duty). Rates are stated per litre of pure alcohol in the product, not per litre of drink or per bottle. The gov.uk Alcohol Duty rates guidance page at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/alcohol-duty-rates had NOT been updated with the February 2027 rates when read on 24 November 2026 — it still showed the 1 February 2026 rates. Draught relief eligibility conditions (container size and ABV) are in separate guidance, 'Check if you can pay less Alcohol Duty on draught alcoholic products', and were not verified here.

title: ISA Compliance Package: New HMRC Powers Over ISA Managers

figures.what: Date the new ISA compliance powers (points-based penalties for late ISA returns, penalties for inaccuracies, and suspension of ISA managers) take effect
Confirmed start date for the new powers in Budget 2026 OOTLAR paragraph 1.86
Estimated HMRC IT and staff cost of delivering the change, as part of the wider Digitalisation of ISAs programme
Exchequer impact of the measure from 2028 to 2029 onwards (2026-27 and 2027-28 cells blank)

scope.who: ISA managers — the banks, building societies and investment firms approved by HMRC to manage Individual Savings Accounts. From 6 April 2028 their monthly digital returns and annual returns come within a points-based penalty regime; HMRC gets new sanctions for inaccuracies in ISA returns, can collect an amount representing the tax lost and apply a penalty scaled to the nature and scope of the failure, and can suspend an ISA manager where withdrawing HMRC approval would not be appropriate. Delivered by amending section 696 of the Income Tax (Trading and Other Income) Act 2005 and Schedule 24 to the Finance Act 2021, with the rest done through amendments to the ISA Regulations.
scope.excluded: Individual ISA savers and investors: the new penalties and suspension powers bite on ISA managers, and HMRC states individual investors' experience of dealing with HMRC is expected to remain unchanged — savers get no new obligation, return or penalty from this package. HMRC also states that civil society organisations are not expected to be affected, and that compliant ISA managers face only a negligible one-off familiarisation cost with no continuing administrative burden.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2028 (policy paper first published 13 July 2026, last updated 17 November 2026)
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — this is a compliance and penalty measure applying automatically to HMRC-approved ISA managers from 6 April 2028. Managers should follow HMRC's Tax-free savings newsletters and the ISA Regulations amendments for the detail.

notes: This is the ISA compliance package that supports the Digitalisation of ISAs programme; the policy paper was updated on 17 November 2026 (the update concerned the suspension powers). It is NOT a change to the ISA allowance and NOT the separate Budget 2026 reduction in the cash ISA limit — keep those apart in any copy. No penalty amounts or points thresholds are published yet: the paper states no figures for penalty levels, so do not quote any. The powers are legislated in Finance Bill 2026 and the ISA Regulations, so the detail can change before 6 April 2028. ISAs are a UK-wide tax wrapper, with the same rules in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

title: Soft Drinks Industry Levy Rates From 1 April 2027

figures.what: Lower-band Soft Drinks Industry Levy rate from 1 April 2027, for chargeable soft drinks with at least 5g but less than 8g of total sugar per 100ml (OOTLAR para 1.67)
Higher-band Soft Drinks Industry Levy rate from 1 April 2027, for chargeable soft drinks with 8g or more of total sugar per 100ml (OOTLAR para 1.67)
Additional annual increase added to the lower and higher rates respectively on top of CPI inflation, part of spreading the April 2018 to April 2024 CPI catch-up over 2025 to 2029
Lower sugar threshold for the levy from 1 January 2028, reduced from 5g per 100ml (the 5g threshold still applies to the 1 April 2027 rates)
Milk content at or above which a pre-packaged milk-based drink is currently exempt from the levy — this exemption is removed from 1 January 2028

scope.who: Businesses registered for the Soft Drinks Industry Levy that produce, package, own the brand of, or bring into the UK liable soft drinks containing at least 5g of total sugar per 100ml — HMRC estimates 500 to 600 businesses. The levy is charged per 10 litres of prepared drink and is uprated each 1 April. Costs may be passed to the hospitality trade and to consumers.
scope.excluded: Drinks with less than 5g of total sugar per 100ml are outside the levy (HMRC says about 89% of soft drink sales are not subject to it). Also not liable: drinks containing at least 75ml of milk per 100ml of prepared drink (cream does not count as milk) until that exemption is removed on 1 January 2028; alcohol-replacement drinks sold and marketed as a direct substitute for an alcoholic drink, not aimed at under-18s and never above 1.2% ABV; infant formula, follow-on formula and baby foods; total diet replacements and dietary food for special medical purposes; drinks made with fruit or vegetable juice and no other added sugar; and drinks packaged or brought into the UK before 6 April 2018. Businesses that only dispense drinks into a cup, glass or takeaway cup are not classed as packagers and do not pay. Sugar replacements such as stevia, aspartame and sucralose do not count as sugar.
scope.from_when: 1 April 2027 for the new rates (they apply to chargeable events on or after that date). Separately, the threshold cut to 4.5g and the removal of the milk-based and milk-substitute exemptions take effect 1 January 2028.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim — the new rates apply automatically to chargeable events on or after 1 April 2027. Registered businesses report and pay on their quarterly SDIL return.

notes: Two separate SDIL changes must not be run together in copy: the RATE rise on 1 April 2027 (£2.25 and £3.01 per 10 litres, from Budget 2026 OOTLAR para 1.67), and the SCOPE changes on 1 January 2028 (lower threshold 4.5g per 100ml, milk-based drinks and sweetened plant-based milk substitutes brought into the levy, legislated in Finance Bill 2026 / Finance Act 2027). The 2028 scope paper carries no 2027 effective date. Drinks still out of scope from 1 January 2028 include open-cup milkshakes prepared in cafes and bars, plain milk and unsweetened milk drinks, unsweetened plant-based drinks, drinking yoghurt that is at least 90% fermented milk with no other liquid added, and plant-based drinks whose only sugar comes from the single principal ingredient such as soya or oats. SDIL is a UK-wide levy, identical in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The gov.uk SDIL rate and liability guidance pages still showed the 1 April 2025 rates (£1.94 and £2.59 per 10 litres) and the 5g threshold when read on 24 November 2026. The small producer position and the registration volume threshold were NOT verified at primary source and must not be stated.

title: Electric Vehicle Excise Duty (eVED) From April 2028

figures.what: eVED rate for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and hydrogen fuel cell electric vehicles (HFCEVs) that are cars, from 1 April 2028
eVED rate for plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) that are cars, from 1 April 2028
Operative date: the date eVED has effect from
eVED rates will be uprated in 2029 to 2030 and in future years in line with Consumer Prices Inflation to maintain real-terms value
Number of vehicles HMRC expects eVED to affect in financial year 2028 to 2029

scope.who: Registered keepers of UK-registered cars that are battery electric (BEV), plug-in hybrid (PHEV) or hydrogen fuel cell (HFCEV). Administered by DVLA as an extension of Vehicle Excise Duty: it is renewed alongside VED. Businesses and fleets are in scope, including company cars.
scope.excluded: Vehicles that are not cars — the measure applies only to BEVs, PHEVs and HFCEVs 'that are cars', so electric vans, HGVs, motorcycles and other non-car vehicles are outside eVED. Petrol, diesel and non-plug-in hybrid cars are also outside it (they pay fuel duty at the pump instead). Vehicles that are not UK-registered are outside it. Leasing and rental businesses are NOT exempt — they get special administrative arrangements, including the ability to estimate mileage for their vehicles centrally.
scope.from_when: 1 April 2028. Motorists will first pay eVED when they next renew their VED after April 2028.
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim — a charge. At eVED/VED renewal the driver provides an odometer (mileage) reading from the car and estimates mileage for the forthcoming tax period (typically a year). They pay an upfront charge based on that estimate or spread payment across the year; the year-end mileage reading triggers a reconciliation. DVLA will cross-check against MOT mileage data, so for a car already subject to an MOT there are typically no additional steps.

notes: Announced at Budget 2025; legislated in Finance Bill 2026-27 by amending the Vehicle Excise and Registration Act 1994 (new rates in Schedule 1 to VERA 1994), with consequential amendments to Part II Road Traffic Act 1988 and Part 3 Road Traffic (Northern Ireland) Order 1995 on odometers. Powers for the Secretary of State for Transport to make commencement regulations are in the Bill, so operational detail is still to come in secondary legislation — the pence-per-mile figures and the April 2028 date are the only settled numbers. This is NOT a replacement for VED: it sits on top of VED, which continues. It is NOT a road-pricing scheme with telematics or GPS — it is self-declared odometer mileage checked against MOT readings. It is NOT a van or HGV charge. Rates uprate from 2029-30 by CPI, so the 3p/1.5p figures hold only for 2028-29.

title: VAT And Climate Change Levy On Public And Workplace EV Charging

figures.what: Standard rate of VAT, which applies to electricity supplied through publicly accessible EV charging points and workplace charging points

Temporary zero rate of VAT on qualifying supplies of domestic electricity in Great Britain, in force from 1 October 2026 (Group 24 of Schedule 8 VATA 1994) — this is the relief that public and workplace EV charging is now excluded from
Reduced rate of VAT that qualifying supplies of domestic electricity remain liable to in Northern Ireland (Group 1 of Schedule 7A VATA 1994)
Date from which the legislation has effect, in relation to supplies made on or after that date

figures.value: 1000 kilowatt hours or less per month
figures.what: The deemed domestic use threshold — new Notes 6A and 5A confirm an Electric Vehicle Charging Supply does not qualify for the domestic reliefs even where supply falls below this threshold

scope.nation: UK-wide (the domestic electricity comparator differs: temporary zero rate in Great Britain, 5% reduced rate in Northern Ireland)
scope.who: Businesses supplying electricity through EV charging points accessible to the public, accessible to a section of the public, or accessible to employees or contractors at their workplace — and the users of those charging facilities. Charge point operators must standard-rate these supplies and must account for Climate Change Levy on them.
scope.excluded: Charging points accessible only to residents of a particular residential building are NOT an Electric Vehicle Charging Supply, so they keep the domestic treatment. Electricity used to charge an EV as part of a general supply of electricity to a home continues to qualify for VAT relief and counts as domestic use for CCL. A separate supply through a stand-alone charging point provided for private residential use at a particular dwelling, residential building or building used for a relevant residential purpose may also qualify for relief. Supplies to a charity for non-business purposes are also outside the standard-rating.
scope.from_when: Supplies made on or after 1 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. The charge point operator applies the standard rate and accounts for CCL. A VAT-registered business recovering VAT on charging its own vehicles follows the normal input tax rules; see VAT Notice 701/19.

notes: This puts HMRC's long-standing policy into statute following the First-tier Tribunal decision in Charge My Street Ltd. Legislation: new Note 6A into Group 1 of Schedule 7A VATA 1994, new Note 5A into Group 24 of Schedule 8 VATA 1994, and new paragraph 9A into Schedule 6 to the Finance Act 2000 for CCL. Note the asymmetry clients ask about: home charging is still relieved (0% in GB under the temporary zero rate, 5% in NI), public and workplace charging is 20%. Workplace charging points are caught, which is new and often missed — a charge point open to employees or contractors at their workplace is not domestic use. This is NOT about the employee benefit-in-kind treatment of workplace charging, and it is NOT a change to input tax recovery. Distinct from the separate temporary GB domestic electricity zero rate, which is a different subject and has its own end date — recheck when that temporary zero rate is reviewed.

title: VAT: Extending Online Marketplace Liability To UK Sellers

figures.what: Minimum annual sales threshold per platform: a UK business that is not VAT registered is brought into marketplace-collected VAT once its sales on that marketplace exceed this figure
The date from which the government intends the measure to be implemented
Number of businesses HMRC expects the measure to have a significant impact on
The consignment value threshold under the EXISTING (January 2021) marketplace liability rules for imported goods, which this measure sits alongside

scope.who: Online marketplaces, which become responsible for collecting and accounting for VAT where they facilitate a sale of goods by a UK-established business to a consumer and the goods are in the UK at the time of sale. It catches sales by UK VAT-registered businesses, and sales by any other UK business whose sales on that particular marketplace exceed £90,000 a year.
scope.excluded: Non-business sales (for example personal sales by individuals) are outside the rules. Second-hand goods are outside the rules. Business-to-business transactions are outside the rules. A UK business that is not VAT registered and whose sales on that platform stay below the £90,000 per-platform threshold is outside the rules. The rules bite only where the goods are in the UK at the point of sale and the sale is to a consumer.
scope.from_when: The government intends implementation from October 2027. Some aspects, including the level of the threshold and the final implementation date, will be set by secondary legislation in 2027.
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. Where the measure applies the marketplace, not the seller, accounts for the VAT on the sale. Sellers should expect marketplaces to review listings and ask for VAT status, and should plan for the cash-flow change of VAT being collected at the platform.

notes: Legislated in Finance Bill 2026-27, extending the existing rules in sections 5A, 5B, 7(5A), 7(5B), 7AA, 37(A1), 77E, 77F and 95A VATA 1994, Group 21 of Schedule 8 and Schedule 9ZC. The existing rules, from January 2021, already apply to overseas sellers of goods located in the UK at the point of sale and to imported consignments of £135 or less; this measure extends them to UK-established sellers. Important caveat for clients: the £90,000 figure and the October 2027 date are both stated by HMRC as intentions, with the threshold level, how it operates, the treatment of second-hand goods and the implementation date all to be fixed by secondary legislation in 2027 — so both could move. The £90,000 happens to match the VAT registration threshold but is a separate per-platform sales test, measured platform by platform, not a cumulative turnover test. HMRC estimates total one-off costs for marketplaces and sellers of £40 million.

title: HMRC Inaccuracy Penalties: The Schedule 24 Penalty Ranges

figures.what: Standard penalty for a careless inaccuracy in a category 1 (domestic) matter, as a percentage of the potential lost revenue — FA 2007 Sch 24 para 4(2)(a)
Standard penalty for a deliberate but not concealed inaccuracy, category 1 — FA 2007 Sch 24 para 4(2)(b)
Standard penalty for a deliberate and concealed inaccuracy, category 1 — FA 2007 Sch 24 para 4(2)(c)
Minimum to which the 30% careless standard percentage can be reduced for the quality of disclosure — FA 2007 Sch 24 para 10(2) Table
Minimum to which the 70% deliberate-not-concealed standard percentage can be reduced for the quality of disclosure — FA 2007 Sch 24 para 10(2) Table
Minimum to which the 100% deliberate-and-concealed standard percentage can be reduced for the quality of disclosure — FA 2007 Sch 24 para 10(2) Table

Standard penalties for careless / deliberate not concealed / deliberate and concealed inaccuracies in category 2 (offshore matter or transfer, category 2 territory, income tax, CGT or IHT) — FA 2007 Sch 24 para 4(3)

Standard penalties for careless / deliberate not concealed / deliberate and concealed inaccuracies in category 3 (offshore matter or transfer, category 3 territory, income tax, CGT or IHT) — FA 2007 Sch 24 para 4(4)
Period from the date of an HMRC assessment within which a person must take reasonable steps to notify HMRC of an under-assessment, or face a penalty under Sch 24 para 2

scope.who: Any person who gives HMRC a document (return, claim, account) containing an inaccuracy that amounts to an understatement of liability, a false or inflated loss, or a false or inflated repayment claim, where the inaccuracy is careless or deliberate. Also any person who fails to take reasonable steps within 30 days to tell HMRC that an assessment HMRC issued understates their liability. Applies across the taxes listed in the Sch 24 para 1 Table (income tax, CGT, corporation tax, VAT, NICs and others).
scope.excluded: No penalty is due where the inaccuracy was neither careless nor deliberate — that is, where the person took reasonable care. 'Careless' means the inaccuracy is due to a failure to take reasonable care (para 3(1)(a)), so an innocent error made despite reasonable care falls outside the penalty altogether. An unprompted disclosure of a careless category 1 inaccuracy can reduce the penalty to 0%. The under-assessment penalty does not apply where the person took reasonable steps to notify HMRC within 30 days, judged by whether they knew or should have known about the under-assessment. HMRC may also make a special reduction for special circumstances (para 11), but 'special circumstances' expressly does not include inability to pay, nor the fact that one taxpayer's lost revenue is balanced by another's overpayment.
scope.from_when: In force since 1 April 2008 to 1 April 2009 depending on tax. The three-category structure and the current 30/70/100 plus offshore uplifts came in on 6 April 2011 (FA 2010 Sch 10); the current para 10 disclosure table was substituted with effect from 2017 (FA 2016 Sch 21, SI 2017/259).
scope.how_to_claim: Nothing to claim. To get the reduction, disclose: tell HMRC about the inaccuracy, give HMRC reasonable help in quantifying it, and allow HMRC access to records so it is fully corrected (para 9(1)). For a deliberate offshore inaccuracy or an offshore transfer you must also provide additional information (para 9(1B)). Disclosure is 'unprompted' only if made when the person has no reason to believe HMRC have discovered or are about to discover the inaccuracy; otherwise it is 'prompted'. Quality of disclosure includes timing, nature and extent.

notes: Source is the statute itself — FA 2007 Schedule 24 on legislation.gov.uk, as amended. The HMRC guidance page and the CCFS7a factsheet URL both 404 as at 24 November 2026, and the Compliance Handbook contents pages carry no percentages, so the statute is the primary source here. The 30/70/100 range is category 1 only, which is the domestic case most clients are in; offshore matters in category 2 and 3 territories carry 45/105/150 and 60/140/200 and have a much longer disclosure table (para 10A) with higher minimums — never quote 30/70/100 for an offshore error. Point clients to the gap between unprompted and prompted: on a careless domestic error unprompted disclosure can take the penalty to nil, prompted only to 15%. Separately, penalties can be suspended for careless inaccuracies subject to conditions, and a penalty can arise on an agent's or third party's deliberate act. The government has consulted on 'Reform of behavioural penalties', so these percentages could change — check that before relying on them beyond the current Finance Bill cycle.

title: Capital Gains Tax rates 2026/27

figures.what: CGT rate for individuals on gains falling within the unused basic rate band (all asset types, including residential property), disposals from 6 April 2026
CGT rate for individuals on gains above the unused basic rate band (all asset types, including residential property), disposals from 6 April 2026
CGT rate on disposals of UK residential property - the same rates as other assets since 30 October 2024; residential property no longer has its own higher rate
CGT rate for trustees and personal representatives - a single flat rate, with no basic rate band available to them
CGT rate on gains qualifying for Business Asset Disposal Relief or Investors' Relief, disposals from 6 April 2026 (was 14% in 2025/26 and 10% before 6 April 2025)

scope.who: Individuals (including sole traders and business partners), trustees and personal representatives disposing of chargeable assets; non-residents on UK land and property and on indirect disposals of UK property-rich companies
scope.excluded: Limited companies and other bodies corporate do NOT pay CGT at all - they pay Corporation Tax on chargeable gains. Trustees and personal representatives do NOT get the 18% rate - they pay a flat 24% with no basic rate band. No CGT arises on assets held in an ISA or PEP, on UK government gilts or Premium Bonds, on betting, lottery or pools winnings, on cars, on personal possessions worth under £6,000, or on gifts to a spouse or civil partner or to charity. Carried interest is outside CGT from 6 April 2026 (Income Tax and NICs apply instead)
scope.from_when: 18%/24% main rates from 30 October 2024; BADR and Investors' Relief 18% from 6 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim - a charge. Report and pay through Self Assessment, or via the Report and pay Capital Gains Tax on UK property service within 60 days for UK residential property disposals. BADR and Investors' Relief must be claimed

notes: The rate depends on total taxable income: gains falling within the unused basic rate band after income is counted are taxed at 18%, the excess at 24%. Losses, the annual exempt amount and the unused basic rate band may be allocated in the most beneficial way. The basic rate LIMIT used is the UK one - Scottish and Welsh rates of income tax do NOT apply to capital gains, so a Scottish taxpayer's CGT band is still the UK basic rate band. The 28% and the earlier separate 24% residential rates are both historic. Not the same thing as the annual exempt amount, which is banked separately. The 32% carried interest rate applied only to 2025/26.

title: Dividend tax rates 2026/27

figures.what: Ordinary (basic) dividend rate for 2026/27, up from 8.75% in 2025/26
Upper (higher) dividend rate for 2026/27, up from 33.75% in 2025/26
Additional dividend rate for 2026/27 - unchanged
Ordinary, upper and additional dividend rates for 2027/28 - no further change announced, rates stay as in 2026/27

scope.who: Individuals receiving dividend income above the dividend allowance and above any unused personal allowance; the rate that applies is set by which Income Tax band the dividend income falls in once added to other income, and more than one rate can apply to the same person
scope.excluded: Dividends on shares held inside an ISA are NOT taxed at all. Dividends covered by the unused personal allowance are NOT taxed. Dividends within the dividend allowance are NOT taxed. Companies receiving dividends do NOT pay these rates - company distributions received are generally exempt from Corporation Tax, not charged at dividend rates. Trusts and estates do not use these individual rates. Dividend income is NOT charged at the Scottish or Welsh rates of Income Tax, so Scottish and Welsh taxpayers pay the same dividend rates as the rest of the UK
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 (tax year 2026 to 2027)
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim - a charge. Tell HMRC if dividends exceed both the unused personal allowance and the dividend allowance; report through Self Assessment, or ask HMRC to change your tax code for smaller amounts

notes: The 2 percentage point rise in the ordinary and upper rates took effect 6 April 2026; the additional rate was left alone, so the gap at the top narrowed. HMRC's public page calls them basic, higher and additional; the statutory and Budget wording is ordinary, upper and additional - the same rates. The dividend allowance is banked separately and is an allowance, not a rate. Dividend rates are UK-wide even though earned income rates are devolved in Scotland and Wales, which is a common error.

title: Class 1A NIC on benefits and the P11D(b)

figures.what: Class 1A National Insurance rate for 2026 to 2027, charged on the total cash equivalent of taxable benefits in kind; it follows the employer's secondary Class 1 rate for the year the benefit is made available
Class 1B rate for 2026 to 2027, on items in a PAYE Settlement Agreement - PSA items are outside Class 1A
Threshold above which Class 1A is due on a non-contractual termination award - on the excess only
P11D and P11D(b) filing deadline - 6 July following the end of the tax year, so 6 July 2027 for 2026/27
Deadline for Class 1A National Insurance to clear HMRC's account if paying electronically - 19 July if paying by cheque

Late filing penalty for form P11D(b): 100 pounds for every 50, or part batch of 50, employees provided with benefits, for each month or part month the return is late, charged if HMRC has not received it by 19 July
Late payment penalties on unpaid Class 1A: 5% after 30 days, a further 5% after 6 months, a further 5% after 12 months

scope.who: Employers (the secondary contributor) providing taxable benefits in kind to employees or directors in an employed earner's employment; occasionally the third party who provided the benefit
scope.excluded: Employees do NOT pay Class 1A at all - HMRC states plainly that Class 1A NICs are not payable by employees. Class 1A is NOT due on: benefits that are not chargeable to Income Tax; anything already liable to, or specifically exempt from, Class 1 NIC, so it is never charged twice on the same item; items included in a PAYE Settlement Agreement, which attract Class 1B instead; benefits provided for business use only or where private use is not significant, an exemption that does not extend to motor vehicles, boats, aircraft or improvements to living accommodation; trivial benefits costing £50 or less that are not cash, a reward, contractual or salary sacrifice; benefits made good in full by the employee by 6 July; employments that are not employed earner's employments; and employees working abroad where no UK NIC liability arises under a social security agreement. Termination awards up to £30,000 are outside the charge
scope.from_when: Tax year 2026 to 2027 at 15%; P11D(b) for 2026/27 due 6 July 2027, payment due 22 July 2027 electronically
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim - an employer obligation. File form P11D(b) by 6 July with the P11Ds, or alone if all benefits are payrolled, and pay the Class 1A by 22 July electronically or 19 July by cheque

notes: Payrolling benefits does not remove the Class 1A charge or the P11D(b) - the P11D(b) is still required even when no P11Ds are needed. Class 1A is employer-only and has no earnings threshold and no upper limit: it is charged on the whole cash equivalent, not just the part above a threshold, unlike Class 1. It is distinct from Class 1B on PSA items and from Class 1 on cash earnings. CAUTION: the CWG5 2026 guide still carries legacy 13.8% figures in its termination-award worked examples - the operative rate for 2026/27 is 15%, so flag it if anyone quotes 13.8% from that guide. UK-wide: NIC is not devolved.

title: Stamp Duty and SDRT on shares

Stamp Duty on a transfer on sale of stock or marketable securities made on paper using a stock transfer form, charged on the consideration and rounded up to the nearest £5
Where the consideration for a paper transfer is £1,000 or under, no 0.5% Stamp Duty charge applies PROVIDED the instrument contains a certificate of value
