Securities admitted to trading on a recognised growth market and not listed on any market are excluded from chargeable securities by s99(4B) FA 1986, so neither the 0.5% nor the 1.5% SDRT charge applies; exemption introduced 28 April 2014
Stamp Duty and Stamp Duty Reserve Tax are to be replaced by a single Securities Transfer Tax from late 2027, carrying over the 0.5% standard and 1.5% higher rates

scope.who: The purchaser or transferee acquiring shares in a UK incorporated company, or in a foreign company that keeps a share register in the UK - electronically under SDRT or on a paper stock transfer form under Stamp Duty
scope.excluded: You do NOT pay Stamp Duty or SDRT if: you are given shares for nothing, a genuine gift with no consideration; you subscribe to a new issue of shares in a company; you buy shares in an open-ended investment company from the fund manager; or you buy units in a unit trust from the fund manager. Shares admitted to trading on a recognised growth market and not listed on any market are exempt from SDRT entirely. Foreign shares bought outside the UK are not normally within either tax. Paper transfers with consideration of £1,000 or under escape Stamp Duty ONLY if the instrument carries a certificate of value - without that certificate the 0.5% still applies. There is NO £1,000 de minimis for SDRT on electronic purchases
scope.from_when: Current rates; growth market exemption from 28 April 2014; replacement by Securities Transfer Tax from late 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim - a charge. Electronic purchases through CREST: collected automatically by the broker or system, nothing to do. Off-market SDRT: send HMRC written notice of the transaction and pay by the accountable date, with interest running from the due date. Paper transfers: send the signed, dated stock transfer form to the Stamp Office and pay within 30 days

notes: Two different taxes, commonly confused. SDRT: 0.5%, rounded to the nearest 1p, electronic agreements to transfer, no £1,000 de minimis, collected automatically in CREST. Stamp Duty: 0.5%, rounded UP to the nearest £5, paper stock transfer forms, 1000 pound certificate-of-value exemption, 30-day deadline. Neither is Stamp Duty Land Tax - SDLT is a different tax on land and buildings and is England and Northern Ireland only, with LBTT in Scotland and LTT in Wales. Stamp Duty and SDRT on shares are UK-wide and not devolved. MAJOR FORWARD CHANGE: Budget 2026 states both taxes will be replaced by a single Securities Transfer Tax from late 2027, keeping the 0.5% and 1.5% rates, so do not treat this subject as stable past 2027.

title: New Style Jobseeker's Allowance: weekly rates and the 182-day limit

figures.what: New Style (contribution-based) JSA maximum weekly personal rate, claimant aged up to 24, 2026/27
New Style (contribution-based) JSA maximum weekly personal rate, claimant aged 25 or over, 2026/27
Maximum length of a New Style JSA award, about 6 months; after that the claim ends
DWP confirmed 2026/27 contribution-based JSA personal rates, under 25 and 25 or over; 2025/26 were £72.90 and £92.05
Weekly hours of work at or above which you cannot usually get New Style JSA

scope.who: People aged 18 or over and under State Pension age who have worked as an employee and paid Class 1 National Insurance contributions in usually the previous 2 tax years, are looking for work and work under 16 hours a week. Savings, yours or your partner's, do not affect the claim, and neither does household income beyond your own earnings and private pension
scope.excluded: People who were self-employed and paid only Class 2 National Insurance, unless a share fisherman or volunteer development worker; anyone without the required Class 1 contribution record in the relevant 2 tax years; under-18s; people at or over State Pension age; people working 16 or more hours a week; people whose illness or disability stops them working, who should claim ESA instead; people involved in a trade dispute with their employer; most full-time students, unless the course is Level 4 or below AND they get no maintenance loan, grant or bursary AND they can meet their work-related requirements; anyone who has already had the full 182 days in the same benefit year. Nobody can make a NEW claim for income-based JSA at all - it is closed, and Universal Credit replaces it
scope.from_when: Rates apply from April 2026 for the 2026/27 tax year; income-based JSA has been closed to new claims since the completion of Universal Credit rollout
scope.how_to_claim: Claim New Style JSA online at gov.uk, then attend an interview at a Jobcentre Plus office and accept a Claimant Commitment. If you cannot apply online, contact Jobcentre Plus. Can be backdated up to 3 months in certain circumstances

notes: Only ONE version of JSA can be claimed now: New Style JSA, which is contribution-based and paid to the individual. Income-based JSA is closed to new claims - Universal Credit replaced it. Because New Style JSA is contribution-based and individual, there is NO couple rate: the gov.uk rates table has age bands only, and the couple figures in the DWP rates tables belong to the closed income-based scheme. New Style JSA can be claimed alongside Universal Credit, but it counts as income and reduces the UC award pound for pound. Northern Ireland: JSA is administered by the Department for Communities, not DWP, with a separate claim route via nidirect. A benefit year runs 12 months from the first Sunday in January, which is what governs repeat claims.

title: New Style ESA: assessment rate, main phase and support component

figures.what: ESA assessment-phase weekly rate for the first 13 weeks, claimant aged under 25, 2026/27
ESA assessment-phase weekly rate for the first 13 weeks, claimant aged 25 or over, 2026/27
Main-phase weekly ESA for a new claimant placed in the work-related activity group, 2026/27 - personal allowance only, because no component is added for claims made on or after 3 April 2017
Main-phase weekly ESA for a claimant in the support group, 2026/27 - £95.55 personal allowance plus £50.35 support component
ESA support component, weekly, contributory and New Style ESA, 2026/27; was £48.50 in 2025/26
Private pension income threshold: half of any private pension income above £85 a week is deducted from New Style ESA
Normal length of the assessment phase, after which the main-phase rate applies; the assessment rate continues, and is backdated, if the decision takes longer
Time limit on New Style and contribution-based ESA for claimants in the work-related activity group; there is no time limit in the support group

scope.who: People under State Pension age with a disability or health condition that affects how much they can work, who have worked as an employee or been self-employed and paid enough National Insurance contributions, usually in the last 2 to 3 years, with National Insurance credits also counting. Can be claimed whether in or out of work. New Style ESA is the only version open to new claims
scope.excluded: Anyone who does not have the required National Insurance contribution record - New Style ESA is contributory, so people with no qualifying work history get nothing and must claim Universal Credit instead; people at or over State Pension age; people already claiming Jobseeker's Allowance; people receiving Statutory Sick Pay, who can apply up to 3 months before SSP ends but cannot claim both; people whose private pension income is high enough to wipe out the award, since half of pension income above £85 a week is deducted; claimants in the work-related activity group once they have had 365 days of New Style or contribution-based ESA. Nobody can make a NEW claim for income-related ESA - it is closed. New claimants placed in the work-related activity group do NOT get a work-related activity component at all: that component is payable only on claims made before 3 April 2017
scope.from_when: Rates apply from April 2026 for the 2026/27 tax year; income-related ESA closed to new claims; work-related activity component unavailable on claims made on or after 3 April 2017
scope.how_to_claim: Claim New Style ESA from gov.uk by phone or online via Jobcentre Plus; you will need your National Insurance number, bank details, employment and private pension details, and fit notes. Separate claim route in Northern Ireland, and a separate route under the special rules if you are nearing the end of life. A Work Capability Assessment decides which group you are placed in

notes: Three distinct figures get confused: the ASSESSMENT RATE (£75.65 under 25, £95.55 aged 25 or over, first 13 weeks, the same as JSA), the MAIN-PHASE support group amount (£145.90 = £95.55 + £50.35), and the main-phase work-related activity group amount, which for a new claimant is just £95.55 because the component was abolished for claims made on or after 3 April 2017. The components are also uprated differently: for contributory and New Style ESA the support component rises to £50.35 in 2026/27, but for the closed income-related ESA the components are frozen. If you are nearing the end of life you go straight into the support group. The benefit cap does not apply to anyone in the support group. ESA is not the same as PIP, which is for extra costs rather than income replacement, and not the same as Statutory Sick Pay. Northern Ireland has its own claim route and administering department.

title: Social Fund Budgeting Loan: an interest-free loan of £100 to £812

figures.what: Minimum Budgeting Loan you can borrow in Great Britain
Maximum Budgeting Loan if you are single with no children, Great Britain
Maximum Budgeting Loan if you have a partner, Great Britain
Maximum Budgeting Loan if you or your partner claim Child Benefit, Great Britain
Qualifying period - you must have been getting a qualifying benefit for the past 6 months
Interest rate - a Budgeting Loan is interest free, so you repay only what you borrow
Normal maximum repayment period, that is 2 years, by automatic deductions from benefit
Total you can owe for Crisis Loans and Budgeting Loans before you are barred from a further Budgeting Loan

figures.value: £1,000, or £2,000 if you or your partner are 63 or over
figures.what: Savings level above which the loan amount is reduced
Northern Ireland Social Fund Budgeting Loan range, which is DIFFERENT from Great Britain and is administered by the Department for Communities

scope.who: People who have been getting Income Support, income-based Jobseeker's Allowance, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, or Pension Credit for the past 6 months. If you moved from Universal Credit to Pension Credit, time spent on Universal Credit counts towards the 6 months. The loan can pay for furniture and household items, clothes and footwear, rent in advance, moving costs, home maintenance, improvements or security, travel within the UK, costs of starting a new job, maternity costs, funeral costs, repaying hire purchase, or repaying loans taken out for any of those items
scope.excluded: Anyone on Universal Credit cannot get a Budgeting Loan - they must apply for a Budgeting Advance instead. This is the single most misunderstood point, and it now excludes most working-age claimants, because the four qualifying benefits are all legacy benefits closed or closing to new claims. Also excluded: anyone on New Style Jobseeker's Allowance or New Style Employment and Support Allowance, because contributory benefits do not qualify, only the income-related versions; anyone on a qualifying benefit for less than 6 months; anyone involved in industrial action, a strike, walkout or lockout; anyone who already owes £1,500 or more in total for Crisis Loans and Budgeting Loans; anyone judged unable to repay. Requests for less than £100 are refused. Savings above £1,000, or £2,000 if you or your partner are 63 or over, cut the award, and an existing loan being repaid cuts it too
scope.from_when: Current amounts in force at 25 November 2026; these figures are long-standing and are not routinely uprated each April
scope.how_to_claim: Apply online at gov.uk, or by paper form SF500 requested from the Social Fund Enquiry Line and returned by post. You must then ACCEPT the offer before any money is paid. Decision in 7 days if by text or email, 21 days if by letter; money within 7 days of accepting online. If refused, write to the address on the decision letter within 28 days to ask for a review, then the Independent Case Examiner within 28 days of the second decision

notes: This is the Social Fund Budgeting LOAN, not the Universal Credit Budgeting ADVANCE - separate schemes with different rules, and you cannot have the loan if you are on Universal Credit. Interest free: repayments are taken automatically out of your benefits at a rate based on what you can afford, normally over no more than 104 weeks; if you come off benefits, DWP Debt Management writes to you. NORTHERN IRELAND is materially different: administered by the Department for Communities, the range is £100 to £1,500 rather than £348/£464/£812, and the application route is nidirect, not gov.uk. Scotland and Wales use the GB gov.uk Budgeting Loan, but each also has its own separate discretionary scheme on top - the Scottish Welfare Fund Crisis Grant and Community Care Grant in Scotland, and the Discretionary Assistance Fund in Wales. Crisis Loans were abolished and are not available anywhere.

title: Discretionary Housing Payments - renamed Housing Payment in England

figures.what: There is no set award figure anywhere in the DWP guidance. The amount and its duration are entirely at the local authority's discretion, decided case by case on the applicant's income, expenditure and shortfall

figures.value: Weekly Housing Benefit or UC housing element
figures.what: The only stated ceiling on an award: where the payment is for rent costs, it should not exceed the weekly Housing Benefit or Universal Credit housing element
Date from which the Housing Payment strand of the Crisis and Resilience Fund replaces Discretionary Housing Payments in England; authorities must name their schemes Housing Payment
Year from which Discretionary Housing Payments have been fully devolved in Scotland, funded by the Scottish Government and administered by Scottish local authorities

scope.who: People entitled to Housing Benefit, or to Universal Credit including housing costs towards a rental liability, who have a shortfall between their housing support and their actual rent, or a one-off housing cost such as a deposit, rent in advance or removal costs. Administered and decided by the LOCAL AUTHORITY, not DWP, out of a cash-limited annual allocation which the council may top up from its own funds without limit
scope.excluded: Anyone NOT entitled to Housing Benefit or to Universal Credit with a housing element gets nothing - the single biggest misunderstanding. That rules out owner-occupiers, people on Universal Credit with no housing costs element, and working people whose earnings take them off Universal Credit altogether. In England, people with no recourse to public funds cannot get a Housing Payment, because the gateway is Housing Benefit or Universal Credit entitlement. There is also no entitlement where the shortfall arises from ineligible service charges, a rent increase caused by outstanding rent arrears, a benefit sanction or other benefit reduction, recovery of an overpayment, or a benefit suspension. Applications can be refused simply because the council's allocation is exhausted - there is no right to a payment even when the criteria are met, because the scheme is discretionary. These payments cannot be used for council tax, which is a different scheme
scope.from_when: England: Housing Payment strand of the Crisis and Resilience Fund from 1 April 2026, over a 3-year funding period to 31 March 2029. Wales: DHP guidance manual updated 1 April 2026. Scotland: fully devolved since 2017
scope.how_to_claim: Never automatic and never paid without an application - the regulations require an application before an authority can even consider a payment. Apply to your own local council, or in Northern Ireland to the Northern Ireland Housing Executive. Each authority sets its own route: paper form, online, telephone or face to face. You must supply income, capital and expenditure details

notes: THE NAME HAS CHANGED IN ENGLAND. From 1 April 2026 Discretionary Housing Payments are replaced by the Housing Payment strand of the Crisis and Resilience Fund, and councils are required to name their schemes Housing Payment. The eligibility rules and exclusions closely replicate the old rules, and councils may keep using existing DHP application routes during the transition, so many council webpages will still say DHP for a while. Where someone fails the Housing Payment test, a separate Crisis Payment may be available regardless of benefit entitlement. WALES: still Discretionary Housing Payments under the DWP guidance manual updated 1 April 2026. SCOTLAND: fully devolved, funded by the Scottish Government and administered by Scottish councils. NORTHERN IRELAND: administered by the Northern Ireland Housing Executive, and Northern Ireland has domestic rates rather than council tax. There is NO right of appeal to a Social Security Tribunal: the council runs an internal review by a different officer, and beyond that the routes are judicial review or a complaint to the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman. It is not a loan and is not repayable, and it is not the same as a Budgeting Loan, a Budgeting Advance or Council Tax Reduction.

title: Faulty goods: the 30-day right to reject and what follows

figures.what: Time limit for the short-term right to reject faulty goods and get a full refund - the end of 30 days beginning with the first day after ownership or possession transferred and the goods were delivered, under section 22(3) Consumer Rights Act 2015
For goods of a kind that can reasonably be expected to perish after a shorter period, the 30 days is replaced by that shorter period - section 22(4)

After the 30 days the remedy is repair or replacement. A price reduction or the final right to reject becomes available, one or the other, where after one repair or one replacement the goods still do not conform, or repair or replacement is impossible or disproportionate, or the trader has failed to do it within a reasonable time - section 24(5)

Reversed burden of proof - goods which do not conform at any time within the period of six months beginning with the day of delivery must be taken not to have conformed on that day, under section 19(14)

The same point stated for traders on gov.uk - you must repair or replace an item if a customer returns it within 6 months, unless you can prove it was not faulty when they bought it; after 6 months the trader can ask the customer to prove the fault existed at purchase
No deduction for use may be made from a refund where the final right to reject is exercised in the first 6 months, except for motor vehicles - section 24(10) and (11)
A refund on rejection must be given without undue delay and in any event within 14 days beginning with the day the trader agrees the consumer is entitled to it, with no fee - section 20(15) and (17)
Limitation period for bringing a claim - customers have up to 6 years to make a claim for an item they have bought, 5 years in Scotland

scope.who: A consumer - an individual acting for purposes wholly or mainly outside that individual's trade, business, craft or profession - buying goods from a trader. Covers all tangible moveable items, and water, gas and electricity supplied in a limited volume or set quantity
scope.excluded: Business buyers: anyone buying wholly or mainly for their trade, business, craft or profession is not a consumer and gets none of these remedies. Buyers from a private seller rather than a trader. Buyers of second-hand goods sold at public auction where individuals could attend in person. Faults originating in materials the consumer supplied. Customers who knew the item was faulty when they bought it, who damaged it by trying to repair it themselves or having someone else do so, or who simply no longer want it. Anyone past the 30 days, or past the shorter period for perishables, loses the short-term right to reject. The six-month reversed burden does not help where the trader establishes the goods did conform on the day of delivery
scope.from_when: In force 1 October 2015 and applies to contracts made on or after that date
scope.how_to_claim: Exercise the right against the trader who sold the goods, not the manufacturer. The short-term right to reject is exercised by indicating to the trader that you are rejecting the goods and treating the contract as at an end - it may be something the consumer says or does, but it must be clear enough to be understood by the trader. The trader must then refund and must bear the reasonable costs of returning the goods

notes: The Act extends to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, so this is a genuinely UK-wide right. Two things are commonly confused with it: the 14-day distance-selling cancellation right for online, mail-order and phone purchases, which applies even when nothing is faulty and is a separate regime; and a manufacturer's warranty or guarantee, which is in addition to these rights, not instead of them - a customer has the same right to free repairs or a replacement whether or not they have a warranty. Requesting or agreeing to a repair or replacement pauses the 30-day clock for the whole waiting period, and if the replacement is also faulty the consumer then has 7 days after the waiting period ends, or the original time limit extended by the waiting period, whichever is later. Only ONE repair or replacement is required before the consumer can move to a price reduction or final rejection. Limitation differs by nation: 6 years in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, 5 years in Scotland.

title: WaterSure: capped water bills for high-use households on benefits

figures.what: The WaterSure cap in law - charges must be based on the water or sewerage undertaker's average charges for household consumers, and adjusted at the end of the entitlement period so the total does not exceed what the consumer would have paid without applying; regulation 3(1), SI 2015/365
Child benefit route to eligibility - the qualifying person must be entitled to child benefit for three or more children under 19 who reside in the premises; regulation 2(2)(a)
Length of a WaterSure entitlement period - it begins when the consumer applies and ends 12 months later, so it must be renewed annually; regulation 3(4)
Average annual bill reduction received by WaterSure customers in 2024/25
Households that received a WaterSure discount in 2024/25 - about 230,000 in England and 30,000 in Wales
Forecast average household water bill for 2026/27, a 5% rise, against £603 in 2025/26; the average pre-WaterSure bill for WaterSure households is around £890
Maximum household income being introduced as a WaterSure eligibility condition by reforms coming into force in early 2027, set in line with the average household receiving Universal Credit

scope.who: Metered household customers, or those on an assessed charge because a meter cannot be fitted, where someone in the household receives a qualifying benefit or tax credit - Housing Benefit, Income Support, income-based Jobseeker's Allowance, Pension Credit, Child Tax Credit, Working Tax Credit, income-related Employment and Support Allowance or Universal Credit - AND the household is a high water user, either because child benefit is received for three or more children under 19 living there, or because someone has a medical condition obliging them to use a significant additional volume of water
scope.excluded: Anyone with nobody in the household on one of the listed benefits or tax credits. Anyone whose water charges are not volume-based, that is unmetered customers who are not on an assessed charge. Households that are neither high-use for the child benefit reason, with fewer than three children under 19, nor for a qualifying medical reason. Home dialysis patients where the health authority contributes to the cost of the water used in dialysis. Premises that are not the consumer's only or principal home, and premises whose principal use is not as a home. Households that water a garden by any apparatus other than by hand, or that automatically replenish a pond or a swimming pool with a capacity over 10,000 litres - a sprinkler system or an auto-topped pool disqualifies you. Anyone who does not apply, or does not renew every 12 months. Households in Scotland and Northern Ireland, which have entirely different water charging arrangements and no WaterSure
scope.from_when: Current consolidated rules in force 1 April 2015; reformed eligibility and a reformed cap are set to come into force in early 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Apply to your water company, or to the sewerage undertaker instead where the water undertaker's area is wholly or mainly in Wales, supplying evidence of the benefit and of the child benefit or medical condition. Must be re-applied for annually; the company must remind you in advance that renewal is needed

notes: NATION: an England and Wales scheme only. Scotland and Northern Ireland are outside it entirely and have different charging systems - in Northern Ireland the Department for Infrastructure pays a subsidy to NI Water in lieu of domestic consumers' contributions, so NI households have no separate domestic water bill to cap, and Scotland's household charges are set by Scottish Water. CONFUSIONS: WaterSure is not a social tariff - it is a statutory cap every English company must offer, whereas social tariffs are each company's own discretionary scheme with its own income thresholds and discounts, so two neighbours on opposite sides of a company boundary can get very different help. A company can discharge its WaterSure duty through its social tariff only if that tariff is at least as generous. The cap is on the volumetric charge, and it is not a cap at the national average bill but at that particular company's average household charge. REFORM IN FLIGHT: from early 2027 DLA, Attendance Allowance and PIP join the qualifying benefits list, a £25,745 household income ceiling is added, the medical note requirement is dropped, and the cap moves to whichever is lower of the company's overall or metered average. Ofwat's own website returns HTTP 403 to automated clients, so the statutory instrument is used as the official page here.

title: Delay Repay: compensation for rail delays

figures.what: Of the single fare, for a delay of 15 to 29 minutes - payable only by operators that have adopted the 15-minute threshold
Of the single fare, for a delay of 30 to 59 minutes
Of the single fare, for a delay of 60 minutes or more
Of the RETURN fare, for a delay of 2 hours or more

figures.value: 30 minutes for all operators, 15 minutes for most but not all
figures.what: The threshold VARIES BY OPERATOR - all the train operating companies provide Delay Repay for delays of 30 minutes or more, and 13 of them also provide compensation for delays of 15 minutes or more

Maximum time an operator may take to deal with a correctly completed claim, from receipt of claim to communication of decision and payment; if evidence is missing the operator must tell the passenger within 5 working days - ORR Delay Compensation Code of Practice paragraphs 4.1 and 4.2

scope.who: Passengers on train companies operating under contract to the Department for Transport. Delay Repay has been introduced on all rail passenger contracts let by DfT, is paid whatever the cause of the delay and on all types of ticket including season tickets, and a claim can be made regardless of whether the train company travelled with was responsible for the delay or it was the responsibility of infrastructure owners
scope.excluded: Passengers whose delay is below their own operator's threshold - under 15 minutes on a 15-minute operator, under 30 minutes on a 30-minute operator, and under 60 minutes on Grand Central, the only operator still using a 60-minute threshold. Passengers delayed 15 to 29 minutes on Merseyrail, London Overground and the Elizabeth line, which offer compensation for delays of 30 minutes or more only. Passengers whose train was removed from the timetable with notice due to industrial action. London Overground passengers whose delay was outside the train company's control. Passengers of open access operators, which are not DfT contracts and each have their own scheme with varying rules. Anyone who misses their operator's claim deadline or cannot evidence travel. Northern Ireland rail passengers, who are outside Delay Repay entirely
scope.from_when: Delay Repay introduced 2007; the 15-minute threshold announced October 2016 and progressively adopted; thresholds as at DfT's 2025 research, which notes they have not changed since 2023
scope.how_to_claim: Claim from the train company you travelled with, not from Network Rail or DfT, and check that operator's own claim deadline, which the operator sets rather than the regulator. Three routes exist: a manual claim, usually a web form; one-click confirmation of a pre-filled email on registered Advance or Smartcard tickets with several operators; and fully automatic payment, which so far exists only on c2c Smartcards. Operators must also accept physical claim forms in person at staffed stations and by post

notes: THE THRESHOLD IS NOT UNIVERSAL - never state one figure as national. Every DfT-contracted operator pays from 30 minutes, most but not all also pay from 15 minutes, and Grand Central alone still starts at 60 minutes. ORR's Code of Practice treats the threshold as the licence holder's own and requires each operator to publish its own eligibility thresholds, compensation entitlements and season ticket provisions. So the scheme is genuinely per-operator: the same delay produces a different payout depending on who you travelled with. DELIBERATELY NOT BANKED: there is no statutory or regulator-set national CLAIM DEADLINE. The commonly quoted 28 days is each operator's own term, and the only regulator source for it is a 2016 ORR review, so copy must say check your operator's deadline rather than give a number. Delay Repay is distinct from a refund for a journey you did not make, which is a different right. Northern Ireland is served by Translink and NI Railways and is outside this scheme. These are contractual terms in DfT passenger contracts and are being folded into Great British Railways, so thresholds may be restated.

title: TV Licence fee and who still gets it free or reduced

figures.what: Annual fee for a TV licence including colour, in force for licences issued on or after 1 April 2026; set in law in the table in Schedule 1 to the Communications (Television Licensing) Regulations 2004 as amended, the previous figure being £174.50
Annual fee for a black and white only TV licence, in force for licences issued on or after 1 April 2026; the previous figure was £58.50
Date the current fees took effect - the Communications (Television Licensing) (Amendment) Regulations 2026 came into force 1 April 2026 and have effect for TV licences issued on or after that date

Size of the April 2026 increase on the colour licence, the equivalent of an extra 46p a month, calculated using the annualised average of CPI from October to September under the 2022 Licence Fee Settlement
When the fee next changes - it will rise in line with CPI inflation in April 2027, the final year of the current Royal Charter and funding settlement
The over-75 concession as it now stands - free only where the person is 75 or over AND they, or their partner living at the same address, receive Pension Credit

Blind, that is severely sight impaired, concession - the fee payable, including any instalment payments, shall be 50 per cent of the amount which would otherwise be payable; regulation 5(1) of the 2004 Regulations. The licence also covers anyone who lives with the blind person

scope.who: Anyone in the UK who watches or records live TV on any channel or service, or uses BBC iPlayer, needs a licence. Concessions: people who are blind, that is severely sight impaired, pay 50 per cent; people aged 75 or over who, or whose partner at the same address, receive Pension Credit pay nothing; and there is a reduced fee for residents of qualifying residential care and sheltered accommodation
scope.excluded: Over-75s who do NOT receive Pension Credit, and whose partner at the same address does not either, pay the full £180.00 - the concession has not been age-only since the BBC took it over, and this is the single biggest misconception about the fee. People who are partially sighted, that is sight impaired, rather than blind or severely sight impaired, get nothing. The blind concession requires each place specified in the licence to be a residence of the blind person, so it cannot be used for a second property that is not their home. The free over-75 licence applies only where the residence is in the UK or the Isle of Man. There are no other concessions: no reduction for low income, unemployment, students, age alone, or for a disability other than blindness
scope.from_when: Fees from 1 April 2026 for licences issued on or after that date; next CPI rise April 2027
scope.how_to_claim: The full fee is payable on application for a licence - nothing is automatic. The blind concession must be claimed with evidence: a certificate or document showing registration as blind issued by a local authority in Great Britain, a Health and Social Services Trust in Northern Ireland, or the Isle of Man Department of Health and Social Care, or a certificate signed by an ophthalmologist; it need not be re-supplied if provided within the previous 5 years. The over-75 free licence must be applied for, with the Pension Credit award, and can be applied for from age 74

notes: NATION: one UK-wide fee, with no devolved variation; the 2026 Regulations extend to England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, and separate Orders cover the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man. A DRAFTING POINT WORTH KNOWING: regulation 6 of SI 2004/692, as published on legislation.gov.uk in the version in force from 1 April 2026, still reads as an unqualified exemption for anyone aged 75 years or more, with no mention of Pension Credit. The concession is now administered by the BBC, and both DCMS and TV Licensing state the free licence requires Pension Credit - so rely on the DCMS position and do not quote regulation 6 as if age alone still qualifies. OTHER CONFUSIONS: the black and white licence is real and still cheaper at £60.50, but it requires a receiver that can only display in black and white, so it is not a loophole for a modern TV. You need a licence to use BBC iPlayer at all, even for on-demand, but not to watch other providers' catch-up only. A reduced-fee licence exists for qualifying care and sheltered housing residents. For the blind concession on a black and white licence, quote the 50 per cent rule rather than a cash figure. TV Licensing's own site returns HTTP 403 to automated clients, so the statutory instrument is used as the official page here.

title: Empty property rates relief, England

figures.what: Period for which no business rates are payable on an empty non-domestic property in England - the hereditament is not liable while it has been unoccupied for a continuous period not exceeding three months
Total exemption period for a qualifying industrial hereditament, that is industrial and warehouse property; gov.uk expresses the same thing as a further 3 months after the first 3
Rateable value below which an empty property in England stays exempt from empty property rates indefinitely - threshold applying for financial years beginning on or after 1 April 2017
Minimum period of re-occupation needed to reset the empty-rates clock - occupation for less than six weeks is disregarded and the property is treated as continuously unoccupied

scope.who: The person entitled to possession of an unoccupied non-domestic property in England, normally the owner or leaseholder. The first 3 months, or 6 months for industrial and warehouse property, are free of rates. Beyond that, exemption continues indefinitely for properties with a rateable value under £2,900, listed buildings and properties subject to a building preservation notice, scheduled ancient monuments, properties the owner is prohibited by law from occupying, properties held by a personal representative of a deceased person, and properties affected by bankruptcy, winding-up, administration or liquidation. Charity-owned property and community amateur sports club buildings stay exempt where the next use will be mostly charitable or mostly as a sports club
scope.excluded: Occupied property gets nothing under this relief - it is for unoccupied property only. Ordinary non-industrial empty property gets no exemption after 3 months, and industrial or warehouse property none after 6 months, unless it falls in one of the indefinitely exempt classes; then full rates are payable by the person entitled to possession. A short re-occupation does not buy a fresh exemption: occupation of under 6 weeks is disregarded. Properties with a rateable value of £2,900 or more do not get the indefinite low-value exemption. Charity and sports club property does not get the extended exemption unless the next use will be mostly charitable or mostly as a sports club. Property in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland is outside this scheme entirely
scope.from_when: Non-Domestic Rating (Unoccupied Property) (England) Regulations 2008, in force from 1 April 2008; the £2,900 rateable value threshold applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 April 2017
scope.how_to_claim: Administered by the billing council that issues the business rates bill, not by HMRC or the Valuation Office Agency. Tell your local council when the property becomes vacant and ask them to check whether you qualify for extended relief; the council applies it to the bill. Changes that affect the property's value are reported separately to the Valuation Office Agency

notes: ENGLAND ONLY. Scotland: Empty Property Relief was devolved to individual local authorities from 1 April 2023, so there is no single Scotland-wide exemption and it depends on the council. Wales: mandatory relief is 3 months for non-industrial and 6 months for industrial property, the property must have been occupied for more than 26 weeks immediately before becoming empty, and the indefinite low-value threshold is a rateable value under £2,600, not £2,900. Northern Ireland: a different system - empty non-domestic property with a Net Annual Value under £2,000 pays no vacant rates at all, NAV of £2,000 or more gets a 3-month free period and then pays 50 per cent of the occupied rate, and the owner must send Land and Property Services a signed declaration or neither applies. NOT the same as Small Business Rate Relief or retail, hospitality and leisure relief, which both require occupation, and not the same as a completion notice rate-free period on new builds.

title: Business rates improvement relief, England

figures.what: Length of the relief - no higher business rates bill for one year; the statutory wording is the period of one year beginning with the day on which qualifying improvement works are completed
gov.uk wording - eligible businesses get the relief for one year starting when the improvements are completed, and the Valuation Office certificate shows when it ends
Earliest completion date for qualifying improvement works - works completed before this date do not qualify
End of the relief - the chargeable day must fall before 1 April 2029, so relief runs to 31 March 2029; the Act allows this date to be changed by regulations

scope.who: Ratepayers in England who complete qualifying improvement works to a non-domestic property they occupy. Two conditions must both be met. The qualifying works condition: the works must have increased the property's rateable value, and must have increased the size or floor area of a building, otherwise improved the physical state of the hereditament such as adding heating, air conditioning or CCTV, or added rateable plant and machinery. The occupation condition: the same ratepayer must have been in occupation of the hereditament on each day since the qualifying works commenced, and must continue to occupy it during the relief period. Where both are met the bill is held at the pre-improvement level for 12 months from completion
scope.excluded: Ratepayers whose works do not increase the rateable value. Works completed before 1 April 2024. Improvements to existing features or equipment do not qualify, and a change of use alone or the addition of land alone does not qualify. Newly constructed hereditaments, and refurbished hereditaments that were removed from the rating list while the works were done. Anyone who was not in occupation throughout the works and afterwards - so a landlord improving an empty unit, a developer, or a new tenant who takes the property on after the works, gets nothing. The relief cannot be transferred to anybody else, and if the ratepayer vacates the relief ends. Chargeable days on or after 1 April 2029. Property outside England, because the regulations apply to England only
scope.from_when: Qualifying improvement works completed on or after 1 April 2024; relief applies to chargeable days before 1 April 2029
scope.how_to_claim: No application form. You report the property change through your business rates valuation account; the Valuation Office decides whether the change could qualify and issues a certificate of qualifying improvement works to you and to your council, showing the rateable value effect and when the relief ends. The billing council then confirms the occupation condition and applies the relief to a reduced bill automatically. If you believe you are eligible but the relief is not showing, contact your local council

notes: ENGLAND ONLY on these sources. Statutory basis: Non-Domestic Rating Act 2023 section 1, inserting a new Schedule 4ZA to the Local Government Finance Act 1988, with detail in the Non-Domestic Rating (Improvement Relief) (England) Regulations 2023. WALES has its own improvement rates relief on the same shape: works completed on or after 1 April 2024, 12 months' relief from completion, the same qualifying works and same-ratepayer occupation conditions, available up to and including 31 March 2029, ending early if the ratepayer vacates. Scotland and Northern Ireland: no equivalent improvement relief was found at primary source, so do not assert one exists. NOT the same as Small Business Rate Relief or retail, hospitality and leisure relief, and NOT a capital allowance - it only freezes the rates bill, it does not give a tax deduction for the spend.

title: Employment related securities annual return: the 6 July deadline and penalties

figures.what: Filing deadline for the ERS annual return or nil return - you must submit a return or nil return by 6 July following the end of the tax year

Registration deadline - new tax-advantaged schemes should be registered by 6 July following the tax year they were set up, and non-tax-advantaged arrangements by 6 July after the tax year of the first reportable event
Automatic initial penalty for a late ERS annual or nil return - a £100 penalty is issued automatically even if the return is just one day late
Further automatic penalty if the return is still outstanding three months after the due date
A further automatic penalty if the return is still outstanding six months after the due date, in addition to the three-month £300
Daily penalties HMRC may charge if the return is still outstanding nine months after the due date
Time employer PAYE registration can take, and it must be done before the scheme can be registered; the scheme reference number itself is issued online about 7 days after registration

scope.who: Employers and other responsible persons who have had a reportable event involving employment related securities in the tax year - including grants and exercises of share options, awards or gifts of shares or other securities to UK employees or directors, even a single one-off gift, and awards of carried interest; and all tax-advantaged schemes, that is SIP, SAYE, CSOP and EMI. The return covers the tax year just ended and is due by 6 July following it. The scheme must be registered with HMRC on the ERS online service BEFORE a return can be filed, and to register the scheme the company must first be registered as an employer with an activated PAYE online service. A nil return must still be filed where there is nothing to report
scope.excluded: An employer does not have to file an end-of-year return for a reportable event only if ALL of these apply: the company, and any company in the same group or ownership, is not registered for PAYE; the arrangements are not tax-advantaged schemes; the company has no PAYE obligation for the reportable event; and the company has no PAYE obligation for anything else it does. Nobody else is let off - there is no de minimis for small numbers of participants or small values, and nothing happened this year does not excuse filing, because a nil return is required once a scheme is registered. A responsible person is relieved of the duty only where another responsible person has already submitted a return containing all the information they were required to report. Using an agent does not transfer liability - if they file late, you remain liable; and where an Employer of Record employs the worker, the Employer of Record remains liable
scope.from_when: Annual and recurring. The return for tax year 2026-27 is due by 6 July 2027
scope.how_to_claim: Not a claim - a filing obligation. Register as an employer for PAYE and activate PAYE online services; register the scheme or arrangement on HMRC Online Services and get the scheme reference number; then file the annual return or nil return online by 6 July following the end of the tax year. Agents must be authorised through the Online Agent Authorisation process

notes: Form 42 is the historic paper name - reporting is now done only as an online ERS return through HMRC Online Services, so content should say the ERS annual return, formerly form 42, rather than treating form 42 as a current form. The £100, £300, £300 and £10-a-day ladder is per return and is charged per responsible person. EMI has an extra trap: options granted before 6 April 2024 had to be notified within 92 days of grant, whereas grants on or after 6 April 2024 follow the 6 July annual-return rule - do not conflate the two. Separately, registering a tax-advantaged scheme late is not just a penalty risk, it can cost the scheme its tax-advantaged status for the company and its employees. UK-wide: ERS is HMRC and non-devolved. NOT the same as the P11D benefits return, and NOT the same as the EMI option notification.

title: Deferring your State Pension: what the increase is worth

figures.what: NEW State Pension, that is State Pension age reached on or after 6 April 2016 - for every 9 weeks you defer, you get 1% added to your regular weekly pension payment for life
NEW State Pension - the minimum deferral before any increase is payable
NEW State Pension - what 52 weeks of deferral works out to as an increase to the weekly pension
NEW State Pension - gov.uk's worked example of the extra weekly amount from deferring 52 weeks, being 5.8% of the full new State Pension of £241.30 a week
Full new State Pension figure used in gov.uk's deferral worked example, the 2026-27 rate
OLD basic State Pension, that is State Pension age reached before 6 April 2016 - 1% of the weekly amount added to the regular payment for life for every 5 weeks deferred
OLD basic State Pension - what 52 weeks of deferral works out to
OLD basic State Pension - the minimum deferral before the one-off lump sum option is available instead of increased regular payments, with interest at 2% above the Bank of England base rate

scope.who: Anyone who has reached State Pension age and does not claim - if you do not claim at State Pension age, it automatically defers. Which rule applies depends ONLY on when you reached State Pension age. Reached State Pension age on or after 6 April 2016, the new State Pension: 1% added for every 9 weeks deferred, minimum 9 weeks, just under 5.8% for a full 52 weeks, which on gov.uk's example of a full new State Pension of £241.30 a week is an extra £13.99 a week for life. Reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016, the old basic State Pension: the more generous rule of 1% for every 5 weeks, minimum 5 weeks, just under 10.4% for a full 52 weeks; and this group alone can instead take the deferred pension as a one-off lump sum after deferring at least 12 months
scope.excluded: You build up no increase for any period in which YOU are receiving Pension Credit, income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Universal Credit, Carer's Allowance, Carer Support Payment, Incapacity Benefit, Severe Disablement Allowance, Widow's Pension, Widowed Parent's Allowance or Unemployability Supplement. You also build up no increase for any period in which YOUR PARTNER is receiving Pension Credit, Universal Credit or income-related Employment and Support Allowance. You build up no increase for any time spent in prison. Deferring for less than the minimum - 9 weeks on the new State Pension, 5 weeks on the old basic State Pension - earns nothing. The lump sum option is NOT available to anyone who reached State Pension age on or after 6 April 2016: they can only have increased regular payments
scope.from_when: The 1 per cent per 9 weeks rule applies to people reaching State Pension age on or after 6 April 2016; the 1 per cent per 5 weeks rule and the lump sum apply to people who reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016. Cash figures quoted are 2026-27 rates
scope.how_to_claim: Deferral itself is automatic - simply do not claim. When you do claim, you tell the Pension Service whether you want the deferred amount as increased regular payments or, in pre-6 April 2016 cases only, as a one-off lump sum

notes: The commonest error on this subject is quoting 1% per 5 weeks, or 10.4% a year, as if it were the current rule. It is NOT: 10.4% applies only to people who reached State Pension age BEFORE 6 April 2016. Anyone reaching State Pension age on or after 6 April 2016, which is everyone retiring now, gets 1% per 9 weeks, just under 5.8% a year, and no lump sum option. The £241.30 and £13.99 cash figures move every April with uprating, so treat them as 2026-27 figures only; the percentage rules themselves do not change with uprating. gov.uk's deferral guidance covers Great Britain - Northern Ireland has its own guidance and administration via nidirect and the Department for Communities, which was not read for this entry, so do not state NI figures from it. NOT the same as paying voluntary National Insurance to fill gaps. The Pension Credit trap matters: time on Pension Credit earns no increase at all, so deferring while on Pension Credit is simply lost money.

title: NHS prescription and dental charges in England, and the Low Income Scheme

figures.what: NHS prescription charge per item dispensed in England, frozen at this level for 2026/27
England prescription charge confirmed frozen for 2026/27 at the preceding Budget
Three-month NHS prescription prepayment certificate, England, frozen for 2026/27
Twelve-month NHS prescription prepayment certificate, England, frozen for 2026/27
NHS dental charge Band 1 in England from 1 April 2026 - examination, diagnosis, advice, X-rays and a scale and polish if needed; urgent treatment is also charged at one Band 1 charge
NHS dental charge Band 2 in England from 1 April 2026 - Band 1 plus fillings, root canal treatment and extractions
NHS dental charge Band 3 in England from 1 April 2026 - Bands 1 and 2 plus crowns, dentures and bridges
NHS Low Income Scheme capital limit in England - savings, investments and property excluding your own home must be below this

Universal Credit household take-home pay limit in the last assessment period for free prescriptions and free NHS dental treatment, where the award has no child element and no limited capability for work element
Universal Credit household take-home pay limit where the award includes a child element or an element for limited capability for work

scope.who: Prescriptions are free automatically for anyone aged 60 or over, anyone under 16, those aged 16 to 18 in qualifying full-time education, pregnant women and those who have had a baby in the previous 12 months with a valid maternity exemption certificate, holders of a valid medical exemption certificate, holders of a valid War Pension or Armed Forces Compensation Scheme certificate for an accepted disability, NHS inpatients, people in a qualifying Universal Credit or Pension Credit Guarantee Credit award, and holders of a valid HC2 certificate. NHS dental treatment is free for under-18s and under-19s in qualifying full-time education, pregnant women and those who have had a baby in the previous 12 months, NHS inpatients treated by the hospital dentist, people in a qualifying Universal Credit or Pension Credit Guarantee Credit award, and HC2 holders. The Low Income Scheme is for people on a low income whose capital is under the limit
scope.excluded: Adults aged 19 to 59 in England who hold no exemption or HC2 certificate and are not on a qualifying benefit pay the £9.90 per item in full. Being aged 60 or over gives FREE PRESCRIPTIONS BUT NOT FREE NHS DENTAL TREATMENT - over-60s pay the full dental band charge. Universal Credit claimants whose household take-home pay in the last assessment period exceeded £435, or £935 where a child or limited-capability element is included, are NOT exempt from either charge. Contribution-based JSA or ESA alone, and Pension Credit Savings Credit alone, do not give exemption - only Pension Credit Guarantee Credit does. HC3 holders get partial help only and must pay the amount shown on the certificate. People with capital over £16,000 cannot get the Low Income Scheme. Private dental treatment is outside the banding system entirely and is never covered
scope.from_when: Prescription charge and prepayment certificate prices frozen for 2026/27; dental band charges apply from 1 April 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Age-based and inpatient exemptions are automatic - you declare the exemption category when you collect the prescription or start treatment and may be asked for proof. Maternity and medical exemption certificates must be applied for through a GP or midwife. Prepayment certificates are bought from the NHS Business Services Authority online or by phone. The Low Income Scheme is claimed on form HC1, online or by post, which returns an HC2 for full help or an HC3 for partial help, valid for between 6 months and 5 years

notes: THIS IS AN ENGLAND-ONLY MONEY SUBJECT. All prescriptions dispensed in Northern Ireland are free of charge for everyone; prescriptions in Scotland are free; and anyone registered with a GP in Wales is entitled to free prescriptions from a pharmacist in Wales. So a prepayment certificate is worth nothing to a Scottish, Welsh or Northern Irish patient, and the £9.90 figure must never be presented as a UK charge. Each item on a prescription is charged separately - a prescription with three medicines costs three charges, which is the point of a prepayment certificate. Contraception and medicines given to hospital inpatients are always free. Free for everyone at the dentist regardless of exemption: stitch removal, stopping bleeding from the mouth, and denture repairs. Further NHS dental treatment within 2 months in the same or a lower band is free, and if treatments span bands you pay only the highest band once. Do NOT confuse the NHS Low Income Scheme with Council Tax Reduction, Healthy Start or the Healthcare Travel Costs Scheme, though the Low Income Scheme does cover travel costs. An HC2 is full help; an HC3 is partial and is the one people wrongly assume means free.

title: Rate Rebate: help with domestic rates in Northern Ireland for people on Universal Credit

figures.what: Capital value threshold for a private rented property - above this, where the tenant is liable for the rates, the Rate Rebate credit goes to the tenant's own rate account instead of the landlord's
End of the Northern Ireland rating year - a homeowner's rebate is credited from the claim start date to 31 March and renews each year unless circumstances change

scope.who: People already entitled to Universal Credit who are liable for domestic rates: owner-occupiers, including a person who is no longer the legal owner but has the right to live in the property; Housing Executive and housing association tenants; and private rented tenants where either the tenant or the landlord is liable for the rates
scope.excluded: Anyone not entitled to Universal Credit cannot get Rate Rebate. Also excluded: people living in supported accommodation; people already receiving Housing Benefit and Rate Relief, who cannot also claim Rate Rebate; and people entitled to Pension Credit, unless their partner already receives Universal Credit. Anyone outside Northern Ireland is excluded - there is no Rate Rebate in England, Scotland or Wales. Rate Rebate is never paid as cash to the claimant, so a person wanting a cash payment gets nothing
scope.from_when: Current scheme, administered by Land and Property Services; the rebate runs from the claim start date to the end of the rating year on 31 March and renews annually
scope.how_to_claim: Apply online to Land and Property Services through nidirect by creating or logging in to a Rate Rebate account. It is a SEPARATE claim from Universal Credit itself: being on Universal Credit does not trigger it. Social housing tenants need their tenancy reference number. Changes of circumstance must be reported. Homeowners have the rebate credited to their rate account; for Housing Executive and housing association tenants it is paid to the landlord monthly in arrears; for private tenants it is credited to the landlord's rate account monthly in arrears, unless the capital value is over £150,000 and the tenant is liable, in which case it goes to the tenant's own rate account

notes: NORTHERN IRELAND HAS DOMESTIC RATES AND NO COUNCIL TAX. Rate Rebate is not Council Tax Reduction, not Council Tax Support and not a council tax discount - none of those exist in Northern Ireland. Rate Rebate replaced Housing Benefit for rates for Universal Credit claimants: it is the Universal Credit route, while Housing Benefit Rate Relief is the legacy route for people not on Universal Credit, such as pensioners on Pension Credit. You cannot hold both at once. Do not confuse Rate Rebate with the separate Rate Relief scheme, Lone Pensioner Allowance, Disabled Person's Allowance or the Low Income Rate Relief scheme, all of which are different Northern Ireland rates reliefs. Because the scheme does not cover England, this subject is deliberately NOT tagged bham.

title: Child Maintenance Service application fee and Collect and Pay charges

figures.what: Child Maintenance Service application fee, payable by the person making the application whether or not a maintenance calculation results - regulation 3, Child Support Fees Regulations 2014
Collect and Pay collection fee charged to the paying parent, ADDED ON TOP of the maintenance due - regulation 7, Child Support Fees Regulations 2014
Collect and Pay collection fee charged to the receiving parent, DEDUCTED FROM each collected payment before it reaches them - regulation 7, Child Support Fees Regulations 2014
Collect and Pay charge on the paying parent as stated on gov.uk - added to the payment
Collect and Pay charge on the receiving parent as stated on gov.uk - taken off the payment
Direct Pay collection fees - gov.uk states you do not pay any collection fees
Age below which an applicant is exempt from the £20 application fee - regulation 4(2), Child Support Fees Regulations 2014

scope.who: Any parent applying to the Child Maintenance Service pays the £20 application fee unless exempt. Collection fees apply only where the Secretary of State collects the maintenance, that is on the Collect and Pay service: the paying parent pays 20 per cent on top of the maintenance owed and the receiving parent has 4 per cent deducted from each payment collected
scope.excluded: The £20 application fee is waived ONLY for an applicant who is under 19 at the time of applying, or who in the Secretary of State's opinion is a victim of domestic violence or abuse, has reported it to a person on the published list of appropriate persons, and declares this and names that person. Everyone else pays it - including a parent on benefits, a parent on a low income, and a parent whose application produces no maintenance calculation at all. There is no exemption from the Collect and Pay collection fees: a paying parent cannot escape the 20 per cent by paying the other parent directly while on Collect and Pay, and a receiving parent cannot opt out of the 4 per cent. Parents who make a private family-based arrangement without applying pay nothing but get no enforcement. Northern Ireland is outside these regulations - it has its own Child Support Fees Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2014
scope.from_when: Child Support Fees Regulations 2014, in force since 2014; the £20 fee and the 20 per cent and 4 per cent collection fees are unchanged
scope.how_to_claim: The application fee is charged on application to the Child Maintenance Service - it is not claimed, it is paid. The under-19 waiver is applied automatically from the applicant's age. The domestic violence or abuse waiver must be claimed: the applicant declares it when applying, or afterwards on a written form, provided the fee has not already been paid. Collection fees are applied automatically on Collect and Pay with no claim or waiver route; the only way to avoid them is to be on Direct Pay, where the service calculates the amount but the parents arrange payment between themselves

notes: The two services are the confusion point. DIRECT PAY: the service works out the amount, parents pay each other directly, and there are NO collection fees, though the £20 application fee is still charged. COLLECT AND PAY: the service collects and passes on the money, and both parents are charged - 20 per cent added to what the paying parent owes, 4 per cent taken off what the receiving parent receives. So on a £100 weekly calculation the paying parent pays £120 and the receiving parent gets £96. Enforcement charges are separate from collection fees and are not covered here. The £20 figure is in the regulations, not on the gov.uk payments page, which covers only the collection fees - so cite the legislation for the £20. Nation point: these regulations cover England, Wales and Scotland, while Northern Ireland runs the equivalent scheme under its own 2014 regulations, so NI figures must be checked separately. Do not call this the CSA - the Child Support Agency scheme is closed. Reform of Direct Pay has been consulted on, so the Direct Pay and Collect and Pay split is the part of this subject most likely to change.

title: Low Earner's Pension Payment for net pay arrangement schemes

figures.what: The government top-up added to pension contributions in a Relief at Source scheme even for non-taxpayers - the benefit net pay arrangement low earners were missing, and which this payment corrects
The first tax year for which the payment applies; eligibility is assessed separately for each tax year thereafter
When HMRC expects to begin contacting eligible individuals

scope.who: Individuals who paid into a workplace pension through a Net Pay Arrangement scheme and did not financially benefit from tax relief on some or all of their pension contributions - that is, low earners whose income was too low for the tax relief built into a net pay scheme to be worth anything to them. HMRC identifies eligible people itself from its own data and contacts them directly. Eligibility is assessed separately for each tax year from 2024-25 onwards
scope.excluded: People whose workplace pension uses a Relief at Source scheme are excluded - they already receive the 20 per cent government top-up on their contributions even if they pay no tax, so there is nothing to correct. People in a net pay arrangement who DID financially benefit from the tax relief on their contributions, that is who paid enough tax for the net pay mechanism to give them full relief, are excluded. Tax years before 2024 to 2025 are excluded - the payment does not apply to earlier years. People who do not pay into a workplace pension at all are excluded. Anyone HMRC does not identify as eligible gets nothing: there is no application route to request the payment
scope.from_when: 2024 to 2025 tax year onwards; HMRC contact begins December 2026
scope.how_to_claim: Automatic identification - no claim or application needed, and you should not contact HMRC before they get in touch. HMRC identifies eligible individuals, calculates the top-up and contacts them by letter or through the Personal Tax Account. The recipient must then supply bank details to receive the money, via the Personal Tax Account, by telephone on the number given in the letter, or in writing

notes: This fixes the long-standing net pay anomaly - the gap between Relief at Source and Net Pay Arrangement schemes, where only Relief at Source gives non-taxpayers a 20 per cent top-up. It is NOT a new tax relief and NOT the same as claiming higher-rate relief on pension contributions. It is not a benefit payment. Which type of scheme an employee is in is chosen by the employer, not the employee, so people cannot opt in. IMPORTANT LIMIT ON WHAT IS KNOWN: no payment amount and no income threshold has been published at primary source - the top-up is calculated individually by HMRC, and the only published document is HMRC's screening equality impact assessment, with no standalone eligibility guidance page as at 25 November 2026. Because HMRC contacts people by letter and asks for bank details, this is an obvious shape for scam imitation, so any copy should point people at HMRC's genuine-letter checker rather than at a phone number.

title: Unpaid time off to accompany a partner to antenatal appointments

figures.what: the maximum number of occasions of time off, under ERA 1996 section 57ZE(2)
the maximum time off on each of those two occasions, under section 57ZE(3)
section 57ZE gives no right to be paid — there is no equivalent of the section 56 pay provision. The only money is a tribunal award if time off is unreasonably refused
date the right came into force
employees have the right from day one
time limit to bring a tribunal claim, from the date of the appointment, raised from three months on 1 October 2026

scope.nation: Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales). Northern Ireland has its own equivalent, whose figures are not verified here.
scope.who: an employee in a qualifying relationship with the pregnant woman or her expected child: husband or civil partner; a partner living with her in an enduring family relationship who is not a relative; the expected child's father; a parent under the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 2008; or certain prospective parental-order applicants. Agency workers have a parallel right on the same caps, also unpaid.
scope.excluded: the third and every later appointment — the right stops at two; any part of an appointment beyond 6.5 hours; non-employees who are not agency workers; the police service, where sections 50 to 57 are disapplied; agency workers who have not completed the 12-week qualifying period or who fall within the equivalent statutory exclusions; and appointments not made on the advice of a registered doctor, midwife or nurse.
scope.from_when: 1 October 2014
scope.how_to_claim: no qualifying service for employees. The employer may require a signed written or electronic declaration of the qualifying relationship, the purpose, the medical advice and the appointment date and time — that is a condition of the right, not a formality.

notes: This right is UNPAID, and that is the point clients get wrong. The pregnant employee's own right is paid and uncapped (see antenatal-care-time-off-pregnant-employee); the partner's is capped at two appointments of 6.5 hours and carries no pay. Do not publish an armed-forces statement for this right without a further check — the provision extending Part VI to the armed forces lists sections 55 to 57, and section 57ZE was inserted later.

title: Household Energy Payment in Wales — £100, on different rules from England

figures.what: single payment per dwelling
the qualifying date in Wales, not 4 January 2027 as in England
eligible council tax bands, plus Council Tax Reduction Scheme recipients in ANY band, plus any band with a disability adaptation band reduction

when payments are encouraged to start

scope.who: households liable for council tax, not exempt, living in the property as their main or primary residence AND responsible for the utility and other regular bills, in bands A to D — plus Council Tax Reduction Scheme recipients in any band, plus any band with a disability adaptation band reduction.
scope.excluded: households whose main residence is in England, even if they pay council tax and bills on a second Welsh property; second homes in Wales; bands E to I with neither Council Tax Reduction nor a disability band reduction; and people who pay the utility bills but are not liable for the council tax. There is also no right of appeal if a claim is declined, though councils should reconsider on new information.
scope.from_when: qualifying date 28 October 2026; payments from January 2027
scope.how_to_claim: automatic where the council already holds current bank details or the household pays by direct debit; otherwise a council registration form must be completed by 5pm on 30 June 2027.

notes: Wales is a separate scheme, not the English one extended. Three differences matter: the qualifying date is 28 October 2026, eligibility reaches Council Tax Reduction recipients in any band, and Wales adds a requirement that the household be responsible for the utility bills. Conflating the two is the single most likely published error on this subject. England's version is household-energy-payment-2027. No Scottish equivalent is published at primary source as at 27 November 2026, and Northern Ireland has domestic rates rather than council tax.

title: Class 2 National Insurance 2026-27 — nothing to pay, but not everyone gets the credit

figures.what: the liability to pay Class 2 was removed from 6 April 2024 — it was not abolished, and the voluntary route remains
Small Profits Threshold for 2026-27, up from £6,845
voluntary Class 2 rate for 2026-27, up from £3.50
Class 2 payable where profits are at or above the Small Profits Threshold
special Class 2 rate for share fishermen, 2026-27
special Class 2 rate for volunteer development workers, 2026-27

scope.who: self-employed earners — sole traders and partners — with profits at or above £7,105, who are treated as having paid Class 2 and pay nothing, with their State Pension and benefit record protected for free.
scope.excluded: anyone with profits below £7,105, or a loss, gets NO credit — their record shows a gap for that year unless they pay voluntarily. Four categories are never treated as having paid and must pay voluntarily to get a qualifying year: examiners, moderators, invigilators and people who set exam questions; ministers of religion with no salary or stipend; people who make investments otherwise than as a business and without fee or commission; and landlords eligible to pay Class 2. Married women and widows holding a reduced-rate election cannot pay voluntary contributions at all.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027 for the rates; the liability was removed on 6 April 2024
scope.how_to_claim: the credit is automatic through the Self Assessment return where profits reach the threshold. Voluntary Class 2 is normally paid through the return; the four special categories cannot use Self Assessment and must register with HMRC and pay against an 18-digit reference, with HMRC issuing a payment request between September and the end of October.

notes: The commonest error is calling Class 2 abolished. The liability went; the contribution and the voluntary route both survive, and the Small Profits Threshold still decides who gets the free credit. Low-profit traders routinely assume 'nothing to pay' means 'year protected' — below £7,105 it does not. The Lower Profits Threshold was removed on 6 April 2024; the £12,570 Lower Profits Limit that survives is a Class 4 figure and must not be described as a Class 2 threshold. For 2027-28 the threshold rises to £7,355 and the voluntary rate to £3.80 a week. gov.uk publishes no annual figure for a full voluntary year, so if one is used say 'about £190' rather than quoting a precise total.

title: Class 4 National Insurance 2026-27 — the age test that catches people out

figures.what: Class 4 main rate on profits between the Lower and Upper Profits Limits, 2026-27
Class 4 additional rate on profits above the Upper Profits Limit
Lower Profits Limit for 2026-27, unchanged
Upper Profits Limit for 2026-27, unchanged
the rates and both limits are announced to stay the same next year

scope.who: self-employed earners carrying on a trade, profession or vocation whose profits exceed £12,570. Partners pay on their share. It is collected automatically through Self Assessment.
scope.excluded: anyone with profits of £12,570 or less; anyone under 16 at the start of the tax year; anyone over State Pension age at the start of the tax year; anyone not UK resident for Income Tax purposes; trustees, executors and administrators on profits received in that capacity; property and land profits, which are not Class 4-able, so most landlords pay none; and post-cessation receipts.
scope.from_when: 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027
scope.how_to_claim: nothing to claim — it is calculated and collected through the Self Assessment return alongside Income Tax, due 31 January. The age and residence exemptions are applied through the return. Special Class 4 payers such as examiners and invigilators cannot pay through Self Assessment and must contact HMRC's National Insurance office.

notes: The age test is taken at the START of the tax year, and HMRC's manual is explicit that someone who reaches State Pension age during the year stays liable for the whole year. That is the most-missed point and is worth a post on its own. Turning 16 or reaching State Pension age mid-year does not pro-rate either. Property income is not Class 4-able, but trading income from a property business run as a trade can be, so do not write 'landlords never pay Class 4' without the qualifier. Class 4 buys NO benefit entitlement — it is a pure tax, and only Class 2 and Class 3 build the contribution record. Where someone is both employed and self-employed there is an annual maximum capping combined contributions; the 2026-27 figure is not verified here, so do not quote one.

title: Voluntary Class 3 National Insurance — and when paying is money wasted

scope.who: people with gaps in their National Insurance record who will actually benefit from filling them. Class 3 is the general route — employees earning under the threshold, the unemployed not receiving credits, and people abroad.
scope.excluded: anyone with no gaps; married women and widows paying reduced-rate National Insurance, who cannot pay voluntary contributions at all; anyone past the deadline for the year in question; people who were contracted out, for whom gov.uk warns voluntary contributions do not always increase the pension; anyone whose starting amount already equals or exceeds the full new State Pension, where extra years add nothing; anyone who will reach the needed years anyway from future working years; anyone eligible for free National Insurance credits instead, such as carers, parents and jobseekers; and anyone who reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016, who is on the old basic State Pension with different rules.
scope.from_when: £18.40 applies 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027
scope.how_to_claim: check the record and forecast on gov.uk, then pay online or against an 18-digit reference. gov.uk's standing instruction is to contact the Future Pension Centre first if below State Pension age, the Pension Service if at or over it, or the International Pension Centre if abroad, to confirm you will benefit BEFORE paying.

notes: The headline is that paying can be money wasted, and gov.uk says so in terms. A post that says 'fill your gaps' without the contracted-out and already-full exclusions is misleading. '35 years' is only right for someone with no record before 6 April 2016 — write it as 'normally 35'. The self-employed with low profits should usually pay Class 2 at £3.65 a week rather than Class 3 at £18.40: paying the wrong class costs about £767 more for a single year. The extended window reaching back to 2006-07 closed on 5 April 2025 and only the 6-year rule now applies; gov.uk does not print the earliest currently-fillable year, so say 'broadly the last 6 years' rather than naming one. Old years are normally paid at the current rate, except Class 3 for the previous two tax years, which is paid at those years' rates. The £19.05 rate for 2027-28 is already announced.

title: The £1,000 trading allowance — and why it is not £3,000 yet

figures.what: the trading allowance as it stands, applying to 2025-26 and 2026-27
the announced increase, for 2027-28 onwards — NOT yet law, as it needs Finance Bill 2026-27
the separate property allowance, which does not share the trading £1,000
