scope.who: individuals with trading or miscellaneous income — self-employment, casual services such as babysitting or gardening, and hiring out personal equipment. Full relief if gross income is £1,000 or less; above that, £1,000 can be deducted INSTEAD of actual expenses.
scope.excluded: trading income from a company you or a connected person owns or controls; income from a partnership in which you or a connected person is a partner, partnership trading income being outside the allowance altogether; and income from your own employer or your spouse's or civil partner's employer. Anyone whose expenses exceed £1,000 may use it but would be worse off doing so.
scope.from_when: £1,000 applies now and through 2026-27; £3,000 from 6 April 2027 if enacted
scope.how_to_claim: full relief needs no entry on a return, though records of the income must still be kept. Partial relief must be claimed on the return.

notes: Do not publish £3,000 as the current figure — it takes effect for 2027-28 and is not yet law. For the 2025-26 returns due 31 January 2027, and for 2026-27, it is £1,000. The test is GROSS income, not profit: £1,100 of takings with £900 of costs is over the threshold. The real trap in Self Assessment season is that you must still register even under £1,000 if you want to claim loss relief, pay voluntary Class 2, or claim Tax-Free Childcare or Maternity Allowance based on self-employment — a low-earning self-employed parent who takes the allowance and files nothing can lose both a qualifying year and a childcare claim. Trading and property allowances are two separate £1,000s. The allowance is per person per tax year, not per trade, and claiming it rules out deducting expenses or capital allowances against that income.

title: Marriage Allowance — £252 a year, and the Scottish cut-off nobody mentions

figures.what: Personal Allowance transferable under Marriage Allowance, 2026-27 and announced the same for 2027-28

Personal Allowance; the lower earner's income must normally be below it

the recipient's qualifying income band in SCOTLAND — starter, basic or intermediate rate

scope.nation: UK, but the recipient's qualifying band differs in Scotland: £12,571 to £43,662 against £12,571 to £50,270 elsewhere. gov.uk gives no separate Scottish figure for the lower earner and no Wales-specific figure.
scope.who: married couples and civil partners where one partner's income is below the Personal Allowance and the other pays basic rate, or in Scotland starter, basic or intermediate rate. The lower earner transfers £1,260 of allowance and the higher earner's tax falls by up to £252.
scope.excluded: couples living together who are not married or in a civil partnership — gov.uk is explicit that they cannot claim; couples where the lower earner's income is at or above the Personal Allowance; couples where the recipient pays higher or additional rate, or in Scotland is above the intermediate rate; and couples already receiving Married Couple's Allowance, as you cannot have both. Receiving a pension or living abroad while still entitled to a UK Personal Allowance is not disqualifying.
scope.from_when: £1,260 and £252 apply for 2026-27; claims can reach back to 2022-23
scope.how_to_claim: apply free online on gov.uk, by post for backdated years, on the Self Assessment return, or by phone. Once granted it renews automatically every year until cancelled.

notes: The nation difference is sharp and worth the whole post: a Scottish couple where the higher earner is on £46,000 cannot claim, while the identical couple in England can. The automatic renewal is the main thing that goes wrong — a couple whose circumstances change must cancel it or risk an underpayment. Do not reuse HMRC's old 'up to £1,242 backdated' line, which dates from August 2022 and no longer matches the window; gov.uk publishes no combined five-year total. And do not repeat the widely circulated claim that a couple can end up worse off where the lower earner's income sits just under the Personal Allowance — that is not stated at primary source and is unverified.

title: Companies House identity checks — the transition period is over

figures.what: date identity verification became a legal requirement and the 12-month transition began
end of the transition window for existing directors — now passed

scope.who: directors and director-equivalents including members, general partners and managing officers; directors of overseas companies registered in the UK; people with significant control; LLP members; and authorised corporate service providers.
scope.excluded: identity verification is still to come, at a later date, for people who merely file at Companies House, for limited partnerships, for corporate directors of companies, for corporate members of LLPs, and for officers of corporate PSCs — none of these must verify yet. The PSC verification service also cannot be used where the PSC has personal information protected at Companies House. Sole traders and ordinary partnerships are outside Companies House entirely.
scope.from_when: legal requirement since 18 November 2025; transition period ended 17 November 2026
scope.how_to_claim: verify free through GOV.UK One Login, or through an Authorised Corporate Service Provider, who may charge. Verifying is only half of it — the resulting Companies House personal code must then be connected to each role.

notes: Clients think verifying is the end of it. It is not: the personal code must be linked to each role, and a PSC who verifies but never submits the code is still non-compliant. Continuing to act as a director without complying is an offence, and the company and its other directors may be committing one too; Companies House has already used financial penalties, prosecutions and Insolvency Service referrals leading to fines and disqualifications. A non-verified person cannot be appointed to an existing company, incorporate a new one, or register as a service provider. Three points matter for non-UK-national directors: a biometric passport from ANY country is accepted, the service-provider route can be used from any country, and one email address can only ever verify one identity. Expired passports are not accepted; an expired DVLA licence is accepted within 90 days, and an expired BRP, BRC or FWP within 18 months.

scope.nation: UK. Scottish and Welsh taxpayers have S- and C-prefixed codes because those nations set their own income tax rates, but the change to how the notice is delivered is UK-wide and does not touch rates.
scope.who: people who already use HMRC's Personal Tax Account or the HMRC app and have not yet gone paperless.
scope.excluded: people who do not use HMRC's online services keep receiving the notice by post; anyone needing an alternative format such as braille, large print or audio continues to get it that way; and anyone whose tax code has changed can still request a paper notice. The self-employed with no PAYE source have no tax code notice at all.
scope.from_when: February 2027
scope.how_to_claim: nothing to apply for. The action is defensive: sign in to the Personal Tax Account or the HMRC app and make sure a current email address is on file, so a notification arrives when the communication is available.

notes: The failure mode is a stale email address — the notice goes online, no email arrives, and the first the client knows of a wrong tax code is a short pay packet. Telling clients to check the email address HMRC holds is the actionable point. This is a first step rather than the full rollout: HMRC says it will watch how the 3.5 million respond before going wider. It pairs naturally with a scam warning, since 'your tax code has changed, click here' is exactly what phishing looks like, and HMRC's own page carries that warning.

title: VAT: medicines dispensed by pharmacy technicians zero-rated from 10 December 2026

figures.what: the Value Added Tax (Drugs and Medicines) (Health and Welfare) Order 2026
date the instrument was made, laid before the Commons the following day
date it comes into force, applying to supplies made on or after it
where the zero-rating amendment sits, as a new note (2D)(k)
where the welfare exemption is amended so that 'Act' expressly includes a Measure or Act of Senedd Cymru

scope.nation: the pharmacy change covers England, Scotland and Wales only. The Welsh welfare-services amendment concerns Wales.
scope.who: community pharmacies and other pharmacy businesses, registered pharmacists and registered pharmacy technicians, and their VAT advisers. From 10 December 2026 the zero rate also applies to prescription medicines dispensed to an individual for personal use by a registered pharmacy technician authorised by a registered pharmacist, or by pharmacy staff supervised by such a technician. Separately, social care providers in Wales regulated by Care Inspectorate Wales.
scope.excluded: Northern Ireland is expressly excluded from the pharmacy change, because pharmacy technicians are not currently a registered healthcare profession there. The change does not alter WHICH drugs and medicines can be zero-rated. Dispensing that is not on prescription, or not for an individual's personal use, is unaffected. On the Welsh welfare point, providers who are not state-regulated remain outside the exemption exactly as before.
scope.from_when: supplies made on or after 10 December 2026
scope.how_to_claim: nothing to claim — it is an automatic change in VAT liability. Pharmacies should check that till and EPOS VAT treatment follows the new supervision arrangements from that date.

notes: This is the one fully enacted tax law change in the week to 27 November 2026: a made SI, laid before the Commons, with a fixed commencement. The trap on the Welsh half is reading Revenue and Customs Brief 15 as new relief. It is not — HMRC is explicit that supplies of welfare services in Wales are exempt before, from and after 10 December 2026. It is a drafting fix: 'Act' listed Acts of Parliament, the Scottish Parliament and the Northern Ireland Assembly but omitted Senedd Cymru. No refund claim arises, and treating it as a reclaim opportunity would be wrong. VAT Notice 701/57 and the VAT Health Manual do not reflect the change yet, so do not cite the Notice for it.

scope.excluded: vehicles of 3,500kg and under, so ordinary vans, car-derived vans and cars get nothing; HGVs in any other tax class; vehicles whose renewal falls outside the window; and the HGV road user levy, which is not included and whose rates are set separately. Under the Budget 2026 transitional rule, where more than one temporary-rate licence has been taken out and together they exceed 12 months, the extra months may be recovered at the normal rate if the last such licence was taken out on or after 28 October 2026 — so licences cannot be stacked to get more than 12 months at £1.

notes: Say 'in effect', not 'in law', and do not name a Finance Act section. The measure is operating, but it is not in enacted primary legislation: Finance Act 2026 sections 92 to 98 set the ordinary VED and levy rates and contain no temporary-rate provision, and the tax information note uses the formula 'will treat as amended' the Vehicle Excise and Registration Act 1994, which is the standard wording for a measure given effect ahead of legislation. The end-of-holiday transitional rule was published as draft legislation on 28 October 2026. What changed in the week to 27 November 2026 is the exchequer-impact table, restated at Budget 2026 — not the rate or the dates — so be straight about that if it is published as news. Of real value to haulage, plant, agricultural contractor and skip or tipper clients, and to owner-driver and small-fleet operators.

title: CBAM: the EU, EEA and Swiss origin exemption is still only draft

figures.what: the CBAM registration threshold, by rolling value of CBAM goods imported
date UK CBAM takes effect, when record-keeping starts even for those not liable, and the intended start of the exemption
date the CBAM registration service opens
when the exemption legislation is expected to receive Royal Assent, taking effect retrospectively once enacted

scope.nation: goods imported into the UK. The CBAM framework itself is in Part 5 of Finance Act 2026.
scope.who: importers of CBAM goods originating in the EU, the EEA or Switzerland. If enacted, CBAM will not be charged on their embodied emissions, they will not count toward the £50,000 threshold, and they will not be reported on a UK CBAM return. The draft also creates a framework to extend exemptions to other countries whose emissions trading schemes link to the UK ETS.
scope.excluded: CBAM goods originating anywhere else — China, India, Turkey and the rest — stay fully in scope and still count toward the threshold. Already out of scope, and this part is in force: goods for private use, goods of UK origin, goods eligible for returned goods relief, goods under temporary admission with full customs duty relief, and goods processed under a special customs procedure. Businesses importing below £50,000 do not register, but everyone importing CBAM goods must keep records from 1 January 2027.
scope.from_when: intended for goods imported from 1 January 2027, if enacted
scope.how_to_claim: an exemption rather than a claim, once enacted. In the meantime keep records, including evidence of the origin of the goods, and register from 1 January 2028 if liable.

notes: This is NOT law. The page states the legislation is expected to receive Royal Assent after 1 January 2027, will take effect retrospectively once enacted, is subject to the parliamentary process and may change, and that until then liable persons must keep meeting the requirements in force. So the line to clients is: assume you are in scope, keep the records and the origin evidence, and do not stand down. Note an inconsistency to be aware of — HMRC's guidance page updated 23 November 2026 says flatly that EU, EEA and Swiss goods do not count toward the threshold from 1 January 2027, while the draft-legislation page says the law is not yet made. Cite the draft-legislation page for status. Failure to notify when required to register attracts penalties. Relevant to any client importing aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen or iron and steel.
